description: Musk mallow is traditionally recorded for snakebite, the most distinctive application in its record. This plant of the Malvaceae family has documented uses in Trinidad, India, Mexico, the Philippines, Guatemala, and Borneo. Its applications include digestive complaints such as colic, stomach ache, and debility, along with respiratory conditions like asthma, chest colds, flu, and hoarseness. Other recorded uses cover nervous system issues such as hysteria, spasms, and nerves, as well as rheumatism, skin itch, and boils.

name: Abies alba

old.description: A European fir tree with essential oil used for respiratory conditions and as an antiseptic.

description: Abies alba, of the family Pinaceae, has recorded traditional use in Spain and Turkey. It was traditionally recorded for respiratory complaints such as cough, catarrh, bronchitis, and lung and tubercle related applications, as well as for expectorant and diuretic purposes. Other recorded uses include the external treatment of wounds, sores, and bruises, along with applications for calculus, gravel, gonorrhea, leucorrhea, and internal ulcers. The plant was also recorded as a laxative and as a liniment, and was described as a rubefacient (a substance that reddens the skin) and a vulnerary (a wound healer).

The plant was also applied to boils, inflammation, and sprains, and was used for stomach complaints. Additionally, it was valued for its lubricative properties and for the relief of sores.

The plant has also been traditionally recorded for respiratory complaints such as cough and bronchitis, for fevers and rheumatism, and for digestive issues including dysentery, colic, and constipation. Other recorded applications include wound and ulcer care, as well as a range of general purposes like tonic, demulcent, diuretic, and refrigerant uses.

It was also traditionally recorded for digestive and urinary concerns such as carminative, dropsy, and dysuria, as well as for skin conditions including eczema and itch, and for other issues like convulsion, beri-beri, and scrotal sores.

Additional applications include as a sialogogue to promote saliva flow, a sternutatory to induce sneezing, and a tonic. These records group into pain relief, bleeding control, and oral or respiratory stimulation.

description: Achillea nobilis, known by its common name noble yarrow, is traditionally recorded for hemorrhage, a distinctive application in its record. This plant belongs to the Asteraceae family, and its use has been documented in Denmark and Turkey. The main medicinal applications group into several areas: it was used as an astringent and hemostat for bleeding, as a carminative and stomachic for digestive complaints, and as a depurative and litholytic for cleansing and stone-related issues. Other recorded uses include treating fever, scurvy, and spasms, as well as serving as an expectorant, sudorific, stimulant, tonic, and vulnerary for wound healing.

The documented applications include anodyne and tonic purposes, as well as uses for rheumatism, lumbago, headache, and toothache. Other traditional recordings cover menstrual and postpartum care, hypertension, and the treatment of malaria and ague.

Its uses include arthralgia, rheumatism, and tension, as well as fever and thirst. The plant was also recorded for liver-related applications such as hepatoma, and for urogenital purposes including as a diuretic and for stone. Additional applications include esophagus-related uses.

name: Grassy Sweet Flag

description: Grassy Sweet Flag, a member of the Acoraceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in China. Its applications are grouped around digestive complaints, including anorexia, dyspepsia, hyperacidity, diarrhea, and stomachic and digestive support. It was also recorded for neurological and sensory conditions such as coma, convulsion, epilepsy, spasm, deafness, and numbness, as well as for respiratory and throat congestion, otitis, and skin eruptions and sores. Additional traditional uses include rheumatism, backache, malaria, leprosy, and as a stimulant, tonic, sedative, diaphoretic, and vermifuge.

name: Ackee

old.description: Jamaican national fruit tree with medicinal bark and leaves in West African and Caribbean medicine.

description: Ackee, a member of the Sapindaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Upper Volta, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Mozambique, the West Indies, and Haiti. Its applications include anodyne and stimulant actions, as well as uses for migraine, epilepsy, and edema. It has also been recorded for eye conditions such as conjunctivitis and ophthalmia, skin and soft tissue complaints including sores, yaws, orchitis, and rib ache, and for smallpox and yellow fever. Other traditional uses include massage and as an antiemetic.

description: Aethusa cynapium, a member of the Apiaceae family, is traditionally recorded for digestive and nervous system complaints. Its use has been documented in the United States, France, Turkey and Belgium. The main applications group around stomach and intestinal disorders, including gastritis and diarrhea, as well as cholera. It is also traditionally recorded for convulsion and spasm, and as a sedative and stomachic.

description: Afzelia africana, a member of the Fabaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications across Upper Volta, Ghana, Ivory Coast, and West Africa. The most frequent therapeutic theme in the record is the relief of abdominal and stomach complaints, with uses also noted for fever, edema, and hernia. Other recorded applications include diuretic and antemetic purposes, as well as treatments for gonorrhea, guinea worms, leprosy, lumbago, and sleeping sickness.

description: Agave, of the family Agavaceae, has traditional use recorded in Mexico, Haiti, Venezuela, Lesotho, India, and Greece. Among its most distinctive applications is the treatment of ascites, a fluid accumulation in the abdomen. The plant is also traditionally recorded for syphilis, leukemia, and dysentery, as well as for scurvy and warts. Other uses include promoting wound healing (cicatrizant), depurative and diuretic purposes, and the production of liqueur, with recorded applications for sores.

Its applications include wound healing and skin care, as well as internal uses such as dysentery and syphilis. The plant is also recorded as a depurative and sudorific, and for leprosy.

description: Aframomum melegueta, a plant in the Zingiberaceae family, was recorded in Egypt, Ghana, China, Nigeria and Liberia for a wide range of applications. Its main medicinal uses include soothing the digestive tract, as seen in records for dysentery, enteritis, gastritis and stomachic complaints, alongside carminative and astringent purposes. It was also traditionally recorded for fever and malaria, as a stimulant and tonic, and for anodyne, sedative and styptic uses. Other applications include preventive uses for migraine and rheumatism, treatment of toothache and tapeworm, and use as an aphrodisiac and excitant.

name: Ageratum Conyzoides

description: Ageratum conyzoides, a member of the Asteraceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Trinidad, Africa, Malaya, Venezuela, Nigeria, and Sierra Leone. The most frequently documented applications relate to wound care and skin complaints, including boils, burns, sores, craw-craw, and wounds, often prepared as a poultice or used for its hemostatic and vulnerary properties. Other recorded uses include treatment of fever, ague, flu, pneumonia, rheumatism, and venereal diseases such as syphilis, as well as digestive issues like colic, dysentery, dyspepsia, and cough. The plant has also been noted for eye applications, as a collyrium, and for gynecological and obstetric purposes, including contraceptive and puerperium uses.

name: Agrimonia pilosa

old.description: East Asian agrimony used in TCM for bleeding conditions, parasites, and digestive complaints.

description: Agrimonia pilosa, known by its common name agrimony, is a member of the Rosaceae family. Its use was recorded in China and the USSR, where it was traditionally recorded for a range of applications. Among the most distinctive is its use as a hemostat, or agent to stop bleeding. Other recorded uses include treating diarrhea and dysentery, addressing fever and heatstroke, and relieving headache and sore throat. It was also recorded for abdominal complaints.

name: Agrostemma githago

description: Agrostemma githago, known as corn cockle, belongs to the family Caryophyllaceae. Its use has been recorded in the United Kingdom, Turkey, Argentina and Europe. Among its most distinctive traditional applications is the expulsion of worms, and it was also recorded as a diuretic and for dropsy, a condition involving fluid retention. Other traditional uses include support for jaundice and use as an expectorant for clearing the airways.

name: Ailanthus altissima

description: Ailanthus altissima, in the family Simaroubaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in China, Iraq, the United States, Europe, and Turkey. Its applications include treatment for fevers such as malaria, digestive complaints like diarrhea and dysentery, and menstrual disorders including dysmenorrhea and metrorrhagia. It has also been recorded as an antiseptic and bactericide for sores and eruptions, as a vermifuge and taenifuge for tapeworm, and for respiratory and cardiac concerns. Other traditional uses include astringent, cathartic, and emetic actions, as well as a hair tonic.

It was also recorded as a diuretic and for fever, as well as for jaundice, liver, and spleen complaints, and as a stomachic and carminative for digestive support. Other traditional uses include rheumatism, lung conditions, and general tonic and vulnerary purposes, with a narcotic application also noted.

Other traditional roles include a sedative and a tonic, as well as a diuretic and a vermifuge. It was also listed as a stimulant and a vulnerary, the latter a term for a wound remedy.

description: Albizia anthelmintica, a member of the Fabaceae family, has been traditionally recorded in Africa and Ethiopia for uses centered on the expulsion of intestinal worms. The most frequent applications are as a vermifuge and taenifuge, both referring to the elimination of parasitic worms. It has also been documented as a purgative, and in some cases the plant's use has been associated with fatal outcomes. These records reflect the plant's long-standing role in local practices for worm-related complaints.

description: Alchemilla alpina, a member of the Rosaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for digestive and urinary complaints in Turkey and Spain. These uses reflect the plant's place in local herbal practice rather than any established medical effect.

Other recorded uses include diarrhea, diuretic and depurative purposes, and a tonic role, alongside stomachic, demulcent, refrigerant, and tonic applications.

Additional applications include diuretic and expectorant uses, as well as a sedative effect and support for wound care.

name: Alchornea

description: Alchornea, a member of the Euphorbiaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use across Africa, including Upper Volta, West Africa, the Central African Republic, Sierra Leone and Nigeria. Its applications are broad and include digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, jaundice and piles, alongside respiratory uses recorded for cough, cold, bronchitis and throat conditions. External and topical applications include wounds, sores, ringworm, craw-craw, yaws and chancre, while eye related uses such as collyrium, conjunctivitis and ophthalmia are also noted. Other recorded purposes range from malaria and rheumatism to gonorrhea, urethritis and venereal complaints, with uses also noted for newborns and for menstrual pain.

These related applications group together as a set of effects on the digestive system, ranging from promoting vomiting to loosening the stools and causing vigorous evacuation.

Respiratory and gastrointestinal complaints also appear, notably colds, coughs, rhinitis, diarrhea, and dysentery, along with tuberculosis.

name: Allium tuberosum

Other recorded applications include hemorrhage and hematemesis (vomiting blood), as well as spermatorrhea and conditions affecting the urethra. It was also traditionally recorded as a depurative, a term for a cleansing agent.

name: Allspice

Its applications also extend to antimicrobial and antioxidant purposes, such as bactericide and fungicide, as well as stimulant and anodyne properties.

These labels point to a role in promoting elimination through urine and sweat, tightening tissues, and supporting general vitality. Other recorded uses include fever and the expulsion of worms, with a separate application for the foot.

name: Amaranth

description: Amaranth, of the family Amaranthaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in the United States and Colombia. description: Asparagus adscendens, known as shatavari, is most distinctive in its traditional record as an aphrodisiac. This plant of the Liliaceae family has been recorded in India and Iran for a range of applications. These include use as a tonic and stimulant, as a demulcent and refrigerant for soothing and cooling purposes, and as a diaphoretic to promote sweating. The applications are traditionally recorded for these purposes rather than as treatments for specific diseases.

name: Atractylodes Rhizome

old.description: Principal TCM spleen tonic used to strengthen spleen qi, dry dampness, stabilize the exterior, and prevent miscarriage. A foundational herb in digestive and immune formulas.

description: Atractylodes Rhizome, of the Asteraceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in China. Its main applications center on digestive complaints, with recorded use for anorexia, dyspepsia, and as an aperient. Related uses include bronchitis and cough, as well as anemia and pregnancy. A viricide application is also documented.

name: Averrhoa bilimbi

old.description: Tropical Oxalidaceae tree used in Malay and Caribbean medicine for hypertension, diabetes, and skin conditions.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Averrhoa bilimbi belongs to the family Oxalidaceae, and its use has been recorded in Java, Belimbing besi, Haiti, the Philippines, Malaya, and Sri Lanka. Traditionally recorded applications include skin complaints such as itch, pimples, and whitlow, as well as swelling and mumps. Other uses include cough, thrush, ophthalmia, and piles, along with proctitis and rheumatism. The plant has also been recorded for syphilis, biliousness, beriberi, and as a diaphoretic, with further uses for osteosis.

name: Bacopa monniera

old.description: Bacopa monniera appears in 3 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

provenance.limitations: LNHPD publishes no per-product indication, so uses are empty rather than invented.

description: Bacopa monniera, known commonly as bacopa, is a plant in the family Scrophulariaceae. Its use has been recorded in China, India, Iraq, the Philippines, and in Hindu medical tradition. The most distinctive application is for epilepsy, and related uses include insanity, lunacy, and hysteria. Other recorded applications cover heart function, as a cardiotonic and for cardiac complaints, and as a diuretic. It has also been noted for sexual and reproductive concerns such as impotency, frigidity, ejaculation, and wet dreams, as well as for rheumatism, backache, hoarseness, and as a general tonic and nervine.

name: Babchi Seed

old.description: Ayurvedic and TCM seed used for vitiligo, psoriasis, bone health, and kidney yang tonification. Contains psoralen — used in PUVA therapy for vitiligo.
traditional_uses: Treat vitiligo in Ayurveda and TCM

description: Babchi Seed, a member of the Fabaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications across China, Vietnam, India, and Nepal. Its uses include skin conditions such as psoriasis, vitiligo, leucoderma, and leprosy, as well as joint and muscle complaints like arthritis, rheumatism, lumbago, and knee pain. The seed was also traditionally recorded for digestive issues including diarrhea and stomach ache, and for urinary and reproductive concerns such as diuretic, polyuria, enuresis, incontinence, impotency, spermatorrhea, and wet-dream. Additionally, it was used as a tonic, stimulant, stomachic, bactericide, and for inflammation, callosity, caries, and vision problems.

name: Bael Fruit

old.description: A sacred tree in Hinduism dedicated to Lord Shiva, whose fruit is one of the most effective anti-diarrheal remedies in Ayurveda.

description: Bael fruit, of the family Rutaceae, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications in India, Java, Turkey, Iran, and Celebes. Its uses include digestive complaints such as constipation, diarrhea, dysentery, dyspepsia, and stomach ache, along with fever, malaria, and cholera. The plant was also recorded for heart-related concerns like palpitation and for the brain, as well as for convulsion, spasm, and nausea. Other applications include astringent, tonic, and restorative purposes, and it was used for skin issues like itch and sore, and for conditions of the breast and during puerperium.

name: Bai Bu Root

old.description: TCM herb that moistens lungs, stops cough, and kills parasites; used for chronic cough and topical for lice and scabies.

description: Bai Bu Root belongs to the Stemonaceae family and is recorded in China. Traditionally recorded uses include respiratory complaints such as cough, pertussis, and sore throat, as well as tuberculosis. It is also documented for intestinal worms, including oxyuriasis, and as a vermifuge and pediculicide.

name: Bai Bian Dou Seed

old.description: TCM food-medicine that strengthens spleen and resolves summer damp; gentle heat for deficient cold spleen.
traditional_uses: Strengthens spleen and resolves summer damp

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

taxonomy.source: Kew POWO (Plants of the World Online)

verified_sources: Kew POWO (Plants of the World Online)

description: Bai Bian Dou Seed, of the Fabaceae family, is traditionally recorded for digestive complaints such as diarrhea, cholera, and as a carminative, as well as for fever, thirst, and sunstroke. Its use has been documented in China, India, the Philippines, and Asia more broadly. Other traditional applications include a poultice for swelling, a tonic, and uses for throat, earache, and leucorrhea. The seed is also recorded for blindness, epilepsy, menorrhagia, megalospleny, and as a preventive for gray hair and antivinous purposes.

name: Bai He Bulb

old.description: TCM herb that nourishes lung yin, clears heat, and calms the spirit; used for dry cough, insomnia, and heart palpitations.

description: Bai He Bulb, of the Liliaceae family, is traditionally recorded for lung-related applications, including cough, hemoptysis, and lung complaints. Its use has been documented in China and Vietnam. The bulb is also traditionally recorded for fever, debility, and as a tonic, as well as for bruises, wounds, sores, and swelling. Additional applications include eczema, eruptions, and as a sedative for neurosis.

name: Bai Hua She She Cao

old.description: TCM herb clearing heat and resolving toxin, widely studied for cancer.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Bai Hua She She Cao belongs to the Rubiaceae family and is traditionally recorded for use in China and Malaya. Its applications include abscesses, boils, bruises, trauma, and snake bite, as well as fever, heatstroke, sore throat, and jaundice. The plant is also noted as a tonic, alexiteric, anodyne, depurative, diuretic, and refrigerant, and has been used for infection and lumbago.

name: Bai Ji

old.description: A TCM herb that stops bleeding, heals ulcers, and reduces swelling of the lungs.

description: Bai Ji, an orchid in the family Orchidaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in China and Japan. Its applications center on bleeding, including hemorrhage from the lungs, stomach, and intestines, as well as hemoptysis and hematemesis, and it is also noted as a hemostatic agent. The plant has been used for wounds, trauma, abscesses, swelling, and skin inflammation, and for coughs, chest complaints, and lung conditions such as tuberculosis and silicosis. Additional traditional uses include dysentery, dyspepsia, stomach ache, piles, and as a demulcent and apertif.

name: Bai Tou Weng

old.description: TCM herb used to clear heat and toxins, cool blood, and treat amoebic dysentery and infectious diarrhea.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Bai Tou Weng has been traditionally recorded for diarrhea, amebiasis, and the passage of bloody stools, as well as for its hemostatic and antiphlogistic properties. It belongs to the Ranunculaceae family, and its use was recorded in China. The plant was also applied to trauma and wounds, reflecting a broader role in managing bleeding and inflammation.

name: Balanites Aegyptiaca

old.description: Desert-adapted tree used across North and sub-Saharan Africa for schistosomiasis control, diabetes, malaria, and as a nutritional food plant.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Balanites aegyptiaca, the only name recorded for this plant in the family Balanitaceae, has a traditional use record spanning Sudan, Africa, Ghana, Chad, Nigeria, and Libya. Among its most distinctive applications is the treatment of Guinea worm, known as the fiery serpent, which stands out in a record that also includes uses for fever, cold, malaria, and sleeping sickness. Other applications group around digestive complaints such as aperient and purgative effects, and vermifuge use, alongside external purposes like wound care, unguent, fumigant, and circumcision. The plant is also traditionally recorded for syphilis, herpes zoster, liver complaints, malignancy, and as a sweetener.

name: Balsam Poplar

old.description: North American poplar with highly fragrant resinous buds; buds used by Indigenous peoples and herbalists for respiratory and pain conditions.
traditional_uses: Respiratory conditions by many Indigenous peoples
Used as Balm of Gilead substitute

image.credit: Lynden Gerdes @ USDA-NRCS PLANTS Database / USDA NRCS. 1995. Northeast wetland flora: Field office guide to plant species. Northeast National Technical Center, Chester. — Public domain

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Balsam poplar, in the family Salicaceae, was traditionally recorded for medicinal use in China and the United States. Its applications include astringent and stimulant actions, as well as uses for diarrhea, dysentery, and cholera. It was also recorded for expectorant and lung-related purposes, and for kidney and stomach complaints. Other traditional uses include wound and fracture care, skin and eye applications, and remedies for rheumatism, gout, and inflammation.

name: Balsam of Peru

old.description: Central American balsam with strong vanilla-cinnamon aroma; used topically for wound healing and respiratory conditions; common allergen.

image.credit: Franz Eugen Köhler, Köhler's Medizinal-Pflanzen — Public domain

description: Balsam of Peru was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications, including respiratory complaints, wound care, and digestive support. It belongs to the family Flacourtiaceae, and its use was documented in South America, the Dominican Republic, Denmark, Panama, and Colombia. The applications include antiseptic and bactericidal purposes, as well as remedies for asthma, bronchitis, catarrh, colds, coughs, and tuberculosis, often grouped with expectorant and pectoral uses. Other recorded uses cover rheumatism, sclerosis, sores, swelling, wounds, and venereal conditions, along with stimulant, stomachic, tonic, and vulnerary actions, and it was also used as a fumigant and for headache and umbilical applications.
traditional_uses: Respiratory complaints such as asthma and bronchitis

name: Bamboo

old.description: Bamboo leaves and shavings are used in TCM to clear heat and in modern nutrition as a rich source of organic silica.

description: Bamboo, a member of the grass family Poaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in Trinidad, Turkey, Haiti, Samoa, Malaya, and Perak. Its applications are broad, with many focused on respiratory complaints such as colds, coughs, catarrh, flu, and pneumonia, as well as fever and biliousness. Other recorded uses include jaundice and liver conditions, dysentery, and the treatment of wounds, burns, and erysipelas. Bamboo is also noted as a tonic, stimulant, and aphrodisiac, and has been used as a vermifuge, purgative, and insectifuge, among other purposes.

name: Bamboo Silica

old.description: Tropical grass with silica-rich nodules for bones.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Bamboo Silica was traditionally recorded for a range of applications, including fever, jaundice, and flatulence. It belongs to the grass family Poaceae, and its use was documented in the United States and in Arab regions. Other recorded uses include a soothing demulcent action, a pectoral application for chest complaints, and an aphrodisiac purpose, along with a larvicidal use and a connection to water. The plant also carries a cyanogenetic note, indicating a documented property rather than a medicinal use.

name: Ban Xia Rhizome

old.description: TCM most important herb for transforming damp-cold phlegm; dries dampness, descends rebellious qi, and stops vomiting.

image.credit: The original uploader was Polyhedron at Chinese Wikipedia. — CC BY-SA 3.0

description: Ban Xia Rhizome was traditionally recorded for digestive complaints, respiratory conditions, and pain. It belongs to the Araceae family, and its use was recorded in China and Japan. The main applications include nausea, vomiting, and dyspepsia, as well as cough, bronchitis, and sore throat. It was also recorded for rheumatism, arthralgia, and snake bite, and as a sedative.

name: Banisteriopsis caapi

old.description: Sacred Amazonian vine; contains MAO inhibitors (harmine, harmaline) used in ayahuasca ceremonies.

image.credit: Original uploader was Wowbobwow12 at en.wikipedia — CC BY-SA 3.0

description: Banisteriopsis caapi, a member of the Malpighiaceae family, has traditionally recorded use in Colombia, Peru, Sa, and by Amerindian peoples. Its main applications are grouped around hallucinogenic, narcotic, and psychedelic purposes, reflecting a role in altered states of consciousness. These related uses are traditionally recorded for their psychoactive effects rather than for treating or curing disease.

name: Baneberry

old.description: European woodland perennial; berries and roots highly toxic but plant documented in historical European herbal medicine.
traditional_uses: Used in folk medicine for rheumatism

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Baneberry, a member of the Ranunculaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for a range of applications in China, Turkey, Spain, Europe, India, and West Germany. Its use centers on the heart and circulation, with records for angina pectoris, cardiotonic purposes, and dropsy, as well as for respiratory complaints such as asthma and pertussis. The plant also appears in records for nervous conditions including hysteria, nerves, and as a nervine and sedative, alongside uses for rheumatism and spasm. Additional traditional applications include phthisis, senility, and preventive purposes related to death, malaria, and miasm.
traditional_uses: Preventive purposes for malaria and miasm

name: Baphicacanthus cusia

description: Baphicacanthus cusia, known by its common name, is a plant in the Acanthaceae family. Its use has been recorded in China. The most distinctive application in its record is for parotitis, and it is also traditionally recorded for fever, rash, and sore throat. These applications group into systemic and topical concerns: fever and sore throat reflect internal discomfort, while rash and parotitis involve visible swelling or skin eruption.

name: Basella alba

description: Basella alba, the sole species name recorded, belongs to the family Basellaceae. Its use has been recorded in China, India, and Gandola. Traditionally recorded applications include skin related concerns such as acne and sores, alongside emollient and demulcent properties. Uses also extend to conditions of the nose like rhinitis, intestinal applications, and recorded instances for syphilis, lymphoma, leukemia, and hepatoma.

name: Bauhinia purpurea

old.description: South and Southeast Asian Bauhinia with pink flowers; leaves and bark used for thyroid and skin conditions.

provenance.notes: 1 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Bauhinia purpurea, a member of the Fabaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for a range of applications in India, Singapore, and Nc. The most frequent theme in the list concerns the nervous system, with uses for convulsions, delirium, epilepsy, and stupefaction. Other recorded applications include snake and tiger bites, wasp stings, and cases of septicemia, hemorrhage, and intoxication. The plant is also traditionally recorded for anasarca, dropsy, rheumatism, sores, and swelling, as well as for rinderpest and as an anodyne.

name: Bauhinia variegata

old.description: South Asian ornamental tree; flower buds (Kachnar) used in Ayurveda for skin, thyroid, and digestive conditions.

image.credit: Peter1968 at English Wikipedia — CC BY 2.5

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Bauhinia variegata, a member of the Fabaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Iraq, Nepal, India, Java, and Turkey. The plant is most often associated with skin applications, including dermatosis, sores, and ulcers, and is also noted as an astringent. Other recorded uses include scrofula, obesity, parturition, and general tonic and alterative purposes.

name: Bawang Dayak

old.description: Kalimantan (Borneo) indigenous plant used by Dayak people for diabetes, hypertension, and cancer.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Bawang Dayak, a plant in the Iridaceae family, was traditionally recorded for several medicinal applications in the Philippines. Its uses include addressing bug bites and boils, as well as spasms and wounds. These applications reflect the plant's role in folk practices for skin issues and muscular discomfort.

name: Bayberry

old.description: A North American shrub whose root bark is a powerful astringent, used by Thomsonian herbalists as a cornerstone remedy.

taxonomy.source: Kew POWO (Plants of the World Online)

verified_sources: Kew POWO (Plants of the World Online)

description: Bayberry, in the family Myricaceae, has a traditional record that includes use for nose polyps, a distinctive application among its many entries. Its use was recorded in the United States, Turkey, Mexico, and Guatemala. Other applications group around digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, and jaundice, and around tonics and stimulants, including a cordial and a stomachic. It was also traditionally recorded for fever, hemorrhage, sore mouth and throat, canker, scrofula, and as an astringent, laxative, emetic, and vermifuge.

name: Beach Morning Glory

old.description: A coastal plant used across Pacific Island and tropical countries for skin conditions and rheumatism.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Beach Morning Glory, a member of the Convolvulaceae family, is traditionally recorded for an unusual application: the evil eye. Its use has been documented in Malaysia, Malaya, Haiti, India, Malagasy, and Java. The plant is also traditionally recorded for a wide range of skin and soft tissue problems, including abscesses, boils, carbuncles, bedsores, ulcers, wounds, whitlow, and swellings, as well as for soothing bug bites and stings. Other recorded uses include digestive complaints such as colic, stomach ache, and cramps, and it has been noted as a diuretic, laxative, purgative, emetic, and vermifuge, with additional applications for rheumatism, piles, and prolapse.

old.description: Young barley leaves harvested before the grain develops. Similar to wheatgrass but with distinct nutritional profile.

name: Benincasa hispida

old.description: Asian cucurbit used in TCM and Ayurveda for urinary conditions, cooling properties, and weight management.

description: Benincasa hispida, in the family Cucurbitaceae, was traditionally recorded for a broad range of medicinal applications in China, Iraq, and Turkey. Its uses include soothing and expelling actions for coughs and lung complaints, including the coughing of blood and wasting conditions, as well as remedies for fever, thirst, and heat. The plant was also recorded for digestive and urinary purposes such as constipation, difficult urination, and gravel, and for skin eruptions, pimples, rashes, abscesses, and wounds.

name: Berberine Metabolic

old.description: Berberine activates AMPK (the metabolic master switch), reducing blood sugar, improving insulin sensitivity, and lowering LDL cholesterol; clinical evidence rivals metformin.
traditional_uses: Blood sugar management in Asian traditional medicine

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Berberine Metabolic, of the family Berberidaceae, was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications in Nepal, India, Turkey, and Hindu regions. Its uses include fever, including malarial fever, and malaria itself, as well as jaundice. The plant was also recorded for skin-related conditions such as dermatosis and condyloma of the anus, for eye applications, and as a tonic and medicine. Additionally, it was used in relation to boils.

name: Berberis lycium

old.description: Northwest Himalayan barberry; bark paste (Rasaut) used in Unani medicine for eye conditions and infections.

provenance.notes: Automatically matched to: WHO Vol.3 (2007). No PubMed citations yet.

description: Berberis lycium, a member of the Berberidaceae family, has a therapeutic theme centered on digestive and eliminative functions. It is traditionally recorded for use as an aperient to encourage bowel movement and as a carminative to relieve flatulence. The plant also appears in records for piles and for a uterine condyloma, a wart-like growth. In addition, it is noted as a febrifuge for reducing fever.

name: Berberis thunbergii

old.description: Ornamental Japanese shrub widely planted in Western gardens, contains berberine, invasive in North America.
traditional_uses: Traditional Japanese medicine for digestive and eye conditions
Used in folk medicine across temperate Asia for infections

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Berberis thunbergii, known by its common name Thunberg's barberry, is a member of the Berberidaceae family. Its use has been recorded in China, where it is traditionally noted for a range of applications. Among the most distinctive is its use for menorrhagia, or heavy menstrual bleeding. The plant is also recorded as an antiseptic and a bitter principle, and for fever, stomachic purposes, as a refrigerant, and as a vermifuge.

name: Bergamot Monarda

old.description: Brilliant red native North American flower used by Oswego tribe for tea after Boston Tea Party and for respiratory and antiseptic uses.
traditional_uses: Oswego tea substitute after Boston Tea Party
treatment of colds and fever in Native American medicine

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Bergamot Monarda is a member of the Lamiaceae family, and its use has been recorded in the United States. Among its applications, one of the most distinctive is as a hair oil, a use that stands apart from its internal applications. Traditionally recorded for digestive support, it has been used as an apertif, carminative, digestive, and tonic, as well as a stimulant and sudorific. Other recorded uses include as a diuretic, hemostat, and medicine, and it has also been taken as a tea.

name: Bethroot

old.description: North American woodland herb used by many Native American tribes for gynecological, wound healing, and respiratory conditions.

description: Bethroot was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications, including uses related to childbirth and women's health, as well as for skin and wound care. It belongs to the Liliaceae family, and its use was recorded in the United States. Other traditional applications include promoting expectoration, supporting digestion, and serving as a tonic or alterative. It was also recorded as an astringent, antiseptic, and hemostat, and as a poultice for skin problems and gangrene.

name: Betula verrucosa

old.description: Betula verrucosa appears in 4 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

provenance.limitations: LNHPD publishes no per-product indication, so uses are empty rather than invented.

description: Silver birch (Betula verrucosa), of the family Betulaceae, has a recorded use in Spain that includes an ointment for skin applications, the most distinctive entry in its ethnobotanical profile. The plant was traditionally recorded for skin care, with an ointment form noted, and for its diuretic and antiseptic properties. It also appears in the record as an irritant, a label that may reflect a caution about topical use rather than a therapeutic aim.

name: Bhumyamalaki

old.description: Annual herb found throughout tropical regions; closely related to P. niruri; used extensively in Ayurveda for liver protection and viral hepatitis.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

taxonomy.decision: GBIF and ITIS both accept this name; NCBI files it under a different genus

description: Bhumyamalaki belongs to the Euphorbiaceae family and has been recorded in Haiti, Trinidad, and Polynesia. Traditionally, it is noted for applications related to diabetes and digestive complaints, as well as for its diuretic properties, which link to its use for oliguria. Other recorded uses include malaria and venereal conditions.

name: Bhumi Niruri Liver

old.description: Liver-specific application; geraniin and corilagin in Phyllanthus niruri directly inhibit hepatitis B surface antigen secretion and protect hepatocytes from damage.

description: Bhumi Niruri Liver, of the Euphorbiaceae family, is traditionally recorded for digestive and liver-related complaints across Haiti, Malaya, the Bahamas, the Marianas Islands, India, and Java. Its applications include dyspepsia, dysentery, diarrhea, colic, and stomach ache, as well as use as a stomachic, carminative, laxative, and aperitif. The plant is also traditionally recorded for fevers such as malaria, typhoid, and flu, and for urinary and kidney conditions including dropsy and blennorrhagia. Other recorded uses include skin complaints such as itch and dermatosis, and a poultice application.

name: Bidens tripartita

old.description: Wetland Bidens used in Russian, Chinese, and Eastern European medicine for skin, allergies, and diuresis.

image.credit: Mentz, August, 1867-1944 & Ostenfeld, C. H. (Carl Hansen), 1873-1931 — Public domain

description: Bidens tripartita, a member of the Asteraceae family, has been traditionally recorded for skin and hair applications across Turkey, China, Iraq and Europe. Its uses include eczema and general skin complaints, as well as a hair-blackening purpose. The plant is also recorded as an astringent and styptic, and for dysentery, fever and scurvy. Other traditional applications include a diuretic and aperient action, a sudorific and sedative use, and a recorded use for spleen sclerosis.

name: Bing Pian

old.description: Southeast Asian tree providing borneol crystals used in TCM to open the orifices, clear heat, and resolve toxins; also used topically as an analgesic.

description: Bing Pian is a plant in the family Dipterocarpaceae, with recorded use in China, Malaya, and Sumatra. It is traditionally recorded for inflammatory and infectious skin conditions such as carbuncle, eczema, ringworm, and chancre, as well as for eye and ear complaints including conjunctivitis, ophthalmia, and opacity. Other traditional applications include respiratory issues like asthma and cough, joint pain in arthritis, and oral or dental problems such as toothache and stomatitis. The plant also appears in records for digestive, nasal, and neurological uses, reflecting a broad range of folk practice across these regions.

name: Bird's Foot Trefoil

old.description: European meadow herb used in folk medicine for digestive complaints, anxiety, and as a mild sedative; related to lotus but distinct properties.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Bird's Foot Trefoil has been traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications, including as a tonic and restorative. It belongs to the Fabaceae family, and its use has been documented in China, the United States, and Spain. The plant was also recorded for fever, thirst, and nerves, as well as for carminative purposes. Additionally, a cyanogenetic application is noted, which may refer to the presence of cyanogenic compounds.

name: Bixa Orellana

old.description: Tropical tree native to tropical America whose seeds produce the red pigment bixin used as a food coloring and medicinally for skin protection and anti-inflammatory conditions.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Bixa orellana, of the family Bixaceae, is traditionally recorded for a broad range of medicinal uses across Mexico, Trinidad, Hawaii, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, and Colombia. Its applications include remedies for fevers and flu, digestive complaints such as dysentery and stomach upset, and kidney and urinary issues including oliguria. The plant is also traditionally recorded for skin conditions like burns, inflammation, and erysipelas, as well as for jaundice, diabetes, and venereal complaints. Other recorded uses include astringent, diuretic, and purgative actions, along with treatments for headache, fainting, and epilepsy.

name: Bitter Orange

old.description: Mediterranean and Asian citrus species whose peel is used in TCM and Western herbal medicine for digestive conditions and weight management.
traditional_uses: Digestive conditions in TCM as Zhi Shi (immature fruit)
Anxiety and insomnia in Mediterranean folk medicine

provenance.notes: Automatically matched to: Commission E. No PubMed citations yet.

description: Bitter orange, a member of the Rutaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications across China, Trinidad, Turkey, Mexico, Curacao, and Haiti. Its uses include digestive complaints such as dyspepsia, flatulence, and diarrhea, as well as respiratory issues like congestion and dyspnea. The plant was also recorded for circulatory and blood-related purposes, including hypertension and menorrhagia, and for nervous system applications such as anodyne and nervine. Other traditional applications include fever, liver and gallbladder support, and external uses like mouthwash and freckle treatment.

name: Black Plum

old.description: TCM herb that astringes the lungs, binds the intestines, generates fluids, and expels roundworms. Key herb in the classical formula Wu Mei Wan for roundworm conditions.

description: Black Plum, a member of the Rosaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in China and Japan. Its applications are broad, with a notable emphasis on digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, and cholera, as well as stomachic and astringent effects. Other recorded uses include fever and malaria, cough and cold, and the promotion of wound healing as a styptic. The plant has also been traditionally recorded for convulsions and epilepsy, and as a vermifuge.

name: Black Horehound

old.description: European herb with characteristic unpleasant smell used in folk medicine for nausea, vomiting, motion sickness, and as a nervine.

description: Black Horehound, a member of the Lamiaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Turkey, Iraq, Europe and Spain. Its main medicinal applications centre on the nervous system, where it was used as a nervine, sedative and for hysteria, alongside a spasmolytic action for spasm. Other recorded uses include a stomachic for digestive complaints, a diuretic, a vermifuge against worms, and a uterine tonic, with additional labels for stimulating, cleansing and resolving actions.

name: Blue Lotus

old.description: An ancient Egyptian sacred plant with mild psychoactive properties, used for relaxation, euphoria, and aphrodisiac effects.
traditional_uses: Ritual and ceremonial use in ancient Egypt

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

taxonomy.source: Kew POWO (Plants of the World Online)

verified_sources: Kew POWO (Plants of the World Online)

description: Blue Lotus, in the family Nymphaeaceae, is most distinctive in its traditional record for dysentery. Its applications also include dyspepsia and a cardiotonic use, alongside astringent and demulcent properties. These latter two suggest soothing and tightening actions that may relate to the digestive complaints for which it was recorded.

old.description: Middle Eastern variety of almond with amygdalin; used historically for cough and as antispasmodic.

name: Blue Vervain

old.description: Native North American nervine herb used for tension, stress, and liver support.

provenance.notes: Automatically matched to: Commission E. No PubMed citations yet.

description: Blue Vervain, a member of the Verbenaceae family, was traditionally recorded for use in the United States. Its applications include promoting sweating (sudorific and diaphoretic) and loosening phlegm as an expectorant, which were often associated with addressing colds and fevers. The plant was also recorded for stomach ache and for albuminuria, a condition involving protein in the urine. Other documented uses include inducing vomiting (emetic) and as a general medicine.

name: Blumea balsamifera

old.description: Philippine medicinal plant used for kidney stones and urinary conditions; approved Philippine traditional medicine.

description: Blumea balsamifera, a member of the Asteraceae family, is traditionally recorded for fevers and malaria across Malaya, the Philippines, Java, and Sumatra. Its applications also include pain relief for headache, stomach ache, lumbago, and rheumatism, as well as a role in childbirth and menstrual regulation. Other recorded uses are as a stomachic, sudorific, vermifuge, and depurative, with additional applications for beriberi, angina, insomnia, and an enlarged spleen.

name: Boehmeria nivea

description: Ramie (Boehmeria nivea), in the nettle family Urticaceae, has a traditional record that includes use for preventing miscarriage, alongside a wide range of other applications. Its use was recorded in China, Haiti, Malaya, Johore, and the Dominican Republic. The plant was traditionally recorded for fevers, dysentery, and flux, as well as for its diuretic, tonic, and refrigerant properties. It also appears in records for wound care and bleeding control, for skin problems such as boils and sores, and for rheumatism and pain, including bites from bugs and snakes.

name: Boerhaavia diffusa

old.description: Boerhaavia diffusa appears in 3 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

description: Boerhaavia diffusa belongs to the family Nyctaginaceae and has been recorded in use in India, Haiti, Sudan, Upper Volta, Africa, and the Dominican Republic. Its applications are broad, with a strong emphasis on the digestive system, where it was traditionally recorded for diarrhea, dysentery, gastritis, and enteritis. It also appears in records for liver and kidney related concerns such as jaundice, dropsy, and Bright's disease, and for fevers including malaria. Other uses include the management of seizures and spasms, as well as skin and inflammatory conditions like swelling and erysipelas.

name: Bolivian Copaiba

old.description: South American tree resin used by Amazonian tribes for anti-inflammatory, wound healing, and respiratory conditions.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Bolivian Copaiba, a member of the Fabaceae family, is traditionally recorded in Turkey for an unusually wide range of purposes, among them the striking use of the plant material against maggots. Its applications include promoting urine flow and bowel movement, with both laxative and purgative uses noted, alongside a stimulant action. The plant was also recorded for venereal complaints, including gonorrhea, and as a vermifuge against worms. Other traditional uses include wound care, massage, and a role in witchcraft practices.

name: Bombax ceiba

old.description: Bombax ceiba appears in 9 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

description: Bombax ceiba, recorded only under that name and placed in the family Bombacaceae, has traditional use documented in India. Its applications cluster around pain and inflammation, with records for anodyne use, neuralgia, rheumatism, toothache, leg ache, sore, swelling, pleurisy and pneumonia. Other traditional records include cholera, hemorrhage, menorrhagia, smallpox, leprosy, caries, stomatitis, megalospleny, atrophy, snake bite and spider lick, along with rinderpest in animals.

name: Brassica juncea

description: Brassica juncea, in the family Brassicaceae, was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal uses in China, Java, Malaya, and Guatemala. Its applications include relief for arthritis, rheumatism, and lumbago, as well as for headache and foot ache. The plant was also recorded as a diuretic, stimulant, and emetic, and as a rubefacient, meaning a substance applied to the skin to produce redness. Other traditional uses include treating syphilis and serving as an anodyne and apertif.

name: Brassica napus

description: Rapeseed (Brassica napus), of the family Brassicaceae, has traditional medicinal use recorded in Haiti, the Dominican Republic, and Europe. Its most distinctive application is as a soporific, a substance traditionally recorded for promoting sleep. Other uses include relief of catarrh and chest colds, as well as pectoral and diuretic applications. The plant is also traditionally recorded for gout.

It also appears in records for its cyanogenetic properties, as a vermifuge, and for intellect and as a soporific. The plant belongs to the Brassicaceae family, and its use was recorded in China, Spain, Haiti, Mexico, Chile, and Germany.

description: Cauliflower, Brassica oleracea var. botrytis, is a member of the Brassicaceae family with a traditional use record spanning China, Spain, Haiti, Mexico, Chile, and Germany. Its most distinctive recorded application is as a soporific, suggesting a traditional role in promoting sleep. Other traditional uses include addressing infection, jaundice, and scurvy, as well as serving as a vermifuge and a cyanogenetic agent. The plant has also been recorded for applications related to intellect, sores, and warts.

description: Brassica oleracea var. capitata, in the family Brassicaceae, was traditionally recorded for uses including jaundice, scurvy, and various infections across China, Spain, Haiti, Mexico, Chile, and Germany. description: Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera, in the family Brassicaceae, has recorded uses in China, Spain, Haiti, Mexico, Chile, and Germany. Traditionally recorded applications include jaundice, scurvy, and sores, as well as warts and infection. Other uses noted are as a vermifuge, a soporific, and for cyanogenetic and intellect-related purposes.

description: Brassica oleracea var. italica was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications, including jaundice, scurvy, and various types of sores and warts. It belongs to the Brassicaceae family, and its use was documented in China, Spain, Haiti, Mexico, Chile, and Germany. Other recorded applications include use for infection, as a vermifuge, and for its cyanogenetic properties, as well as for intellect and as a soporific.

description: Brassica oleracea var. viridis, a member of the Brassicaceae family, has traditional use recorded in China, Spain, Haiti, Mexico, Chile and Germany. Its applications center on the skin and on the liver, with traditional use recorded for sores and warts, and for jaundice. Other traditional uses include scurvy, infection, intestinal worms and a soporific purpose, alongside a cyanogenetic application and one relating to intellect.

name: Breadfruit Leaf

old.description: A Pacific Island staple tree whose leaves are used in traditional Polynesian and Caribbean medicine for hypertension and diabetes.

image.file: Starr-120606-6998-Artocarpus altilis-leaf on ground-Kahanu Gardens Hana-Maui (25118304516).jpg
image.credit: Forest and Kim Starr — CC BY 3.0 us

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Breadfruit leaf, of the family Moraceae, is traditionally recorded for use in Haiti, Trinidad, Fiji, the Dominican Republic, Tonga, and Brazil. The applications documented for this leaf are varied, including its use for pain relief and for inflammatory joint complaints such as gout and rheumatism. It is also traditionally recorded for skin and wound-related purposes, including boils, burns, and sores, as well as for fractures. Other uses include diabetes, hypertension, and as a laxative or for oliguria.

name: Bridelia Ferruginea

old.description: West African tree used across Nigeria, Ghana, and Cameroon in traditional medicine for diabetes, inflammation, and skin conditions.

description: Bridelia ferruginea, a member of the Euphorbiaceae family, is traditionally recorded for use in Africa, Togo, and Nigeria. Its applications are broad, with internal uses noted for diarrhea, dysentery, and intestinal complaints, as well as for diabetes mellitus, edema, and bladder issues. The plant is also traditionally recorded as a diuretic and laxative, and for fever, headache, and rheumatism. External and topical uses include a mouthwash, and applications for skin eruptions, thrush, and gonorrhea, while it has been recorded as a preventive for syphilis.

name: Broom Corn Millet

old.description: Ancient grain used across Europe and Asia as food medicine. Used in TCM for digestive complaints, and in European folk medicine as a nutritive warming food for the elderly and weak.
traditional_uses: Nutritive food for weak and elderly

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Broom corn millet (Poaceae) has been traditionally recorded across China, Turkey, Europe, the USSR, and Ethiopia, with applications centering on the relief of fever and inflammatory skin conditions. It was used for abscesses, boils, sores, and venereal complaints, as well as for cough and other pectoral concerns. Other recorded uses include as a demulcent, diuretic, refrigerant, and intoxicant, and for flux, hematuria, labor, and pyrosis.

name: Broussonetia papyrifera

old.description: An East Asian tree used in TCM for liver and kidney conditions and as a nutritive tonic.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Broussonetia papyrifera, a member of the Moraceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in China, Taiwan, Samoa, and Hawaii. Its applications center on the digestive and urinary systems, with uses for diarrhea, dysentery, dyspepsia, and flux, as well as for anuria, ascites, and nephritis. Other recorded uses include wound healing and skin eruptions, alongside astringent and tonic purposes. The plant has also been noted for rheumatism, menorrhagia, and complications of pregnancy.

name: Brucea javanica

old.description: Southeast Asian Simaroubaceae; seeds (Ya Dan Zi) used in TCM for dysentery, malaria, and anti-tumor effects.

description: Brucea javanica, of the family Simaroubaceae, is traditionally recorded for malaria and dysentery across China, Malaya, Java, Kelantan, Indochina and Sumatra. Its applications include fevers and malaria, digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery and colic, and a range of skin conditions including boils, sores, ringworm, mange, scurf, warts, corns, piles and condyloma. The plant is also recorded as a vermifuge and nematicide, for rheumatism, cough, labor, splenomegaly and as an emetic, cathartic, anodyne, anticoagulant and cholagogue, with use against centipede bites.

name: Buckthorn

old.description: European laxative shrub whose berries were used in medieval medicine as a strong purgative.

image.credit: Köhler, F. E. (Franz Eugen) — Public domain

provenance.notes: Automatically matched to: Commission E. No PubMed citations yet.

description: Buckthorn, a member of the Rhamnaceae family, has a traditional record that includes Turkey, Europe, and Spain. Its most distinctive recorded application is as a purgative, and it was also traditionally recorded for laxative, emetic, and diuretic purposes. These applications group into effects on bowel function (purgative and laxative), the induction of vomiting (emetic), and the promotion of urine flow (diuretic). The plant's use across these regions reflects a broad historical interest in its strong effects on the body.

name: Buckwheat Herb

old.description: Grain herb whose leaves and flowers are used medicinally as a source of rutin for capillary strengthening. The grain is an important gluten-free nutritive food.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Buckwheat Herb, of the Polygonaceae family, is traditionally recorded in China and Iraq for a wide range of applications, including an unusual use for frostbite and gangrene. Its record also covers circulatory and bleeding-related complaints such as hemorrhage, hemoptysis, hemophilia, and telangiectasia, alongside eye conditions like glaucoma and retinitis. Digestive and intestinal uses include diarrhea, cholera, colic, and enterorrhagia, while other entries note abscesses, carbuncles, sores, eruptions, and gonorrhea. Additional traditional purposes include gravel, diabetes, hypertension, and a hair tonic.

name: Buddleja officinalis

description: Buddleja officinalis was traditionally recorded for eye complaints, including cataracts, conjunctivitis, opacity, photophobia, and general vision problems. The plant belongs to the family Loganiaceae, and its use was recorded in China. It was also traditionally recorded for fever and for applications relating to the liver. These labels group into two broad areas: conditions of the eyes and vision, and internal uses involving fever and the liver.

name: Bugleweed Herb

old.description: North American herb used in traditional medicine for hyperthyroid conditions, heart palpitations, and anxiety. One of the few herbs with evidence for reducing thyroid activity.

description: Bugleweed Herb, of the mint family Lamiaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in the United States and Turkey. Its applications center on the lungs and digestion, with cough, lung complaints, and tuberculosis grouped alongside digestive, aperitif, and diarrhea uses. Other recorded uses include astringent and hemorrhage applications, as well as sedative and narcotic effects, and diabetes.

name: Bupleurum Chai Hu

old.description: A fundamental TCM herb that harmonizes Shao Yang patterns; saikosaponins modulate immune function and protect the liver; major herb in Xiao Chai Hu Tang formula.
traditional_uses: Liver qi stagnation and alternating chills and fever
Menstrual irregularities from liver qi stagnation

image.credit: Photo by David J. Stang — CC BY-SA 4.0

description: Chai Hu, in the Apiaceae family, is traditionally recorded for use in China. Its applications include fever and malaria, as well as cold and related sweating. It is also traditionally recorded for liver complaints, nausea, and thirst. Other traditional uses include headache and backache, and it has been noted as a diaphoretic and for metroxenia.

name: Burnet Salad

old.description: European herb used in traditional medicine as an astringent, diuretic, and digestive herb. The fresh leaves were eaten in salads and the herb drunk as a wound-healing tea.

description: Burnet Salad is traditionally recorded for its astringent and hemostatic properties, applications that appear most often in its ethnobotanical use. This plant belongs to the Rosaceae family and has been documented in Turkey and the United Kingdom. Its recorded uses also include serving as an aperitif, a purpose that rounds out its traditional profile.

old.description: Ornamental plant widely used in Mexican folk medicine for respiratory conditions, cough, and as a diuretic; the flowers are the medicinal part.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

name: Bursera simaruba

old.description: Central American and Caribbean tree with resin sacred in Mesoamerican cultures; diverse medicinal uses.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Bursera simaruba, in the family Burseraceae, is traditionally recorded for use in Mexico, Haiti, the Bahamas, Dominican Republic, Venezuela, and Salvador. Its applications include wound care and skin complaints such as sores, rashes, and swelling, as well as digestive issues like diarrhea, dysentery, and stomach ache. Other recorded uses cover fever, rheumatism, and venereal conditions, along with diuretic and purgative purposes. The plant is also traditionally recorded for snake bite, debility, and various inflammatory and urinary complaints.

name: Butea monosperma

old.description: Sacred South Asian tree; gum (Butea gum) and bark used in Ayurveda for digestive conditions and anthelmintic.

description: Butea monosperma, a member of the Fabaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications in India and Java. Its uses included treating diarrhea and dysentery, as well as fevers and gravel. The plant was also recorded for skin complaints such as itch, dhobi itch, and herpes, and for eye conditions like ophthalmia. Other traditional applications include its use as an astringent, diuretic, purgative, vermifuge, and rubefacient, and for menorrhagia and as an aphrodisiac.

name: Butterfly Pea Flower

old.description: Climbing vine of Southeast Asia and India with vivid blue flowers used in Ayurveda for cognitive enhancement and now popular as color-changing tea.
traditional_uses: Cognitive enhancement and memory in Ayurveda
Culinary color in Southeast Asian cuisine

description: Butterfly pea flower, of the Fabaceae family, is traditionally recorded for venomous bites, including scorpion and snake bites, across Iraq, Sudan, Java, Venezuela, the Philippines, and Samoa. Its applications also cover inflammatory skin conditions such as abscesses, boils, eruptions, and swelling, along with joint complaints like arthritis. The plant appears as a digestive aid, recorded as an aperient, apertif, cathartic, laxative, and purgative, and as a diuretic for cystitis. Additional uses include cough and a refrigerant purpose.

name: Callicarpa macrophylla

old.description: Callicarpa macrophylla appears in 3 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

description: Callicarpa macrophylla belongs to the Lamiaceae family and its use is recorded in India. Traditionally recorded applications include anodyne and rheumatism uses, which relate to pain relief and joint discomfort. Other recorded uses are for dysentery and stomach complaints, as well as for glossitis and stomatitis, which involve inflammation of the tongue and mouth.

name: Cajanus cajan

old.description: Tropical legume staple; leaves and roots used in Caribbean and African folk medicine for anemia and sickle cell.

description: Cajanus cajan, a member of the Fabaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a broad range of medicinal applications across Trinidad, Malaya, China, Mexico, Haiti and India. Its uses included respiratory complaints such as cough, cold, flu, bronchitis and sore throat, along with digestive and intestinal troubles including diarrhea, dysentery, colic, enteritis and jaundice. The plant was also recorded for skin and wound care, for swelling and urticaria, and for astringent, diuretic, laxative, sedative and vermifuge purposes. Further traditional applications included earache, convulsion, vertigo, leprosy, ciguatera and even bat bite, alongside uses connected with witchcraft.

old.description: Thai tuberous root; phytoandrogen compounds; used in Thai traditional medicine for male virility and aging.

name: Calophyllum inophyllum

old.description: Coastal tropical tree from Pacific Islands and Indian Ocean, seed oil used extensively for wound healing.
traditional_uses: Sacred healing tree of Pacific Island peoples for wound and skin conditions
Used across Indian Ocean and Pacific for skin diseases and wound healing

description: Calophyllum inophyllum, commonly known as Alexandrian laurel, is a member of the Clusiaceae family. Its use has been recorded in Samoa, Java, the Philippines, Malaya, the Solomon Islands, and New Caledonia. The most distinctive application in its record is for leprosy, but it is also traditionally recorded for a wide range of skin complaints, including scabies, rashes, sunburn, sores, wounds, and boils. Other uses include eye conditions such as conjunctivitis and rheum, digestive issues like diarrhea and piles, and women's health concerns including parturition, puerperium, and metrorrhagia.
traditional_uses: Skin conditions such as scabies and rashes

name: Calotropis

old.description: Widespread tropical weed used across Africa and Asia in traditional medicine, though toxic requiring very careful use.

description: Calotropis, of the family Asclepiadaceae, has a traditional use record spanning India, Egypt, Sudan, Africa, Latin America, and the Bahamas. Its applications include respiratory complaints such as asthma, cold, and cough, alongside gastrointestinal uses like dyspepsia and purgative action. The plant is also traditionally recorded for serious infections and neurological conditions, including leprosy, smallpox, malaria, epilepsy, and hemiplegia, as well as for childbirth and labor. Notably, the record contains entries for suicide, homicide, and infanticide, reflecting a history of toxic use.

name: Calotropis gigantea

old.description: Pan-tropical weed; latex used in Ayurveda for skin diseases, joint pain, and as purgative; cardiac glycosides.

image.credit: Jeevan Jose, Kerala, India — CC BY-SA 4.0

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Calotropis gigantea, in the family Asclepiadaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in India, Java, Malaya, Burma, Sanscrit and the United States. Its applications include treatment for respiratory complaints such as asthma, cough, cold and pneumonia, as well as gastrointestinal issues like dysentery, dyspepsia and cholera. It has also been recorded for skin conditions including boils, carbuncles and leprosy, and for neurological and musculoskeletal problems such as neuralgia, myalgia, paralysis and epilepsy. Other uses include labor and parturition, bites from bugs and dogs, and as an alterative, anodyne, emetic, purgative and diaphoretic.

name: Calystegia sepium

old.description: European climbing vine; roots used in folk medicine as laxative and for gallbladder conditions.

description: Calystegia sepium, a member of the Convolvulaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in China and Spain. Its applications cluster around internal cleansing and topical care: it was used as a diuretic, a purgative, a demulcent, and a tonic, and was also applied as a poultice. The poultice was recorded for bones and tendons, while the other uses reflect broader soothing and eliminative purposes.

name: Camellia japonica

old.description: A Japanese ornamental with medicinal seed oil used for hair, skin, and anti-inflammatory properties.

description: Camellia japonica, of the family Theaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in China and Japan, with bleeding as the most recurrent theme. The plant was recorded for hemorrhages including hematemesis, hemoptysis, and enterorrhagia. It also appears in connection with heart and circulation, recorded for cardiotonic use and for endocarditis and pericarditis. External applications include burns and scalds, along with use as an oil and as an ointment base, and it was recorded for tea.
traditional_uses: Bleeding from the lungs and stomach

name: Cananga odorata

old.description: A tropical Asian tree with fragrant essential oil used in aromatherapy for anxiety, hypertension, and aphrodisiac effect.

description: Cananga odorata, of the family Annonaceae, is traditionally recorded for boils, a use that stands out among its applications. Its use has been documented in Haiti, Tonga, the Solomon Islands, the Dominican Republic, Turkey, and Samoa. The plant is also traditionally recorded for digestive complaints such as diarrhea, stomach issues, and as a carminative, as well as for headache (cephalgia), gout, rheumatism, and malaria. Other recorded uses include eye inflammation (ophthalmia).

name: Canavalia ensiformis

old.description: Tropical cover crop legume; Concanavalin A (ConA) used in immunology research; seeds used in folk medicine.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Canavalia ensiformis, commonly known as jack bean, is a member of the Fabaceae family. Its use has been recorded in China, the West Indies, India, Panama, and in Voodoo traditions. Traditionally recorded applications include a role as an anodyne for pain relief, a tonic for convalescence and general strengthening, and a digestive aid. It also appears in records for kidney-related uses, as a coffee substitute, and in weaning practices, with a mitogenic application noted.

name: Canarium album

old.description: Canarium album is a botanical used in Traditional Chinese Medicine. Health Canada has licensed 1 natural health product containing it, and 1 of their labels were read for this entry. The regulator records no specific indication beyond the traditional-medicine basis, so this entry claims none.

provenance.limitations: LNHPD publishes no per-product indication for TCM licences and no TCM energetics (nature, flavour, meridians). Those fields are deliberately empty rather than filled from an unlicensed source.

description: Canarium album, a member of the Burseraceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in China. Its applications center most often on the throat and respiratory tract, where it was used for sore throat, pharyngitis, and lung complaints. Other recorded uses include stomachic and aperitif purposes, as well as astringent and antiphlogistic (anti-inflammatory) actions. The plant was also traditionally recorded for intoxication and antinvins (countering the effects of alcohol), thirst and sialogogue (promoting saliva), flux, herpes, eruption, and apprehension.

name: Cang Zhu

old.description: TCM rhizome for dampness elimination, digestive bloating, and joint pain from dampness.

description: Cang Zhu is a member of the Asteraceae family, and its use has been recorded in Japan and China. Traditionally, it has been recorded for digestive complaints such as dyspepsia, and it is also classified as a stomachic. Other recorded applications include diaphoretic and diuretic purposes, as well as use for edema, eczema, and nyctalopia. In addition, it has been noted as a balsamic.

name: Canna indica

old.description: Tropical American ornamental; rhizome starch used as food; leaves and seeds used in folk medicine.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Canna indica, the sole species in the Cannaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for applications that most often center on promoting sweating and urine flow. Across India, Turkey, Haiti, Iraq, Latin America, and Samoa, it was used as a diaphoretic and sudorific to encourage perspiration, and as a diuretic and for dropsy to support urine output. Other recorded uses include relieving fever and inflammation, soothing sore throat as a demulcent, and addressing fluid retention. These applications reflect a consistent theme of influencing body fluids and temperature.

name: Capparis spinosa

old.description: A Mediterranean shrub whose flower buds (capers) have anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic, and liver-protective properties.

description: Capparis spinosa, in the family Capparaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in Turkey, Egypt, Spain, and Iraq. Its applications include digestive and urinary support, such as alterative, aperient, diuretic, and expectorant uses, as well as tonic and stimulant properties. The plant is also traditionally recorded for joint and musculoskeletal complaints like gout, rheumatism, and paralysis, and for glandular and splenic conditions including hepatitis, splenitis, and sclerosis of the spleen. Additional uses include astringent and cold remedies, scurvy, and toothache.

name: Capsicum annuum var. annuum

old.description: Capsicum annuum var. annuum appears in 15 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.
