description: Capsicum annuum var. annuum, in the family Solanaceae, has recorded uses in Turkey, Hawaii, China, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, and Iraq. It is traditionally recorded for digestive complaints such as dyspepsia and as a carminative, stomachic, and tonic. Other applications include stimulant and diaphoretic purposes, as well as external uses for skin sores, rheumatism, lumbago, neuralgia, and pharyngitis. The plant is also noted for asthma, gonorrhea, scrofula, ciguatera, and as an aphrodisiac and styptic.

name: Capsicum baccatum

old.description: South American Capsicum with fruity flavor; Aji amarillo used in Peruvian medicine and cuisine for pain and digestion.

description: Capsicum baccatum, a member of the Solanaceae family, is traditionally recorded for digestive and stimulant applications. Its use has been documented in Turkey, Haiti, Europe, and the Dominican Republic. The plant has been used as a carminative, stomachic, and digestive, as well as a stimulant and CNS stimulant. Other recorded uses include aphrodisiac, piles, rubefacient (a substance that produces redness when rubbed on the skin), and styptic (to stop bleeding).

name: Carissa African

old.description: East African shrub fruit and root used for infections and chest pain.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Carissa African, in the family Apocynaceae, has been traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications across Ghana, East Africa, South Africa, Tanzania, the Central African Republic, and Sudan. Its uses include aphrodisiac and virility purposes, as well as remedies for cough and chest complaints. Other recorded applications are adenopathy, internal ulcers, lumbago, venereal conditions, and as a vermifuge, tonic, and general medicine.

name: Carob Pod

old.description: Mediterranean legume tree whose pods are used as chocolate substitute and medicinally for diarrhea, digestive conditions, and as a nutritive food. Rich in tannins and natural sugars.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Carob pod was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal and culinary purposes. It belongs to the Fabaceae family, and its use was documented in Turkey, Spain, and Egypt. The main applications include astringent and laxative or purgative actions, as well as remedies for cough, catarrh, and other pectoral complaints. It was also recorded in connection with hepatitis and mononucleosis, and as a coffee substitute, liqueur ingredient, and treatment for warts.

name: Caryota Mitis

old.description: Clustering palm native to Southeast Asia used in Filipino and Indonesian traditional medicine for joint pain and as a nutritive food source.

description: Caryota mitis, a palm in the family Arecaceae, has been traditionally recorded for wound care and related applications in Cambodia and Malaysia. The most frequently documented theme is the treatment of wounds, with the plant also noted as a cauterizant, a substance used to burn or sear tissue. Additionally, it is recorded as a masticatory, chewed for oral or other purposes. These uses reflect regional practices without implying proven efficacy.

name: Carum Copticum

old.description: Annual herb widely used in South Asian and Middle Eastern cooking and medicine for digestive disorders, respiratory conditions, and antimicrobial purposes.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Carum Copticum, a member of the Apiaceae family, has recorded uses across India, Malaya, Java, Iran and Malaysia. It is traditionally recorded for a wide range of digestive complaints, including colic, dyspepsia, diarrhea, gastrosis and stomachic and carminative purposes, alongside respiratory applications such as cough, cold, bronchitis, asthma, emphysema and pneumonia. Other recorded uses cover fever, rheumatism, epilepsy, spasm and syphilis, as well as antiseptic and bactericide applications, vermifuge use and tonic and stimulant purposes. The plant also appears in records for sore throat, fistula, prolapse and a range of other conditions.

name: Casimiroa Edulis

old.description: Fruit tree native to Mexico and Central America whose seeds and leaves contain potent sedative compounds used traditionally for sleep and hypertension.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Casimiroa edulis, a member of the Rutaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications in Mexico, Latin America, and the United States. Its uses included sedation and sleep, with records for hypnotic, sedative, and soporific purposes, as well as for convulsions and as a nervine. The plant was also traditionally recorded for pain and rheumatism, fever, diarrhea, and as a vermifuge. Other applications included sores, ulcers, and suppurative conditions, along with vulnerary use for wound healing.

name: Cassia Cinnamon

old.description: Chinese cinnamon species; bark used as warming digestive and circulatory spice in TCM for Yang deficiency and digestive conditions.

description: Cassia cinnamon, a member of the Lauraceae family, has been traditionally recorded in China for a range of applications. One of its most distinctive uses is for snake bites, while it is also noted for colic and as a sedative. Other recorded uses include promoting a healthy complexion and managing perspiration, as well as support during the postpartum period. These applications reflect the plant's historical role in folk practice, though modern evidence is not implied.

description: Cassia tora, a member of the Fabaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications across China, Mexico, India, Malaya, Venezuela, and Japan. Its uses include treating skin conditions such as eruptions, furuncles, herpes, itch, leprosy, psoriasis, ringworm, scabies, sores, and ulcers, as well as eye complaints like ophthalmia, photophobia, and pterygium. Internally, it was recorded as a cathartic, laxative, and purgative, and for constipation, fever, cold, cough, and liver and kidney issues. Other recorded applications include bites from bugs and snakes, epilepsy, vertigo, typhoid, plague, and use as a bactericide, parasiticide, and viricide.

name: Cassytha Filiformis

old.description: Parasitic vine widespread across tropical regions used medicinally in Australia, the Caribbean, and Africa for skin conditions, blood pressure, and kidney health.

description: Cassytha filiformis belongs to the Lauraceae family and has been recorded in India, Java, and the Solomon Islands. Traditionally, it is recorded for fluid retention conditions such as anasarca and dropsy, as well as for bilious complaints and dysentery. Other applications include skin sores, sclerosis, urethritis, and use as a vermifuge, with additional uses as a collyrium for eye complaints and as a hair oil.

description: Caterpillar Fungus is traditionally recorded in China for a notably wide range of applications, including one as a panacea, a general remedy for all ailments. Its family is not recorded. Among the more specific uses, it was traditionally recorded for jaundice and phthisis, and as a restorative, stimulant, and tonic. It was also traditionally recorded for opium addiction.

name: Castanea sativa

old.description: A European tree with medicinal leaves used for whooping cough, other respiratory conditions, and as a nutritive food.

description: Castanea sativa, in the family Fagaceae, has recorded traditional use in China, Turkey, Spain, and Europe. Its applications include astringent and tonic actions, as well as uses traditionally recorded for fever, cough, and pertussis. Other documented uses address digestive complaints such as nausea and stomach issues, circulatory and kidney concerns, and musculoskeletal conditions like rheumatism and myalgia. The plant is also traditionally recorded for skin-related purposes including complexion, sores, wounds, and inflammation, and for a range of other conditions such as hernia, hydrocoele, scrofula, and hematochezia.

name: Cay Hy Thiem

description: Cay Hy Thiem was traditionally recorded for a wide range of applications, including fever and malaria, skin and soft tissue problems, and pain and inflammatory conditions. It belongs to the Asteraceae family, and its use was recorded in China, India, and the Philippines. The plant was also traditionally recorded for circulatory and nervous system complaints such as hypertension, numbness, and hemiplegia, as well as for digestive and metabolic issues. Other recorded uses include bites from bugs, dogs, and tigers, and parasitic skin infections.

name: Cayenne

old.description: One of the most powerful circulatory stimulants in the herbal kingdom, used as a catalyst to enhance other herbs.

description: Cayenne, a member of the Solanaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of applications across Turkey, Hawaii, China, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, and Iraq. Its uses include digestive complaints such as dyspepsia and as a carminative, stomachic, and tonic, as well as stimulant and diaphoretic purposes. The plant was also recorded for pain related conditions like neuralgia, rheumatism, and lumbago, and for skin applications including sores and as a styptic and rubefacient, which refers to a substance that produces redness when rubbed on the skin. Additional traditional records include use for asthma, gonorrhea, scrofula, ciguatera, pharyngitis, and as an aphrodisiac.

description: Celosia argentea var. cristata, in the family Amaranthaceae, is traditionally recorded for uses that most often concern the eyes and vision. In China, India, Thailand, Bayam tuju, Sudan, and Malaya, applications include conjunctivitis, ophthalmia, photophobia, retinitis, and general vision support. Other recorded uses cover bleeding and wounds, such as hemorrhage, epistaxis, metrorrhagia, enterorrhagia, fractures, sores, and eruptions, along with digestive complaints like diarrhea and dysentery. Additional traditional applications include cough, headache, scurvy, beri-beri, pellagra, stomatitis, and use as a tonic, astringent, vermifuge, and aphrodisiac.

name: Centaurea Cyanus

In Turkey, Iraq, and Spain, it has also been documented as a diuretic, astringent, and stimulant, as well as a tonic and a pectoral for chest conditions. Additionally, it has been used in cases of fever. These applications reflect a broad range of traditional practices across the regions where its use was recorded.

description: Cephalanthus occidentalis, a member of the Rubiaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications in Mexico and the United States. Its uses include astringent and tonic purposes, as well as a laxative and an emetic. The plant was also traditionally recorded for fever and malaria, and for cough and pleurisy. Other applications include palsy, venereal complaints, and skin uses.

name: Centaurium umbellatum

description: Centaurium umbellatum, a member of the Gentianaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Turkey, Europe, and Spain. Its main medicinal applications center on the digestive system, where it was used as a stomachic, digestive, and tonic, as well as a cholagogue to support bile flow. Other recorded uses include a depurative and detersive action, a vermifuge for expelling worms, and treatment for dysentery and fever.

name: Cerinthe major

old.description: Mediterranean ornamental with traditional uses for skin wounds and bee forage; honey medicinal properties.

description: Cerinthe major, known by its common name honeywort, is a plant in the Boraginaceae family. Its use was recorded in the United States, where it was traditionally recorded for jaundice and scurvy, and also as a diuretic. These applications reflect a historical interest in the plant for liver-related and nutritional conditions, though no claims of efficacy are made here.

name: Cerbera manghas

old.description: Coastal Indo-Pacific tree; all parts highly toxic (cerberin); bark used topically in folk medicine for skin.

description: Cerbera manghas, commonly known as the dogbane or sea mango, is a member of the Apocynaceae family. Its use has been recorded in Samoa, the Philippines, Java, the Marquesas Islands, and Malaya, where it is traditionally noted for a distinctive canicide application. Other recorded uses include treatments for skin wounds and yaws, as well as remedies for rheumatism and colds. The plant has also been documented as an emetic, cathartic, and purgative, and as a vermifuge and pediculicide, with some applications related to heart conditions.

name: Ceterach Officinarum

old.description: Small fern found in rocky habitats across Europe and North Africa used in traditional European herbal medicine for kidney stones and respiratory conditions.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Ceterach officinarum, a fern of the family Aspleniaceae, was traditionally recorded in Egypt for a range of medicinal applications. Its uses include astringent and diuretic actions, with traditional applications for the bladder and kidneys. It was also recorded as a pectoral for chest complaints, an emollient for soothing purposes, and a vermifuge for expelling worms, as well as for the spleen.

name: Chamaesyce hirta

Traditionally recorded for asthma, bronchitis, and cough, it has also been used for fever, diarrhea, and debility. Other applications include a diuretic effect, a vermifuge purpose, and the treatment of warts, while it has been noted for discutient, narcotic, and antispasmodic properties.

name: Che Qian Zi

old.description: TCM herb that promotes urination, clears heat, and benefits the eyes.

description: Che Qian Zi is traditionally recorded for urinary and kidney complaints, a theme that appears most often in its list of applications. The plant belongs to the family Plantaginaceae, and its use was recorded in China and Japan. It was also traditionally recorded for digestive issues such as diarrhea and gastritis, for skin conditions including itch, swelling, and impetigo, and for fever, cough, and hypertension. Other applications include eye and ear complaints, headache, toothache, and wound care.

name: Chia Seed

old.description: Ancient Aztec food crop rediscovered as omega-3 superfood with excellent fiber and mineral content.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Chia seed was traditionally recorded for constipation, bilious complaints, and liver conditions. It belongs to the Lamiaceae family, and its use was recorded in Mexico. The applications group around digestive and biliary health, with constipation as a specific concern and bilious and liver issues as related internal uses.

name: Chimaphila Umbellata

old.description: Small evergreen subshrub of northern forests used by many Native American tribes for urinary conditions, rheumatism, and skin diseases.

description: Chimaphila umbellata, in the family Ericaceae, has a traditional record that includes use in the United States, Canada, and Danish regions. Among its most distinctive recorded applications is the use of a collyrium, a wash for the eyes. The plant was also traditionally recorded for diabetes and for kidney and bladder stone, as well as for digestive and stomach complaints. Other applications include fever and typhus, rheumatism, muscle pain, and stiffness, along with use as an astringent, diuretic, tonic, and antiseptic, and as a liniment and vulnerary for external care.

name: Chaparro Amargo

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Chaparro Amargo, a plant in the Simaroubaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Mexico. Its applications center on the intestines, where it was used as an astringent and tonic, and it was also recorded for eczema and fever. These uses reflect a broad traditional role in digestive and general health support.

name: Chios Mastic v2

description: Chios Mastic, a member of the Anacardiaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in China, Turkey, Mexico, Europe, the Mediterranean, and Malaya. Its applications include digestive purposes such as stomachic, carminative, and aperitif uses, as well as astringent and hemostatic actions. It is also recorded for respiratory complaints like cough and as an expectorant, and for oral care including gingivitis and halitosis. Other traditional uses encompass analgesic, stimulant, and sudorific purposes, along with applications for skin and soft tissue conditions such as boils and mastitis.

name: Chiranthodendron

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Chiranthodendron, a member of the Sterculiaceae family, has been traditionally recorded in Mexico and Guatemala for a range of medicinal applications. The most frequently noted theme is the relief of pain, with uses as an anodyne and for treating ulcers and piles. Other recorded applications include epilepsy, heart complaints, and ophthalmia, reflecting a broad spectrum of traditional use.

name: Chitrak Root

description: Chitrak root, of the family Plumbaginaceae, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications across Ghana, India, Java, Nigeria, Malaya, and Africa. Its uses include digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dyspepsia, and piles, as well as fever, flu, and malaria. The root was also recorded for skin conditions like abscess, dermatosis, itch, ringworm, and wart, and for swelling, rheumatism, and leprosy. Other applications include its use as a tonic, vermifuge, and in childbirth, alongside external uses as a counterirritant and vesicant.

name: Chokecherry

old.description: Widespread North American shrub used extensively by Plains, Plateau, and Woodland indigenous peoples as food medicine, antimicrobial, and tonic.

Pemmican and pemican ingredient across Plains cultures
Cough and cold in many traditions

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Chokecherry, a member of the Rosaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications in the United States. Its uses included relief from pain and headaches, treatment of digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, and dyspepsia, and management of fever and malaria. The plant was also recorded for respiratory conditions like colds, lung ailments, and tuberculosis, as well as for eye-related applications such as collyrium and sore eyes. Additional traditional uses encompassed women's health during parturition, treatment of piles, and its role as a sedative, emetic, purgative, and vermifuge.

name: Christmas Rose

old.description: Toxic perennial blooming in winter; extensively used in historical and medieval European medicine as purgative and for mental illness.
traditional_uses: Treatment of melancholia and mental illness in ancient medicine

description: Christmas Rose, a member of the Ranunculaceae family, is most distinctly recorded as a rodenticide. Its use was documented in Turkey, Spain, Europe, and the United Kingdom, where it was traditionally recorded for cardiac and cardiostimulant purposes, as well as for cathartic and diuretic effects. Other applications include hydragogue, mydriatic, narcotic, and nervine uses.

name: Chives

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Chives, a member of the Liliaceae family, have traditionally been recorded for uses relating to the blood and circulation, with anemia and general blood complaints among the applications noted. Records from Iraq, Turkey, Haiti, and the United Kingdom also describe digestive purposes, including carminative and digestive uses, alongside a diuretic application and a role as an antiseptic. One further use recorded is for a wen, a term for a localized swelling or lump. These applications reflect traditional practice rather than demonstrated effects.

name: Chrysanthemum Bai Ju

The plant has also been noted for addressing inflammatory skin conditions such as abscesses and boils, and for eye-related issues including conjunctivitis and trachoma. Additionally, it is traditionally recorded for vertigo, tinnitus, and as a sedative and anodyne.

name: Chrysanthemum Flower

description: Chrysanthemum Flower, of the Asteraceae family, is traditionally recorded for use in China. Its most distinctive recorded application is as a collyrium, a wash for the eyes, and it is also noted for eye-related conditions such as conjunctivitis and trachoma. The flower is further recorded for feverish and cold-related complaints, including fever, cold, and flu, and for headache, vertigo, and tinnitus. Additional traditional uses include abscess and boil, along with applications described as alexiteric, anodyne, carminative, refrigerant, and sedative.
traditional_uses: Eye wash for conjunctivitis and trachoma

description: Chuan Bei Mu Bulb belongs to the Liliaceae family and is traditionally recorded for use in Nepal and China. The bulb is most often associated with respiratory complaints, and the documented applications group around three related conditions. These are asthma, bronchitis, and tuberculosis, which together reflect a pattern of use for breathing difficulties and chronic lung concerns.

name: Chuan Lian Zi

description: Chuan Lian Zi is a plant in the Meliaceae family, traditionally recorded for use in China. Its most distinctive application in the ethnobotanical record is for ascariasis, a parasitic worm infection. The plant was also traditionally recorded for parasiticidal purposes more broadly, and for tinea, a fungal skin condition. Other documented uses include an anodyne or pain-relieving application, with specific records for abdominal pain, chest complaints, dysmenorrhea, and tympanitis, which is inflammation of the middle ear.

name: Cichorium endivia

description: Endive, Cichorium endivia, is a member of the Asteraceae family, and its use has been recorded in Turkey. Other applications include use as a refrigerant and fever remedy, as a diuretic, and as a demulcent, while its resolvent action was described in terms of helping to disperse swellings or congestion.

It is also traditionally recorded for contraceptive purposes and for suicide. These uses reflect the plant's association with serious and often lethal consequences rather than with routine medicinal treatment.

name: Cinchona

description: Cinchona, a member of the Rubiaceae family, was traditionally recorded for fevers and malaria in regions including Turkey, Mexico, China, and Italy. Other recorded uses include astringent and antiseptic purposes, as well as a tonic and stomachic, with additional applications for neuralgia, sciatica, and lumbago.

The plant is characterized by opposite leaves and a capsular fruit with winged seeds.

Other traditional uses include cough, pneumonia, gonorrhea, scurvy, and headache or stomach ache, with applications spanning antiseptic, carminative, laxative, and tonic purposes.

image.file: EB1911 - Ericaceae - Fig. 1.—Vaccinium vitis-idaea, with leaf and flower.jpg

description: Cowberry Leaf, a member of the Ericaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Turkey and Japan. Its applications centre on the urinary and genital tract, with antiseptic and disinfectant actions noted for the urethra and urogenital system, alongside a diuretic effect. The leaf is also documented as an astringent and styptic, and as a bitter aperitif and depurative. Other recorded uses include a nervine for debility and a remedy for rheumatism and diabetes.

name: Cranesbill Geranium

old.description: Native North American perennial with deeply divided leaves; one of the best astringent herbs used by Indigenous peoples and Eclectic physicians.
traditional_uses: Diarrhea and dysentery by many Indigenous tribes
Used by Menominee, Potawatomi and many tribes

description: Cranesbill Geranium, a member of the Geraniaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in the United States, Turkey, and the United Kingdom. Its most distinctive application is as a styptic, a hemostat, and a vulnerary, meaning it was used to stop bleeding and to help wounds heal. Related uses include poultices for swelling and sores, as well as astringent and tonic purposes. The plant was also recorded for diarrhea, dysentery, and cholera, and for throat soreness, diuretic action, and enterorrhagia.

name: Creeping Jenny

old.description: European ground-covering plant used in folk medicine for wound healing, hemorrhage, and respiratory conditions.

description: Creeping Jenny, a member of the Primulaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Turkey and Europe. Its main medicinal applications group around digestive and respiratory support, including antacid and astringent actions alongside expectorant use. Other recorded uses include fever, scurvy, tea, and a vulnerary application for wound care. These applications reflect the plant's historical role in folk practice rather than proven medical effects.

name: Crateva nurvala

old.description: An Ayurvedic tree used for urinary stones, BPH, liver conditions, and as an anti-inflammatory.

description: Crateva nurvala, known by its common name, is a plant in the Capparaceae family whose use has been recorded in Malaya, Baroendoj and Sempol wada. Among its most distinctive traditional applications is the management of calculus, and it was also recorded for urogenital complaints. Other recorded uses include fever and malaria, digestive purposes such as aperitif, cholagogue, laxative and tonic, and the relief of cramps. It further appears as an astringent and demulcent, and as a rubefacient and vesicant, terms describing substances applied to the skin to produce redness or blistering.

name: Crescentia Cujete

old.description: Tropical American tree producing large gourd-like fruits used medicinally across Latin America for respiratory conditions, wound healing, and as a traditional cough syrup.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Crescentia cujete, in the family Bignoniaceae, is traditionally recorded for respiratory complaints, with applications including asthma, cough, chest cold, catarrh, and use as an expectorant. Records from Curacao, Mexico, Haiti, Trinidad, Cuba, and Panama also note uses for digestive issues such as diarrhea, dysentery, and as a laxative or aperient. Other traditional applications include fever and flu, inflammation, bruising, and skin conditions like erysipelas and mange, as well as a hair tonic and treatments for lice. The plant is additionally recorded for snake bite and coral cuts, and for menstrual and childbirth-related purposes.

name: Crinum bulbispermum

traditional_uses: Traditional Zulu and Sotho medicine for fevers and infections

description: Crinum bulbispermum, a member of the Liliaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Lesotho. Its main recorded applications are for colds and as a lactogogue, a term for a substance used to support breast milk production. A further recorded use is as a charm, reflecting a cultural rather than strictly medicinal purpose.

name: Crinum asiaticum

old.description: Large bulbous plant of tropical Asian coastlines with fragrant white flowers, used in traditional medicine.
traditional_uses: Traditional South and Southeast Asian medicine for wounds and pain
Used in Ayurveda and Indonesian folk medicine for infections and fever

description: Crinum asiaticum, a plant in the Liliaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications across Malaya, Java, Samoa, Egypt, India, and China. Its uses include internal purposes such as a tonic, laxative, emetic, and expectorant, as well as remedies for fever, bilious conditions, and dysuria. Externally, it was recorded for swellings, sores, wounds, carbuncles, whitlows, chafing, orchitis, lumbago, and headache. Other traditional applications include anodyne, diaphoretic, and preventive use for yaws.

name: Crotalaria juncea

old.description: South Asian fiber crop; seeds and leaves used in folk medicine for skin conditions and as fiber source.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Crotalaria juncea belongs to the Fabaceae family and its use was recorded in Iraq. It was traditionally recorded for depurative purposes, a term used for agents considered to purify the blood. The plant also has recorded applications for skin conditions, specifically impetigo and psoriasis.

name: Crotalaria retusa

old.description: Pantropical weed with pyrrolizidine alkaloids; folk use for respiratory and skin conditions; hepatotoxic.

description: Crotalaria retusa, a member of the Fabaceae family, was traditionally recorded for fever and for coughing up blood (hemoptysis). In Java and the United States, its use also extended to skin conditions, including impetigo and scabies. These applications reflect a historical practice of using the plant for both internal and external complaints.

name: Croton tiglium

old.description: Asian Euphorbiaceae; croton oil from seeds is a purgative; phorbol esters used in cancer research.

description: Croton tiglium, in the family Euphorbiaceae, has recorded uses in China, Java, Turkey, Malaya, the Philippines, and Hainan. It was traditionally recorded for severe digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, and colic, and for fever and cold. Other applications include skin sores, carbuncles, and throat conditions, as well as paralysis and apoplexy. The plant was also used as a purgative, emetic, and diaphoretic, and for toothache and schistosomiasis.

Traditionally recorded applications center on the urinary and digestive systems, including dysuria, oliguria, micturition difficulties, jaundice, dyspepsia, and digestive complaints generally, alongside a diuretic role. Other recorded uses include cough, cold, coryza, eczema, stomatitis, bruises, and the expulsion of worms, with notes on use as a refrigerant and as a preventive for sunstroke.

Its use has been documented in Iraq, Venezuela, Brazil, Kurdistan, Malaya, and Peru. The plant is also traditionally recorded for external applications such as poultices and cataplasms for burns, carbuncles, rashes, warts, and inflammation, as well as for internal uses including fever, chest complaints, teething, and as a diuretic, tonic, and nervine.

Its uses include treating abdominal complaints and fever, as well as acting as a laxative. The plant was also recorded as a spasm remedy and for expelling tapeworms and other intestinal worms, with both taenifuge and vermifuge applications noted.

description: Cumaru belongs to the Fabaceae family and has recorded uses in Trinidad, Turkey, China, and Venezuela. It is traditionally recorded for digestive complaints such as dyspepsia, stomach ache, carminative and stomachic purposes, and for fever and pertussis. Other applications include cardiotonic, stimulant, and diaphoretic uses, as well as fumigant and narcotic purposes.

name: Culver's Root

description: Culver's Root belongs to the family Scrophulariaceae and its use was recorded in the United States. Traditionally, it was recorded for applications that include causing vomiting and evacuating the bowels, with uses grouped as emetic, laxative, and purgative. These applications reflect a strong action on the digestive system, and the plant was also listed more broadly as a medicine.

name: Curculigo Latifolia

description: Curculigo latifolia, of the family Liliaceae, was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal and related purposes in Malaya, Johore, Pahang and Java. Its applications included use as a stimulant and stomachic, as a diuretic, and for fever and urogenital complaints. It was also recorded for menorrhagia, delirium and ophthalmia, and as an aperitif and sweetener.

name: Cupressus sempervirens

old.description: A Mediterranean tree whose essential oil and cones are used for venous insufficiency, respiratory conditions, and wound healing.

description: Cupressus sempervirens belongs to the family Cupressaceae, and its use has been recorded in Turkey, Portugal, Spain, Egypt, and Europe. It is traditionally recorded for respiratory complaints such as cough, flu, pertussis, and as an expectorant and pectoral, as well as for digestive and urinary conditions including diabetes, diuretic, kidney issues, and piles. Other recorded applications include gynecological and rectal concerns like metrorrhagia, uterine sclerosis, myofibroma, and prolapse of the uterus or anus, along with rheumatism, nose polyps, and as an antiseptic, astringent, styptic, vasoconstrictor, sudorific, vermifuge, and vulnerary (wound healing).

name: Curculigo Root

old.description: TCM and Ayurvedic kidney yang tonic used to warm kidney fire, strengthen the sinews, and treat impotence and low libido. More warming than epimedium.

description: Curculigo Root, of the Liliaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in China, the Philippines, and India. Its applications often center on kidney and urinary complaints, including enuresis, diuresis, and support for the kidneys, as well as on digestive and liver issues such as diarrhea, jaundice, and piles. Other recorded uses include asthma, skin conditions like dermatosis and itch, and as a tonic, restorative, and aphrodisiac for impotency.

It was also traditionally recorded for diarrhea, fever, and gravel, a term for urinary stones or sediment.

The plant was used as a stimulant and carminative, and was also applied to bruises and sprains. In addition, it was described as balsamic, a term reflecting a soothing or restorative use.

description: Cuscuta Seed, of the family Cuscutaceae, is traditionally recorded in China and India for a cluster of uses centering on the genitourinary system. These include emission, spermatorrhea, impotency, hypogonadism, enuresis, polyuria, and prostatitis. Other recorded applications cover fluid accumulation such as anasarca and dropsy, as well as lumbago, notalgia, vertigo, neurasthenia, and fracture. The seed is also traditionally recorded in connection with pregnancy and, separately, for rinderpest.

Other traditional applications include night blindness, plague, and smallpox.

description: Quince is traditionally recorded for diarrhea and dysentery, its most distinctive application, and for related astringent and tonic uses. The plant belongs to the Rosaceae family, and its use has been recorded in Turkey, China, Mexico, Iraq, Venezuela, and Chile. Other applications include digestive and carminative purposes, as well as demulcent, emollient, and pectoral uses for the chest and throat. It is also noted as a refrigerant, diuretic, and stimulant, with additional uses for headache, skin lotion, and scald.

The plant was also recorded for digestive complaints such as biliousness and as a carminative, and for spasms and as a stimulant and sudorific. In addition, it was noted as an adulterant, a non-therapeutic use.

name: Cynodon dactylon

description: Cynodon dactylon belongs to the grass family Poaceae and has been recorded in traditional use across India, Egypt, Turkey, Nepal, Sicily, and Mexico. Its applications are broad, with a strong emphasis on the urinary system, where it was traditionally recorded for kidney and urogenital complaints, stones, calculus, and dropsy. It also appears in records for digestive disturbances such as diarrhea and dysentery, and for circulatory and nervous conditions including hypertension, hemorrhage, convulsion, epilepsy, hysteria, and insanity. Other traditional uses include snake bite, wounds, sores, carbuncles, warts, cough, headache, and general purposes described as alterative, astringent, and laxative.

Other traditional applications include leprosy, obesity, and use as a stimulant and vermifuge. These records reflect the plant's place in traditional practice, but no claims of efficacy are made.

name: Cyperus Articulatus

description: Cyperus articulatus belongs to the Cyperaceae family and has been recorded in Egypt, Africa, and Hawaii. Traditionally, it has been used for a range of digestive complaints, including colic and dyspepsia, as well as for ache. The plant has also been recorded as a fumigant and a sedative.

Other traditional uses include arthritis, bruising, and skin conditions like furunculosis and dermatitis, along with astringent, sedative, and tonic purposes.

The plant has also been recorded for cough and fever, as well as for skin sores, wounds, bruises, and trauma. Other traditional uses include anthelminthic, tonic, and vesicant applications.

description: Dioscorea alata, a member of the Dioscoreaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in India, Hawaii, the West Indies, and Mexico. The main applications grouped together include fever and gonorrhea, alongside uses as a laxative and vermifuge. Other recorded uses are for leprosy and piles.

name: Dioscorea Yam

old.description: TCM spleen, lung, and kidney tonic used to tonify qi and yin, stabilize essence, and treat digestive weakness, chronic cough, and urinary frequency.

provenance.notes: Automatically matched to: WHO Vol.3 (2007). No PubMed citations yet.

description: Dioscorea, a member of the Dioscoreaceae family, has recorded traditional use in India and Japan. Its applications include digestive complaints such as diarrhea and dysentery, and respiratory issues like cough. The plant is also traditionally recorded for inflammatory conditions of the male reproductive system, including epididymitis, hydrocoele, orchitis, and swelling. Additionally, it has been used as a nutrient, tonic, and for thirst, as well as for sores.

name: Diospyros kaki

old.description: East Asian fruit tree with medicinal leaves and astringent fruit used in TCM for blood pressure and digestive conditions.

description: Diospyros kaki, of the family Ebenaceae, is traditionally recorded for use in China, India, and Malaya. Its applications include astringent and antidiarrheal purposes, such as diarrhea, flux, and enterorrhagia, as well as remedies for cough, dyspnea, and hiccup. Other recorded uses are for hemorrhage, piles, wounds, and sores, along with fever, hypertension, nausea, and as a stomachic, restorative, vermifuge, and anodyne.

old.description: Woolly-leaved foxglove from Southeast Europe used as primary source of digoxin for heart failure treatment.
traditional_uses: heart failure treatment in European folk medicine

name: Dipsacus Root

old.description: TCM herb that tonifies liver and kidney, mends sinews and bones; used for trauma, fractures, and threatened miscarriage.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Dipsacus root, of the family Dipsacaceae, is traditionally recorded for use in China. Its applications include the relief of pain, as in dysmenorrhea, lumbago, notalgia, and rheumatism, and the management of bleeding such as hemorrhage and menorrhagia. It is also recorded as a tonic for debility and for support during parturition and the puerperium, as well as for trauma and incontinence.

name: Djibouti Desert Tamarisk

old.description: Drought-tolerant tree from Horn of Africa and desert regions used medicinally for skin, digestive, and anti-inflammatory purposes.
traditional_uses: treatment of skin conditions in Horn of Africa folk medicine

description: Djibouti Desert Tamarisk, a member of the Tamaricaceae family, was traditionally recorded for astringent and skin-related applications in Egypt and Algeria. Its uses include eczema and other skin conditions, as well as a gargle. It was also traditionally recorded for sclerosis of the spleen.

name: Dok Khem

old.description: An ornamental shrub used in Thai traditional medicine for menstrual disorders and hypertension.

description: Dok Khem, a plant in the Rubiaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for parturition and the puerperium, as well as for urogenital concerns such as dysuria. Its use is documented in Malaya, Malaysia, and the Philippines. Other applications include hemorrhage and tuberculosis.

name: Dodonaea Viscosa

old.description: Pantropical shrub used in traditional medicine across Africa, Asia, Australia, and Americas for fever, toothache, wound healing, and inflammation.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Dodonaea viscosa, known as hopbush, is a member of the Sapindaceae family and has been traditionally recorded for use in India, Iraq, Mexico, New Guinea, Sudan, and Samoa. Its most distinctive recorded application is funereal, setting it apart from the plant's other uses. Medicinally, it was traditionally recorded for fevers and colic, for joint and muscle complaints such as gout, rheumatism, sprains, and shoulder soreness, and for skin and wound care including bruises, burns, sores, and swellings. It also appears as an astringent, styptic, and stimulant, and was used as a dentifrice.

name: Doku Chini

old.description: A highly valued Thai and Ayurvedic vine rich in berberine used for liver, diabetes, and infections.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Doku Chini was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications, including the care of wounds and sores, the management of fever, and support for debility. It belongs to the Menispermaceae family, and its use was recorded in India and Malaysia. Related applications include antiseptic and fungicide purposes, as well as the relief of dyspepsia and stomach complaints, with tonic and stomachic roles also noted. The plant was additionally recorded in connection with Candida.

name: Dong Kui Zi

old.description: TCM herb promoting urination and benefiting lactation.

image.credit: Nathaniel Lord Britton (1859-1934), and A. Brown — Public domain

description: Dong Kui Zi is a Malvaceae plant traditionally recorded for uses that center on the urinary system and bowel regulation. In China and Indochina, it was used as a diuretic and for dysuria and edema, while its aperient and laxative properties were applied to constipation and dysentery. Other traditional applications include soothing demulcent effects, support for lactation, and relief for keratitis, pertussis, and scabies.

name: Dorema ammoniacum

old.description: Middle Eastern Apiaceae resin plant used in Unani and Persian medicine for respiratory and liver conditions.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Dorema ammoniacum, known commonly as ammoniacum, is a plant in the Apiaceae family whose use has been recorded in Turkey, Europe, France, India, and Iran. Its most distinctive recorded application is for asthma. The plant has also been traditionally recorded for bronchitis, catarrh, and as an expectorant, as well as for hepatitis and splenitis. Other uses include as a carminative, diuretic, stimulant, antiseptic, and for spasm.

name: Doronicum pardalianches

old.description: European alpine herb historically used as stimulant and for heart conditions; toxic alkaloids limit use.

provenance.notes: 1 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Doronicum pardalianches, known by its common name leopard's bane, is a member of the Asteraceae family. Its use has been recorded in India, where it was traditionally recorded for a range of applications including cardiac and cardiotonic purposes, as well as for depression and melancholy. It was also considered a nervine and a tonic, and was used for scorpion stings and warts.

name: Dracocephalum moldavica

old.description: European and Central Asian herb with lemon fragrance; used for digestive and nervous conditions.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Dracocephalum moldavica belongs to the Lamiaceae family, and its use has been recorded in India and Europe. The plant is traditionally recorded for fever and for tonic purposes, as well as for its astringent and demulcent properties. It is also noted as a vulnerary, a term used for applications related to wound care.

name: Dracaena cinnabari

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Dracaena cinnabari, a plant in the family Agavaceae, was traditionally recorded for use in Egypt. It was valued as an astringent and for helping to close wounds (cicatrizant). The plant was also traditionally recorded for diarrhea and dysentery, as well as for hemorrhage. These applications reflect its historical role in managing bleeding and digestive complaints.

name: Dragon's Blood

old.description: Red resin from tropical palm trees used across Chinese, Greek, and South American medicine for wound healing.

description: Dragon's Blood was traditionally recorded for a range of applications in China, including wounds, bruises, and other trauma. It belongs to the Arecaceae family. Related uses include stopping hemorrhage and promoting cicatrization, as well as supporting circulation. It was also recorded as an anodyne and sedative for pain, spasm, and chest or abdominal complaints, and as a tonic in cases of metroxenia.

name: Drimys winteri

old.description: Aromatic tree from Patagonia whose bark was used by Captain Winter on early sea voyages against scurvy.
traditional_uses: Traditional Mapuche sacred tree Canelo for digestive and fever conditions
Used by Captain Winter against scurvy in 1579 sea voyage

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Drimys winteri, a member of the Winteraceae family, was traditionally recorded for a range of digestive and general health purposes. Its use was documented in Turkey, Mexico, Brazil, Venezuela, and Chile. The plant was recorded as a stomachic, gastric, and tonic, and for gastritis, dysentery, and scurvy. It also served as an aperitif, astringent, balsamic, carminative, and stimulant, and was used for toothache.

name: Drynaria fortunei

description: Drynaria fortunei, a member of the Polypodiaceae family, was traditionally recorded in China for a range of musculoskeletal and related complaints. Its applications include relief of pain and inflammation in the joints and muscles, such as arthralgia, arthritis, rheumatism, myalgia, lumbago, and backache. It was also used for trauma and contusion, and for supporting bones, the kidneys, and the legs, as well as for marasmus and neurasthenia. Additionally, it was noted as a carminative and anodyne.

name: Dryopteris crassirhizoma

description: Dryopteris crassirhizoma, a member of the Dryopteridaceae family, is traditionally recorded for use in China. Its main medicinal applications group into two areas: the expulsion of parasitic worms, specifically hookworms and tapeworms, and the management of bleeding, including hemorrhage and the puerperium period. It is also traditionally recorded for prophylaxis, suggesting a preventive role in folk practice.

name: Dryopteris filix-mas

description: Male fern (Dryopteris filix-mas), of the family Dryopteridaceae, has a traditional record that includes use as a taenifuge, a means of expelling tapeworms, which stands out as its most distinctive application. Its use was recorded in Turkey, the United States, Spain, Europe and Egypt. Other applications grouped as digestive and eliminative uses include aperient and vermifuge, while astringent and pectoral uses relate to toning and chest complaints; a cyanogenetic label also appears in the record.

name: Duchesnea indica

description: Duchesnea indica belongs to the Rosaceae family, and its medicinal use has been recorded in China. Traditionally recorded applications include inflammatory skin conditions such as abscesses, boils, eczema, and ringworm, as well as swelling. The plant has also been noted for use in relation to bug bites and snake bites, and for inflammatory conditions of the mouth and throat, including stomatitis, tonsillitis, and laryngitis. Additionally, it has been recorded as a refrigerant and as a decoagulant.

name: Dulawali

old.description: Filipino vine related to Guduchi (Tinospora cordifolia); used in Philippine folk medicine for fever, malaria, diabetes, and as a general tonic.

description: Dulawali was traditionally recorded for stomach complaints and diarrhea, as well as for use as a cordial and a general panacea. It belongs to the Menispermaceae family, and its use was recorded in the Philippines. The plant was also applied to sores, and its overall reputation included a broad role as a panacea.

name: Durian Leaf

old.description: The leaves of the infamous durian fruit tree are used in Southeast Asian folk medicine for fever and skin conditions.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Durian leaf, of the family Bombacaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in Malaya and Java. Its most distinctive application is for parturition, and it was also used for dermatosis, fever, and jaundice. In addition, the leaf was regarded as a tonic. These uses reflect the plant's place in the traditional medicine of those regions.

name: Duoc Lieu Trinh Nu

old.description: The sensitive plant used in Vietnamese medicine for insomnia, anxiety, and as an anti-inflammatory.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Duoc Lieu Trinh Nu, a member of the Fabaceae family, has recorded traditional use in Haiti, Trinidad, Panama, Venezuela, Java, and Guatemala. It was traditionally recorded for a range of applications, including adenopathy and glandular swelling, as well as sores and swelling. The plant was also used as a calmative and sedative for insomnia and headache, and for digestive complaints such as diarrhea and dysentery. Other recorded uses include alopecia, hoarseness, sinus issues, and urogenital and urinary concerns like gravel and oliguria.

name: Dusty Miller Artemisia

description: Dusty Miller Artemisia was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications in China. It belongs to the Asteraceae family. The plant was used for digestive complaints such as carminative and stomachic purposes, and for colds and sore-related applications. Other recorded uses include a hair tonic, skin applications, and a nervine for the intellect.

name: Ecballium elaterium

traditional_uses: Constipation in Greek and Arab folk medicine

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Ecballium elaterium, a member of the Cucurbitaceae family, was traditionally recorded for cathartic and purgative purposes in Turkey, Greece, and Spain. Its use was also noted for dropsy, a term for fluid retention, and for nephritis, or kidney inflammation. These applications reflect a historical practice of using the plant to promote bowel cleansing and address fluid-related conditions.

name: Elaeagnus Umbellata

old.description: Shrub native to China, Japan, and Korea used in traditional medicine for its antioxidant-rich fruits and leaves with anti-inflammatory and antidiarrheal properties.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Elaeagnus umbellata belongs to the family Elaeagnaceae, and its use was recorded in India. Traditionally recorded for astringent, cardiac, cough, lung, and stimulant applications, the plant's medicinal profile groups respiratory and cardiac uses alongside a general stimulant and astringent role. The astringent quality is noted separately from the lung and cough applications, while the cardiac and stimulant labels point to uses for circulation and vitality. These five applications together reflect the plant's recorded place in regional practice.

name: Elaeis guineensis

description: Elaeis guineensis, a palm in the family Arecaceae, has traditional use recorded in Nigeria, Turkey, Nc, and Haiti. The most frequent therapeutic theme is pain relief, with applications traditionally recorded for headache and as an anodyne. Other uses include an aphrodisiac, a hair oil, and a role in witchcraft. These applications reflect the plant's place in local practice rather than proven medical effects.

name: Embelia Ribes

old.description: Woody climber of South and Southeast Asia used in Ayurvedic medicine as the primary anthelmintic herb for intestinal worm expulsion.

image.credit: Earthshine.. at English Wikipedia — Public domain

description: Embelia ribes, in the family Myrsinaceae, has recorded traditional use in India, Java, Iran, Sanscrit, Malaya, and the United States. It was traditionally recorded for digestive complaints such as diarrhea and stomachic and carminative purposes, as well as for cough and chest applications. Other recorded uses include fever, skin and ringworm conditions, and as an anthelminthic, taenifuge, and vermifuge. It was also listed as an alterative, astringent, diuretic, stimulant, and tonic.

name: Elecampane Root

old.description: A tall European and Asian perennial; alantolactone and isoalantolactone are the first sesquiterpene lactones shown to have antibiotic activity; classic respiratory herb.
traditional_uses: Chronic bronchitis and respiratory catarrh in Europe

provenance.notes: Automatically matched to: Commission E. No PubMed citations yet.

description: Elecampane root, a member of the Asteraceae family, has been traditionally recorded for cough and lung complaints, including bronchitis, asthma and pertussis. Its use is documented across China, Turkey, Europe, Argentina, India and the United Kingdom. Related applications group around clearing the respiratory tract, such as expectorant, diaphoretic and sudorific uses, alongside digestive purposes including stomachic, carminative, laxative and cholagogue. Other recorded uses include antiseptic and tonic applications, skin and wound care, and the expulsion of worms.

old.description: Melon seeds from West Africa used medicinally for hypertension, diabetes, and as protein-rich nutritive food medicine.

description: Enterolobium cyclocarpum, known commonly as the ear pod tree, is a member of the Fabaceae family. Its use has been recorded in Mexico, Guatemala, Venezuela, Haiti, and the Dominican Republic. Traditionally, it has been recorded for bronchitis, chest complaints, colds, and tuberculosis, with the most distinctive application being for tuberculosis. These applications group into respiratory conditions affecting the chest and bronchial passages.

name: Entada phaseoloides

old.description: Tropical coastal legume with huge seed pods; bark used as soap substitute and in folk medicine for hair and wounds.

description: Entada phaseoloides, a member of the Fabaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal uses across India, Java, Malaya, the Philippines, South Africa, and Malaysia. Its applications often center on digestive complaints, with records for abdominal issues, enterosis, and hematochezia, as well as its use as an emetic and vermifuge. The plant is also traditionally recorded for inflammatory conditions, including sores, swelling, and wounds, and for malaria and parturition. Other documented uses include a tonic, a shampoo, and a source of water or water vine.

name: Ephedra distachya

old.description: A European ephedra with lower ephedrine content; used in folk medicine for respiratory and urinary conditions.

description: Ephedra distachya, known as sea grape, is a member of the Ephedraceae family. Its use was recorded in Russia and Japan, where it was traditionally recorded for scabies, a distinctive application in its record. Other applications include cough suppression and chest complaints, as well as sweating promotion and fever reduction. The plant was also traditionally recorded for syphilis.

name: Ephedra equisetina

old.description: A Chinese ephedra species from dry regions; similar ephedrine content to E. sinica.

provenance.notes: 1 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Ephedra equisetina, a plant in the family Ephedraceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in China and Japan. Its main applications center on the respiratory system, where it was documented for cough, cold, and dyspnea, as well as for its antitussive and diaphoretic properties. Other recorded uses include the relief of fever and typhoid, the management of arthritis and swelling, and anodyne and febrifuge purposes.

name: Ephedra intermedia

old.description: Central Asian ephedra species used in Chinese and Mongolian medicine; contains ephedrine alkaloids.

description: Ephedra intermedia, known as intermediate jointfir, is a plant in the family Ephedraceae. Its use was recorded in China. Traditionally recorded for fever, colds, cough, and dyspnea, it was also used for arthritis, swelling, and as an anodyne. Other applications include typhoid and use as an adulterant.

name: Equisetum telmateia

old.description: Largest European horsetail with high silica content; used similarly to E. arvense for mineral supplementation.

description: Equisetum telmateia belongs to the family Equisetaceae, and its use has been recorded in Canada and Spain. Traditionally, it has been recorded for a diuretic purpose, as well as for the care of sores and wounds. These applications group into internal and external uses, with the latter focusing on skin injuries.

name: Ephedra sinica

old.description: An ancient Chinese herb containing ephedrine; used for respiratory conditions; now regulated due to cardiovascular risks.

provenance.notes: 1 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Ephedra sinica, in the family Ephedraceae, is a plant whose use has been recorded in China and Japan. It is traditionally recorded for respiratory complaints such as cough, bronchitis, trachitis, asthma, and dyspnea, as well as for colds, flu, and fever. Other recorded applications include arthritis, edema, swelling, and oliguria, along with sweating-related uses like diaphoretic and night-sweat. It is also noted as an anodyne and for hayfever, typhoid, and lung-related purposes.

name: Erigeron canadensis

description: Erigeron canadensis, a member of the Asteraceae family, has recorded uses in the United States, Turkey, Africa, Lesotho, and Iraq. It is traditionally recorded for astringent and hemostatic purposes, including hemorrhage and metrorrhagia, as well as for parturition and uterine and urogenital applications. Other documented uses include respiratory conditions such as bronchitis, catarrh, and sore throat, and urinary and kidney complaints including cystitis, dropsy, and diuretic use. It is also traditionally recorded for diarrhea, dysentery, piles, eczema, ringworm, gonorrhea, and as a sedative and tonic.

description: Buerger's Pipewort is a plant in the family Eriocaulaceae, traditionally recorded in China for a range of medicinal applications. Among these, its use for eye complaints is the most distinctive, with the plant traditionally recorded for nyctalopia, ophthalmia, and eye ache. It is also traditionally recorded for fever and for headache and toothache, grouping these pain related uses together.

name: Eritrean Rue

old.description: Sacred plant of Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Christians used medicinally as antispasmodic and abortifacient herb.

description: Eritrean rue was traditionally recorded for eye complaints, sores, spasms, and as a vermifuge. It belongs to the Rutaceae family, and its use was documented in the Mediterranean region and Morocco. The plant was applied to eye and skin problems, and was also used to address muscle spasms and intestinal worms.

description: Eruca sativa, a member of the Brassicaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in the United States. Its applications include support for liver sclerosis and scurvy, alongside uses as a diuretic and stomachic. The plant has also been noted as a stimulant, a vesicant, and a rubefacient, with cyanogenetic properties documented.

name: Erva Cidreira

old.description: Aromatic Lippia species of tropical America used from Mexico to Argentina for anxiety, insomnia, digestive conditions, and as lemon-scented herbal tea.
traditional_uses: Anxiety and insomnia in Brazilian and Mexican folk medicine

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Erva Cidreira, a member of the Verbenaceae family, is traditionally recorded for digestive complaints, which appear most often among its uses. Across Trinidad, Panama, Curacao, Haiti, Brazil, and Paraguay, it has been documented for stomach ache, stomachic and stomach uses, dyspepsia, colitis, and general digestive support. Related applications include colds, chest colds, cough, flu, and fever, as well as hepatitis, alongside nervine, sedative, and spasm uses. It is also recorded as a pectoral, sudorific, and simply as a medicine or tea.

name: Eryngium foetidum

old.description: Tropical American and Caribbean Apiaceae with strong coriander scent; used medidinally for fever, convulsions, and digestive complaints.

description: Eryngium foetidum, a member of the Apiaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for a broad range of applications, with digestive complaints appearing most frequently. Its use is documented in Trinidad, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Venezuela, Panama, and Malaya, where it was recorded for stomach and intestinal issues such as colic, constipation, and stomach complaints, as well as for colds, coughs, flu, and pneumonia. Other recorded uses include fever and malaria, rheumatic and arthritic pain, and a variety of other purposes, from scurvy to hypertension and diabetes. The plant was also traditionally recorded in contexts involving witchcraft and as a panacea.
traditional_uses: Digestive complaints such as colic and constipation

The plant was further recorded as a cardiotonic and stimulant, as well as an emetic and parasiticide, and it was traditionally recorded for malaria.

description: Eupatorium fortunei, a member of the Asteraceae family, is traditionally recorded for use in China, with a notably distinctive application for tapeworm. Its medicinal applications include addressing worm infestations such as ascariasis, filariasis, and helminthiasis, as well as fever, flu, measles, and hepatitis. The plant has also been traditionally recorded for digestive complaints like anorexia, nausea, and halitosis, and for respiratory issues such as chest congestion and headache. Additional uses include as a diuretic, a refrigerant, a decoagulant, and a preventative, with an aperitif and alexiteric role also noted.

Its use has been documented across India, Africa, China, Samoa, Trinidad and Upper Volta. Traditional records include respiratory complaints such as asthma, bronchitis, catarrh, cough and flu, alongside digestive issues like colic, dysentery, enteritis and nausea. Skin applications cover athlete's foot, ringworm, itch, dermatosis, eruptions and bruises, while other uses include fever, conjunctivitis, ophthalmia and post-natal care.

description: Euphorbia lathyris, commonly known as caper spurge, is a member of the Euphorbiaceae family. Its ethnobotanical record includes uses from China, Turkey, Argentina, Spain, France, and Japan. The most distinctive application is for melanoma, a use that stands apart from the others. Other recorded uses include antiseptic and skin applications for sores and warts, as well as internal uses as a diuretic, emetic, and purgative, with diarrhea also noted. The plant has also been recorded in connection with gangrene and sore throat, and as a coffee substitute and for corn.

These applications reflect its historical use in folk practices across these regions.

The remaining uses cluster around skin and digestive complaints: abscesses, corns, pimples, and excrescences on the skin, as well as diarrhea and enteritis. All of these are traditionally recorded applications rather than confirmed medical uses.

Other recorded uses include pain relief for arthralgia, backache, neuralgia, and as a general analgesic, as well as astringent and tonic purposes for diarrhea, spermatorrhea, polyuria, and as a restorative. It has also been traditionally recorded for fever, thirst, hernia, placenta-related uses, gonorrhea, and as a deobstruent, a term for clearing obstructions.

The plant was also documented as an analgesic, a tonic, and a blood-related remedy, and was used as an antiseptic and parasiticide. Other recorded applications include stimulating appetite and serving as a refrigerant.

The plant was also recorded for women's health concerns, including female complaints, menorrhagia, and as a lactagogue, and for inflammatory and infectious conditions such as abscesses, sores, pimples, and venereal disease. Additional applications include the treatment of snake bite, convulsions, paralysis, cough, cold, eye and ear complaints, toothache, and as an astringent, diuretic, laxative, vermifuge, and anodyne.

Other recorded uses include digestive complaints such as colic and as an apertif, alongside remedies for cough, fever, and headache, as well as diuretic, emetic, and vermifuge actions.

Digestive and respiratory purposes also appear, including colic, bronchitis, croup, and as a laxative, while other recorded uses range from an aphrodisiac to a vermifuge.

The plant also appears in records for rheumatism, smallpox, and otitis, reflecting a broad range of traditional applications.

The plant was also traditionally recorded for skin and soft tissue problems including abscesses, corns, warts, pimples, and scrofula, and for oral and throat issues such as sore throat, gingivitis, and stomatitis. Other recorded uses include measles, as a vermifuge, and as a disinfectant, fumigant, and rennet.
