Other recorded uses include memory and amnesia, apprehension and nerves, and a restorative or tonic role, alongside rheumatism, arthritis, lumbago, fever, diarrhea, and circulation. A smaller set of records concerns virility and aphrodisiac use, and carminative purposes.

name: Gelsemium elegans

old.description: Poisonous vine of Southeast Asia used in TCM in minute controlled doses for pain and cancer treatment.
traditional_uses: Traditional Chinese medicine Gou Wen for pain and skin cancer
Used in Southeast Asian folk medicine in controlled doses

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Gelsemium elegans, a member of the Loganiaceae family, has a traditional record that includes the most distinctive application of homicide. Its use was recorded in China, Borneo, Asia, and India. The plant was traditionally recorded for pain relief in neuralgia and rheumatism, and for cough, skin eruptions, sores, wounds, and scrofula. Other applications include caked breast, perspiration, and fatality, with suicide also noted.

name: Genista tinctoria

old.description: European shrub with isoflavones and sparteine; traditional diuretic and lymphatic herb.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Genista tinctoria, a member of the Fabaceae family, has recorded traditional use in Turkey, the United States, Spain, and the United Kingdom. Its applications include promoting urine flow and bowel movements, with diuretic, laxative, and purgative uses grouped together. Other recorded uses are as an emetic to induce vomiting, a sudorific to encourage sweating, and a home remedy, along with a use for a wen.

name: German Iris

old.description: Rhizomes of Iris germanica have been used in traditional perfumery and medicine for centuries, prized for the violet-scented irone compounds.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: German Iris, a member of the Iridaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Egypt, Turkey, Spain, and Greece. Its applications center on the respiratory system, with uses for colds, bronchitis, and as an expectorant. The plant is also noted for promoting bowel movements, including laxative, purgative, cathartic, and emetic actions, as well as for supporting digestion as a stomachic and stimulant. Additional recorded uses include diuretic and cholagogue effects, and applications for sciatica, sclerosis, and splenitis.

name: Glaucium flavum

old.description: European coastal herb with glaucine alkaloid; antitussive properties; glaucine used in cough medicines.

description: Glaucium flavum, a member of the Papaveraceae family, was traditionally recorded for uses in Spain and France. It was employed as a purgative and hydragogue, applications that promote bowel movements and fluid expulsion. The plant also served as a sedative and was used as an adulterant, while its application to warts reflects a distinct external use.

name: Germander

old.description: A European herb once popular for gout and weight loss, now known to cause hepatotoxicity — a cautionary tale.

description: Germander is a plant in the Lamiaceae family, and its use has been recorded across Turkey, Eurasia, Europe, France, Iraq, and Spain. Traditionally, it has been recorded for a wide range of applications, including as a tonic and stimulant, as well as for digestive complaints and as a diuretic. It has also been noted for fever, gout, rheumatism, and skin-related conditions such as scrofula and fibroma. Other recorded uses include its role as an astringent, antiseptic, and vermifuge.

name: Glycyrrhiza echinata

old.description: Eastern European and Central Asian licorice species used in Russian folk medicine and Unani tradition.

description: Glycyrrhiza echinata, a member of the Fabaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in China, Japan, and Greece. Its applications center on respiratory relief, with antitussive, expectorant, and demulcent uses noted for coughs and throat irritation. Other recorded uses include anodyne and antispasmodic properties for pain and spasms, as well as tonic and alterative roles for general health and rejuvenation. Fever, thirst, and minor sores also appear among the traditional applications.

name: Gloriosa superba

old.description: Spectacular climbing lily of tropical Africa and Asia with crimson-yellow flowers, highly toxic colchicine source.
traditional_uses: Traditional African and Indian medicine for gout and pain in tiny doses
Used as pesticide and poison in parts of Africa

image.credit: Macvivo at English Wikipedia (Original text: Samwise Gamgee) — CC BY-SA 3.0

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Gloriosa superba, a plant in the Liliaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal and other applications across India, Thailand, Malaysia, and Africa, with historical references also noted in Hindu and Sanskrit contexts. Its recorded uses include treatment for skin conditions such as scabies, erysipelas, leprosy, piles, and sores, as well as remedies for snake bite, malaria, gonorrhea, and syphilis. The plant was also documented as a laxative, stomachic, tonic, and for labor and parturition, alongside uses as a vermifuge and pediculicide. Notably, records also associate it with homicide and suicide, reflecting a complex and potentially dangerous profile.
traditional_uses: Skin conditions including scabies and leprosy

name: Glycyrrhiza lepidota

old.description: A North American licorice used by Native American tribes for coughs, fever, and as a food source.

description: Glycyrrhiza lepidota, a member of the Fabaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications in the United States. Its uses included relief for coughs, sore throats, and fevers, as well as an expectorant to help clear respiratory passages. The plant was also applied to arthritis, rheumatism, and backache, and was used as a poultice for localized pain such as earache and toothache. Other recorded applications include afterbirth and placenta, and internal ulcers.

name: Gmelina Arborea

old.description: Fast-growing deciduous tree of tropical Asia, one of the Dashamoola herbs in Ayurveda used as a tonic, diuretic, and treatment for various systemic conditions.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Gmelina arborea, a member of the Lamiaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in India across a wide range of applications. The most frequent theme in the record is the management of fever and related serious conditions, including asthma, bronchitis, and septicemia. Other recorded uses include digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dyspepsia, and cholera, as well as neurological and mental disturbances like convulsion, epilepsy, and delirium. The plant is also noted for its use in bites and stings, skin and soft tissue swellings, and a variety of other ailments, reflecting a broad ethnobotanical role.

old.description: Creeping aromatic perennial of European meadows and hedgerows, used in traditional medicine and historic brewing.
traditional_uses: Traditional European remedy for coughs and respiratory conditions
Used in historic ale brewing before hops

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

name: Goat Rue

old.description: A European herb that inspired the development of metformin; guanidine compounds (galegine) reduce blood sugar through AMPK activation; used for diabetes and lactation enhancement.
traditional_uses: Diabetes management in European folk medicine

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Goat Rue is a plant in the Fabaceae family, traditionally recorded for diabetes in Turkey and Spain. Its applications also include promoting milk flow in nursing mothers, as a diuretic and diaphoretic to increase urine and sweating, and as a tonic and astringent. Other traditional uses address spasms and intestinal worms.

name: Gobernadora

old.description: Sonoran Desert shrub used by Native Americans and Mexican communities for pain, infections, and cancer; highly controversial due to hepatotoxicity risk.

description: Gobernadora, a member of the Zygophyllaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for wound care and skin complaints such as bruises, chafing, and sores. Its use is documented in Mexico and the United States, where it was also applied to joint and muscle conditions including arthritis, rheumatism, and knee discomfort. Other recorded applications include digestive issues like diarrhea and gastritis, as well as urinary concerns such as dysuria and as a diuretic. The plant was additionally noted for antiseptic, emetic, and venereal uses, and for intestinal and tuberculous conditions.

name: Gou Ji

old.description: TCM tree fern used to strengthen the Kidney and lower back; prescribed for weakness of the lumbar spine, incontinence, and vaginal discharge.

image.credit: From Svenska Familj-Journalen, Vol. 18, 1879 — Public domain

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Gou Ji was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications, including the relief of pain and the management of joint and muscle complaints. It belongs to the family Dicksoniaceae, and its use was recorded in China and Malaya. The applications include analgesic and hemostatic purposes, as well as tonic and vermifuge uses. It was also traditionally recorded for arthritis, rheumatism, lumbago, and backache, and for trauma, wounds, and numbness.

name: Gou Teng

old.description: TCM herb used to calm liver wind and clear heat; used with Tian Ma for headache, dizziness, hypertension, and epilepsy.

description: Gou Teng, in the family Pedaliaceae, has been traditionally recorded in China for a range of applications that centre on the nervous system. It was used as a sedative and antispasmodic, and was recorded for convulsions, vertigo, and headache. Other traditional uses include hypertension, fever, and complaints of the liver, including hepatitis and bilious conditions. It was also recorded for dysentery, cold, flushing, apoplexy, and support during the puerperium, with an additional astringent application.

name: Gratiola officinalis

old.description: Gratiola officinalis appears in 9 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

provenance.limitations: LNHPD publishes no per-product indication, so uses are empty rather than invented.

description: Gratiola officinalis was traditionally recorded for its diuretic, emetic, and purgative effects, and for an enlarged spleen. It belongs to the family Scrophulariaceae, and its use was recorded in Turkey, Spain, and possibly Poland. The applications group around promoting urine and bowel movements, inducing vomiting, and addressing splenomegaly.

name: Greater Galangal

old.description: Already entered as galangal-root — distinct entry for emphasis on its anticancer and digestive properties researched in modern medicine.

description: Greater Galangal is a plant in the Zingiberaceae family whose use has been recorded in India, Turkey, Java, and the United States. It is traditionally recorded for digestive complaints, including carminative, stomachic, and digestive applications, as well as for respiratory conditions such as bronchitis, catarrh, and expectorant use. Other recorded applications include rheumatism, ringworm, splenomegaly, parturition, and use as a stimulant and for cardiodepressant purposes.

name: Griffonia Simplicifolia

old.description: A West African climbing shrub whose seeds contain 5-HTP (5-hydroxytryptophan), the direct precursor to serotonin; clinically effective for depression, anxiety, insomnia, and appetite control.
traditional_uses: Mood enhancement and anti-depressant in West African folk medicine

description: Griffonia simplicifolia was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications, including wound care, digestive complaints, and other conditions. It belongs to the Fabaceae family, and its use was recorded in Africa, West Africa, and Ivory Coast. The main applications include antiseptic and wound-related uses, as well as digestive issues such as diarrhea, nausea, and constipation, for which it was used as a laxative and purgative. Other recorded uses include an aphrodisiac, a treatment for chancre, congestion, and as a pediculicide.

name: Grifola Umbellata

old.description: A diuretic medicinal mushroom used in TCM for edema, urinary conditions, and immune support.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Grifola umbellata is a fungus traditionally recorded in China for a small set of medicinal applications. Its most distinctive use is as a diuretic, a purpose that relates to the other two applications in its record: edema and diarrhea. The plant's family is not recorded. All uses are traditional and are not claims of proven efficacy.

name: Gromwell

old.description: Perennial of European roadsides; seeds used in folk medicine as diuretic; roots studied for contraceptive properties and anti-gonadotropic effects.
traditional_uses: Historical contraceptive use (Shoshone tribe in North America)

image.credit: Kristian Peters -- Fabelfroh 09:04, 21 February 2007 (UTC) — CC BY-SA 3.0

description: Gromwell, a member of the Boraginaceae family, has recorded use in Iraq, China, Japan, Turkey, Spain, and Europe. Traditionally, it was recorded for fever and measles, as well as for skin eruptions, itching, and smallpox. Its applications also include bladder and kidney complaints, kidney stones, and gout, along with use as a sedative, contraceptive, and blood purifier.

name: Guayusa

old.description: An Amazonian holly tree related to yerba mate, traditionally used by Kichwa for lucid dreaming and sustained energy.

description: Guayusa, a member of the Aquifoliaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of applications in Ecuador and Colombia. Its uses include stimulant and narcotic effects, as well as digestive, stomach, and diuretic purposes. It was also recorded for amenorrhea, fertility, and venereal complaints, and as a diaphoretic, expectorant, and emetic. Additional applications include chill, mouthwash, divination, and as a stimulant.

old.description: South Asian tiliaceae fruit shrub used in Ayurveda and Unani medicine for cooling, digestive, and respiratory conditions.
traditional_uses: cooling summer drink in South Asian folk medicine

image.credit: Asit K. Ghosh Thaumaturgist — CC BY-SA 3.0

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

name: Guduchi

old.description: Called Amrita (nectar of immortality) in Ayurveda, guduchi is a potent immunomodulator and rejuvenative herb used for fever, liver disorders, and diabetes.

image.credit: Tmd at Thai Wikipedia — Public domain

description: Guduchi belongs to the Menispermaceae family and has been traditionally recorded for use in India, China, Sanscrit, Malaysia, and the United States. Its applications include fever, malaria, and tuberculosis, as well as liver and jaundice related uses. Other recorded uses are for inflammation, rheumatism, gout, and skin sores such as erysipelas, along with leprosy. The plant has also been noted as a tonic, stimulant, sedative, diuretic, emetic, stomachic, aphrodisiac, and bactericide, and for asthma.

name: Gurjun Balsam

old.description: South and Southeast Asian tree oleoresin used for respiratory and skin conditions.

description: Gurjun Balsam is traditionally recorded for gonorrhea, a distinctive application in its record. This plant belongs to the family Dipterocarpaceae, and its use has been documented in India and the United States. Other traditional applications group around skin conditions, including leprosy and psoriasis, as well as general skin uses.

name: Gumweed

old.description: North American herb used by indigenous peoples for respiratory conditions and poison ivy rash treatment.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Gumweed, a member of the Asteraceae family, has been traditionally recorded for a wide range of therapeutic uses in the United States. The most frequent applications relate to the respiratory system, including cough, cold, bronchitis, asthma, pertussis, and pneumonia, often with expectorant and antitussive purposes. Other recorded uses address inflammatory and rheumatic conditions such as arthritis and rheumatism, as well as fevers, stomach ache, and various internal organs including the kidney, liver, and lung. Additional traditional applications include rash, smallpox, tuberculosis, gonorrhea, syphilis, and urogenital concerns, along with spasm and stimulant effects.

name: Hai Jin Sha

old.description: TCM spore that clears heat and promotes urination for stones.

image.credit: harum.koh from Kobe city, Japan — CC BY-SA 2.0

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Hai Jin Sha is a plant in the family Schizaeaceae, with recorded use in China. It has been traditionally recorded for fever and cold, as well as for inflammatory conditions. Its applications also include urinary and kidney concerns such as dysuria, hematuria, edema, nephritis, and stones, along with uses as a diuretic, expectorant, and cathartic.

name: Haematoxylum campechianum

old.description: Central American tree; heartwood red dye source; bark used in folk medicine for diarrhea and fever.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Haematoxylum campechianum, a member of the Fabaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for uses across China, India, Mexico, Haiti, Venezuela, and Turkey. The most frequent theme in its applications is the control of bleeding and tissue repair, with uses recorded for trauma, sores, gangrene, bedsores, and as a hemostat. Other documented applications include astringent and antiseptic actions, as well as uses for diarrhea, dysentery, and dyspepsia. It has also been traditionally recorded for amenorrhea, leucorrhea, and the puerperium period.

name: Harshingar

old.description: Indian tree with flowers and leaves used in Ayurveda and folk medicine for fever and rheumatism.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Harshingar was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications, including fever, bilious complaints, and rheumatism. It belongs to the Verbenaceae family, and its use was recorded in Java and China. The plant was also valued as a tonic and for its cholagogue, diaphoretic, diuretic, and laxative properties, which together reflect a broad role in traditional practice.

name: He Ye

old.description: TCM herb from lotus leaf used to clear Summer-Heat, stop bleeding, and reduce obesity; prescribed for heat stroke, bleeding disorders, and weight management.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

taxonomy.reason: removed preparation/cultivar qualifier from a taxon field; qualifier carries no taxonomic meaning

description: He Ye, a member of the Nelumbonaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in China, India and Egypt. Its applications center on bleeding control, including hemorrhage, hemostasis, epistaxis, hemoptysis, hematemesis, hematuria and hematochezia, along with a coagulant-related use. Digestive and intestinal complaints also feature prominently, such as diarrhea, dysentery, enteritis, dyspepsia, cholera and abdominal conditions, alongside antiemetic and demulcent purposes. Other recorded uses include fever, heart and circulation concerns, insomnia and neurasthenia, labor and post-partum care, and applications for complexion and hair.

name: Haemanthus coccineus

old.description: South African bulb with brilliant scarlet flower heads, traditional Khoikhoi medicine plant.
traditional_uses: Traditional Khoikhoi and Cape Coloured folk medicine for colds and fevers
Used in South African folk medicine for infections and pain

provenance.notes: 1 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Haemanthus coccineus was traditionally recorded for asthma and related respiratory complaints, as well as for conditions involving fluid retention. It belongs to the family Liliaceae. Its applications include use as a diuretic and for dropsy, both connected to the elimination of excess fluid. The plant was also recorded as an expectorant, a use that aligns with its application for asthma.

name: Heather

old.description: Iconic Scottish and European moorland shrub used in traditional folk medicine for urinary infections, arthritis, cough, and insomnia. Sacred to Celtic peoples.

description: Heather, a member of the Ericaceae family, has recorded uses in Turkey, Europe and Spain. It is traditionally recorded for urogenital and bladder complaints, with diuretic and depurative actions noted alongside these applications. Other recorded uses include antiseptic and astringent purposes, as well as relief of inflammation and rheumatism. The plant also appears in records for sedative and narcotic effects, including use for insomnia.

name: Hedera helix

old.description: A European climbing plant with ivy leaf extract well-studied for bronchitis and respiratory conditions.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Ivy (Hedera helix), the only species name recorded for this plant in the Araliaceae family, has a traditional use record that includes Turkey, India, Iraq, France, South Africa, and Italy. Among its most distinctive applications is the treatment of corns, warts, and wens, alongside uses for toothache and nasal polyps. The plant was also traditionally recorded for rheumatism, uterine sclerosis, and various types of swelling. Other applications include digestive stimulants and laxatives, as well as emetic, cathartic, and vermifuge actions, while its astringent, antiseptic, and diaphoretic properties were noted for skin and systemic balance.

old.description: TCM uses the flower spike as Xia Ku Cao for liver fire and thyroid conditions; cooling and anti-inflammatory. The dried flower spikes of self-heal used in TCM to clear liver fire and dissipate phlegm nodules — important for thyroid and lymph node conditions.

name: Hedychium Coronarium

old.description: Fragrant ginger family flower from Asia and Americas used in folk medicine for headache, fever, and anti-inflammatory conditions.
traditional_uses: headache and fever remedy in Asian folk medicine

description: Hedychium coronarium, known as the ginger lily, is a member of the Zingiberaceae family. Its use has been recorded in India, China, Hawaii, Java, Indonesia, and the United States. The most distinctive application in its record is for the nostrils, alongside uses for the throat such as gargle, sore throat, tonsillitis, and halitosis. Other traditional applications include carminative, stomachic, and tonic purposes, as well as for rheumatism, rhinitis, and swelling.

old.description: A tropical climbing vine whose extract is used in European dermatology as a cortisone-free anti-inflammatory for eczema.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

name: Helenium autumnale

old.description: North American Asteraceae used by Native Americans as sneezing powder and for respiratory conditions.
traditional_uses: Respiratory conditions in Native American medicine

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Sneezeweed, Helenium autumnale, is a member of the Asteraceae family, and its use was recorded in the United States. The most distinctive application in its record is as a sternutatory, a substance that provokes sneezing. It was also traditionally recorded for colds, hayfever, and as a decongestant, grouping these respiratory complaints together. Additionally, it was used as a vermifuge, a traditional term for an agent intended to expel intestinal worms.

name: Hedyotis Herb

old.description: Major TCM cancer-support herb that clears heat and fire toxin, promotes urination, and dispels blood stasis. One of the most commonly used herbs in traditional Chinese cancer formulas.

description: Hedyotis Herb, of the Rubiaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of applications across India, China, Singapore, and the Philippines. Its uses include fevers such as malaria, digestive complaints like biliousness and gastritis, and blood-related purposes. The plant was also recorded for debility, depression, and support of the nerves, as well as for conditions of the liver and spleen including hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Other traditional applications include gonorrhea, lymphadenitis, toothache, and care during the puerperium.

name: Hedyosmum brasiliense

old.description: Shrub or small tree of Brazilian Atlantic forest, used in Brazilian folk medicine for neurological conditions.
traditional_uses: Traditional Brazilian medicine for headaches and neurological conditions
Used in Atlantic forest folk medicine for anxiety and pain

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Hedyosmum brasiliense belongs to the family Chloranthaceae and is recorded from Brazil, where its use has been documented. The plant is traditionally recorded for stomachic and tonic purposes, reflecting a role in supporting digestive comfort and general vitality. It also appears as a sudorific, a use associated with promoting sweating, and as an aphrodisiac. These applications are grouped around digestive, restorative, and stimulant related practices.

name: Helianthus tuberosus

old.description: Helianthus tuberosus appears in 18 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

provenance.limitations: LNHPD publishes no per-product indication, so uses are empty rather than invented.

description: Helianthus tuberosus, a member of the Asteraceae family, has been traditionally recorded for uses in Turkey, Iraq, and Spain. Its applications cluster around reproductive and hormonal themes, with records for androgenic, aphrodisiac, and spermatogenic purposes. Other documented uses include digestive support as an aperient, stomachic, and tonic, alongside cholagogue and diuretic actions. The plant is also traditionally recorded for diabetes and rheumatism.

name: Helichrysum arenarium

old.description: Eastern European Asteraceae used for liver, gallbladder, and digestive conditions.
traditional_uses: Liver conditions in Eastern European folk medicine

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Helichrysum arenarium, a member of the Asteraceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Turkey and Europe. Its main medicinal applications center on the digestive system, where it was used as a cholagogue to promote bile flow and as a diuretic to increase urine output. Other recorded uses include an astringent action and the expulsion of worms.

name: Helleborus viridis

old.description: Helleborus viridis appears in 4 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

provenance.limitations: LNHPD publishes no per-product indication, so uses are empty rather than invented.

description: Green hellebore (Helleborus viridis), a member of the Ranunculaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Turkey, Spain, and Europe. Its most distinctive application is as a sternutatory, a substance that induces sneezing. Other recorded uses include cardiac and diuretic applications, as well as use as a nervine. These applications reflect the plant's historical role in folk medicine, though its effects are not supported by modern evidence.

name: Helminthostachys zeylanica

old.description: Helminthostachys zeylanica appears in 4 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

provenance.limitations: LNHPD publishes no per-product indication, so uses are empty rather than invented.

description: Helminthostachys zeylanica, the sole name recorded for this plant in the family Ophioglossaceae, has a traditional record that includes its use as an intoxicant, a distinctive application among its medicinal uses. Its use was recorded in Java, India, Malaya, Malaysia, Tapah, and China. The plant was traditionally recorded for fevers and malaria, as well as for catarrh, pertussis, and phthisis, which is an older term for tuberculosis. Other recorded applications include dysentery, syphilis, sciatica, and general tonic and anodyne purposes.

old.description: Mediterranean weed with historical uses for skin ulcers and warts; significant hepatotoxicity risk.

name: Helonias dioica

old.description: Helonias dioica appears in 27 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 6 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

provenance.limitations: LNHPD publishes no per-product indication, so uses are empty rather than invented.

description: Helonias dioica belongs to the family Liliaceae. Traditionally recorded applications include use as an alterative, a diuretic, a tonic, and a vermifuge. It has also been recorded for leucorrhea. These uses group into general restorative and cleansing purposes, urinary and reproductive support, and the expulsion of intestinal worms.

name: Hemp Agrimony

old.description: A European wetland herb used for immune support and liver conditions, the Old World counterpart to boneset.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Hemp Agrimony, a member of the Asteraceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Turkey, Spain, Indochina, Hungary, Belgium, and Iraq. Its applications include digestive and liver related purposes such as aperitif, bilious, cathartic, cholagogue, emetic, and laxative, along with diuretic and dropsy uses. It is also recorded for fever and flu, catarrh, scurvy, and as a tonic, alterative, and depurative. Additional traditional uses include anodyne, nervine, vermifuge, and vulnerary applications for sores.

name: Herb Paris

old.description: European woodland plant with highly toxic berries used historically in European folk medicine for nervous conditions and as an antidote.
traditional_uses: Nervous conditions and spasm historically in European folk medicine
Eye conditions topically in medieval practice

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Herb Paris belongs to the Liliaceae family and has been recorded in Europe, Turkey, China, Spain and Germany. Traditionally recorded for gout, rheumatism and neuralgia, it has also been noted for headache, palpitation and spasm. Other applications include use as an emetic, purgative and narcotic, as well as for longevity, hair blackening and homeopathy. A preventive use is also documented.

name: Herb Bennet

old.description: Variant form of wood avens with similar clove-scented root properties used throughout European folk medicine for digestive and antimicrobial conditions.
traditional_uses: Digestive conditions in European folk medicine

description: Herb Bennet, a member of the Rosaceae family, has been traditionally recorded in France, Germany, Turkey, Europe, India, and Iraq for applications centered on digestive and systemic balance. Its uses include digestive complaints such as dyspepsia, constipation, diarrhea, and dysentery, along with stomachic and tonic roles for debility. The plant was also recorded for fever and chill patterns, including ague and malaria, and for respiratory and oral concerns like catarrh, sore throat, and halitosis. Additional traditional applications include astringent, antiseptic, and sedative actions, as well as uses for leucorrhea and hypochondria.

name: Hibiscus Flowers

old.description: Tropical ornamental hibiscus used medicinally across Africa, Asia, and Latin America for hair health, diabetes, and as a blood purifier. Different from Hibiscus sabdariffa.

image.file: Chinese hibiscus (Hibiscus × rosa-sinensis) flower, Estufa Fria, Lisbon, Portugal julesvernex2.jpg
image.credit: Jules Verne Times Two — CC BY-SA 4.0

description: Hibiscus flowers, of the Malvaceae family, are recorded for use in Samoa, Iraq, Malaya, Turkey, China, and Trinidad. The flowers are traditionally recorded for respiratory complaints such as cough, cold, bronchitis, asthma, and catarrh, and for fever and flu. They also appear in records for digestive and eliminative purposes, including laxative, purgative, and aperient uses, as well as for diarrhea. Other applications include menstrual and childbirth-related concerns, eye and skin conditions, and use as a soothing demulcent or astringent.

name: Hibiscus mutabilis

old.description: Hibiscus mutabilis appears in 3 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

provenance.limitations: LNHPD publishes no per-product indication, so uses are empty rather than invented.

description: Hibiscus mutabilis belongs to the family Malvaceae, and its use has been recorded in China, Malaya, and Indonesia. Traditionally, it has been recorded for a wide range of applications, including the care of wounds, sores, burns, scalds, abscesses, fistulas, and other inflammatory swellings. It has also been used for fever and as an alexiteric, a term for a protective remedy against poisons or bites, including snake bite. Other recorded uses include cough, bronchosis, and related pectoral and expectorant purposes, as well as dysuria, menorrhagia, and general anodyne, demulcent, emollient, and refrigerant applications.

name: Hibiscus Suratensis

old.description: Prickly herb widespread in the tropical Old World used as a leafy vegetable and medicinally for respiratory conditions, wound healing, and urinary complaints.

description: Hibiscus suratensis, a member of the Malvaceae family, is traditionally recorded for cough and other pectoral complaints. Its use has been documented in India, Reunion, Indochina, and Malaya, where it is also noted as an emollient and laxative. Related applications include skin conditions such as dermatosis and sores, as well as urethritis and gonorrhea.

name: Hibiscus Sabdariffa

old.description: The deep red calyces of this tropical plant are rich in anthocyanins; one of the most clinically studied herbal teas for lowering blood pressure, rivaling some medications.
traditional_uses: Hypertension in Egyptian and Mexican traditional medicine

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Hibiscus sabdariffa (Malvaceae) is traditionally recorded for a wide range of uses in India, Turkey, Mexico, Iraq, Haiti, and the Dominican Republic. The most frequent theme is digestive and eliminatory support, with applications for dyspepsia, biliousness, and as a cholagogue and choleretic, alongside diuretic and laxative uses. It also appears as a refrigerant and fever remedy, a tonic for debility, and a sedative for the nerves, with further uses for heart and hypertension concerns. Additional recorded applications include antiseptic, astringent, and emollient actions, as well as uses for scurvy, hangover, and as a tea or coffee substitute.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Hibiscus tiliaceus, a member of the Malvaceae family, has traditional medicinal uses recorded in India, Samoa, Mexico, Haiti, Java, and Hawaii. The most frequent applications relate to the respiratory system, where it was traditionally recorded for cough, bronchitis, chest complaints, congestion, and throat issues. Other uses include the treatment of wounds, sores, boils, and skin itch, as well as remedies for fever, rheumatism, and dysentery. It was also recorded for gynecological and obstetric purposes such as labor and parturition, and as a diuretic and laxative.

name: Hierba Santa Cruz

old.description: A succulent used across Mexico and the Caribbean for wounds, burns, ulcers, and infections.

description: Hierba Santa Cruz, a member of the Crassulaceae family, is traditionally recorded for asthma, one of its most distinctive applications. Its use has been documented in the Bahamas, the Philippines, and Malaya, where it was also recorded for chest colds and fever. Other traditional applications include ear complaints, sores, strains, and headache.

name: Hippeastrum puniceum

old.description: Tropical American bulb with showy red flowers, used in Caribbean and South American folk medicine.
traditional_uses: Traditional Caribbean folk medicine for fever and inflammation
Used in Venezuelan and Colombian folk medicine for infections

description: Hippeastrum puniceum, a member of the Liliaceae family, is traditionally recorded for use in Haiti and the Dominican Republic. Its applications include a diuretic purpose and a pectoral use, which relates to the chest and respiratory system. The plant is also traditionally recorded for malaria and for spasm. These four applications represent the main medicinal uses documented for this species in the region.

old.description: A Mexican folk herb used by Huichol and Nahua peoples for wound healing and skin conditions.

name: Hollyhock

old.description: Garden plant with flowers rich in mucilage used in European and Middle Eastern folk medicine for respiratory catarrh, sore throat, and urinary tract conditions.

description: Hollyhock, a member of the Malvaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Iraq, Kurdistan, and Spain. Its applications include soothing properties for inflammation and sore throat, alongside expectorant and demulcent uses that may ease irritation. The plant is also noted as a diuretic and astringent, and has been applied for toothache and spasm-related complaints.

name: Hoheria Populnea

old.description: Small New Zealand tree used by Maori in rongoā for wounds, skin conditions, and as a soothing mucilaginous remedy.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Hoheria populnea belongs to the mallow family, Malvaceae, and its use has been recorded in New Zealand. Traditionally, it was recorded for colds, as a demulcent to soothe irritated tissues, and for eye complaints. These applications group around respiratory and soothing uses, with the eye use standing separately.

old.description: East and West African Lamiaceae herb used for epilepsy, malaria, and skin conditions.
traditional_uses: Epilepsy treatment in East African medicine

description: Hoslundia opposita, a member of the Lamiaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications across Ghana, Upper Volta, Africa, Tanzania, Kenya, and Nigeria. Its uses include the management of fevers such as yellow fever, and for digestive complaints including stomach and abdominal issues, jaundice, and liver problems. The plant was also recorded for venereal and genital conditions such as gonorrhea, blennorrhea, and cystitis, as well as for skin and mucous membrane complaints including sores, wounds, swelling, herpes, shingles, and conjunctivitis. Other recorded applications include snake bite, epilepsy, mental conditions, vertigo, colds, chest complaints, and as a diuretic, laxative, purgative, cholagogue, anodyne, and for throat sores.

Its uses include addressing the effects of alcohol, such as intoxication and inebrity, and calming nervous system disturbances like convulsions, spasms, and restlessness. The plant was also recorded as a diuretic, laxative, stomachic, and refrigerant, and for fever and applications related to the rectum.

old.description: TCM herb that clears heat, nourishes yin, and moistens dryness. Used in kidney yin deficiency formulas and to reduce excess fire. Key herb in Bai Hu Tang and Zhi Bai Di Huang Wan.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Huang Qi Zhi Mu is a plant in the Liliaceae family, with recorded use in China and Japan. It is traditionally recorded for fever and related symptoms such as thirst and sweating, as well as for cough and as an expectorant. Other applications include promoting urine flow and addressing dysuria, and easing constipation as a laxative. It has also been noted for hyperglycemia, ejaculation, skin eruptions, and for symptoms like lumbago, tinnitus, and vertigo, with sedative and soothing uses.

name: Houseleek

old.description: European succulent traditionally grown on rooftops to ward off lightning and fire. The fresh leaf juice is used topically for burns, insect stings, and skin inflammations.

description: Houseleek, a member of the Crassulaceae, has recorded traditional use in Turkey, Spain, Germany, the United Kingdom, Yugoslavia and elsewhere in Europe. It was traditionally recorded for fever and inflammation, with refrigerant and spasm-related applications also noted, and for bleeding as a hemostat. Skin and surface uses include corns, calluses, warts and bee stings, alongside astringent, detersive and wound-related applications. Further recorded uses include diuretic, depurative, alterative and vermifuge purposes, as well as toothache.

name: Hydrocotyle asiatica

description: Hydrocotyle asiatica, in the family Apiaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in Malaya, Java, and India. The most frequent theme in its applications is the relief of respiratory and febrile complaints, with asthma, bronchitis, and catarrh alongside fever. Other recorded uses include the treatment of skin and infectious conditions such as leprosy, sores, and wounds, as well as internal disorders like dysentery, dropsy, and rheumatism. The plant also appears in records for nervous system complaints including epilepsy, hysteria, and vertigo, and for urinary and liver related issues.

name: Hymenaea courbaril

description: Hymenaea courbaril, known commonly as courbaril, is a member of the Fabaceae family. Its use has been recorded in Haiti, Mexico, Panama, Venezuela, the Dominican Republic, and Honduras. Traditionally, it has been recorded for a wide range of applications, including respiratory conditions such as asthma, bronchitis, and catarrh, as well as musculoskeletal complaints like arthritis, rheumatism, and fractures. It has also been noted for digestive issues, including diarrhea, dyspepsia, and indigestion, and for various types of sores, ulcers, and mouth complaints. Other recorded uses include as a vermifuge, for malaria, and for headache.

name: Hydrocotyle vulgaris

old.description: A European wetland plant related to gotu kola; used in folk medicine for skin conditions and digestive complaints.

description: Hydrocotyle vulgaris, known by its common name marsh pennywort, has a traditional record that includes wound healing as a distinctive application. This plant belongs to the Apiaceae family, and its use was recorded in Spain and the United Kingdom. The main medicinal applications traditionally recorded for marsh pennywort group into two related areas: it was used as a depurative and diuretic, and also as a purgative and sudorific, while a separate application was as a vulnerary for wound care. These uses reflect a historical practice of employing the plant for cleansing and eliminative purposes as well as for external skin support.

description: Hypericum japonicum, in the family Clusiaceae, is traditionally recorded for use in China, Malagasy, and the Philippines. Its applications include alterative and astringent properties, as well as uses for asthma, colds, and jaundice. The plant is also traditionally recorded for dysentery, hernia, and contusions, and as a styptic and vulnerary, meaning it was used to stop bleeding and aid wound healing. Additional recorded uses include toothache, snake bite, leech infestation, and odontectomy.

name: Ichnocarpus Frutescens

description: Ichnocarpus frutescens, a member of the Apocynaceae family, is traditionally recorded in India for a broad range of uses, with fevers and infectious illnesses among the most prominent. It was traditionally recorded for fevers, asthma, bronchitis, cough, and phthisis, as well as for smallpox, measles, and cholera. Other applications include jaundice, diabetes, bladder and stone complaints, hemorrhage, and skin sores and pimples. The plant also appears in records for convulsions, cramps, palsy, and delirium, and as a tonic, alterative, and laxative.

description: Illicium anisatum was traditionally recorded for digestive complaints, including carminative and colic uses, and for dermatitis. It also appears as a galactogogue, a stimulant, and a ranicide, and was used for toothache. The plant belongs to the family Illiciaceae, and its use was recorded in China, Mexico, Japan, and Malaya.

name: Illicium verum

old.description: East Asian spice; rich in anethole and shikimic acid (Tamiflu precursor); digestive and antiviral properties.

description: Illicium verum, commonly known as star anise, belongs to the family Illiciaceae. Its use has been recorded in China, Turkey, Malaya, and India. Traditionally recorded for a wide range of applications, it has been used for digestive complaints such as colic, constipation, dyspepsia, and dysentery, and as a carminative, stomachic, and laxative. It also appears in records for respiratory and urinary purposes, including as an expectorant and diuretic, and for pain and inflammation such as rheumatism, lumbago, and otalgia. Other recorded uses include antiseptic, stimulant, and spasm-related applications, as well as external uses for skin conditions like scabies and favus.
traditional_uses: Digestive complaints including colic and dyspepsia

name: Impatiens balsamina

description: Impatiens balsamina, the sole species name recorded, was used across China, Turkey, Central America, the Philippines, the United States, and Haiti for a wide range of applications. This member of the Balsaminaceae family was traditionally recorded for wound care and skin sores, as well as for inflammation and as an astringent. Other uses include digestive complaints such as dysphagia and as a laxative or cathartic, along with menstrual and uterine concerns like dysmenorrhea and uterine polyp. The plant was also recorded for eye problems, neuralgia, lumbago, and to support circulation.

It belongs to the family Aquifoliaceae, and its use was recorded in Turkey, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Europe more broadly. The applications include diuretic, purgative, emetic, and sudorific actions, alongside uses for fever, malaria, jaundice, and gout. It was also recorded as a tonic and emollient, and for swelling and warts.

name: Impatiens noli-tangere

old.description: A European balsam used for skin conditions and as a diuretic in folk medicine.

description: Impatiens noli-tangere, commonly known as touch-me-not, is a plant in the family Balsaminaceae. Its use was recorded in the United States. Traditionally recorded for wounds, corns, and as a diuretic and laxative, it groups these applications around external skin complaints and internal elimination. The plant's most distinctive recorded use is for corns.

description: Imperata cylindrica, a grass of the family Poaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in China, India, Japan, Sumatra, Lesotho, and Malaya. Its applications center on the control of bleeding, with records for hemorrhage, epistaxis, hemoptysis, hematemesis, and hematuria, alongside uses as a hemostatic and astringent. Other recorded uses include fever, cough, cold, asthma, and lung complaints, as well as jaundice, dropsy, and nephritis. The plant has also been noted for diarrhea, dysentery, piles, and debility, and as a tonic, restorative, and sedative.

name: Indian Valerian

description: Indian Valerian, a member of the Valerianaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Nepal. Its applications center on calming the nervous system, with sedative and antispasmodic effects noted. It was also traditionally recorded for chorea, epilepsy, and neurosis, reflecting a broader use for neurological and stress-related conditions.

name: Indian Pipe

old.description: A ghostly white parasitic plant with no chlorophyll, used by Native Americans as a powerful nervine for pain and anxiety.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Indian pipe, a plant in the heath family (Ericaceae), has been traditionally recorded for use in the United States. Its applications center on the nervous system, with records for convulsions, epilepsy, spasms, and as a nervine, sedative, and opiate-like remedy. Other traditional uses include an analgesic for pain, a bactericide, a tonic, and an eye wash or collyrium for eye complaints. These applications reflect the plant's historical role in folk medicine, though modern scientific evidence is lacking.

name: Indigo Naturalis

old.description: Tropical shrub of Southeast Asia; processed leaves yield indigo dye also used medicinally in TCM for anti-inflammatory and antitumor conditions.
traditional_uses: Anti-inflammatory for IBD in Asian medicine

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Indigo Naturalis, a plant in the Acanthaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Malaysia. Its main applications group around the urinary system, where it was used as a diuretic and as a lithontriptic, meaning a substance traditionally taken to break up or dissolve stones. Other recorded uses include an astringent action and a traditional role for ague, a term for a fever with chills. These applications reflect the plant's place in local practice rather than any confirmed medical effect.

name: Indigofera oblongifolia

old.description: African and Asian Indigofera used in traditional medicine for epilepsy and liver conditions.

description: Indigofera oblongifolia, a member of the Fabaceae family, is traditionally recorded for applications that centre on the liver and spleen, with the term megalohepaty and megalospleny reflecting an emphasis on these organs. It also appears as a purgative and as an aperitif, while other recorded uses address rheumatism and syphilis. A further application is as a dentifrice, indicating a role in oral care. These uses are documented without accompanying regional information.

name: Indigofera

old.description: Tropical shrub cultivated for centuries as primary indigo dye source; leaves used in traditional Indian and East Asian medicine for liver and skin conditions.
traditional_uses: Skin conditions in traditional Indian medicine

description: Indigofera, a member of the Fabaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for a wide range of applications across China, Turkey, India, Cambodia, Venezuela, and the Dominican Republic. Its uses include addressing inflammatory and lymphatic conditions such as adenopathy, lymphoadenitis, mumps, and struma, as well as fevers, bronchitis, and dysentery. The plant is also noted for its astringent, antiseptic, and anodyne properties, with applications for sores, bruises, rashes, and scabies, and for nervous system concerns like convulsions, epilepsy, and depression. Additionally, it has been used as an emetic, purgative, and stimulant, and as a preventive for alopecia.

name: Intellect Tree

old.description: A climbing shrub whose seeds yield an oil used in Ayurveda as a potent brain tonic and for intellectual enhancement.

description: Intellect Tree belongs to the Celastraceae family and is traditionally recorded for use in India. Its applications include a range of fever related and inflammatory conditions, such as fever, rheumatism, and colic, alongside a traditional role as a central nervous system stimulant and an anodyne for pain. Other recorded uses address anemia, syphilis, and skin related issues like carbuncle and sores.

description: Inula cappa, a member of the Asteraceae family, was traditionally recorded in China for a broad range of medicinal applications. Its uses include the relief of pain such as headache, backache, and leg ache, as well as the management of inflammatory and rheumatic conditions. The plant was also recorded for respiratory complaints like asthma and colds, and for skin issues including sores, swelling, and itching. Other traditional applications include gynecological and postpartum care, and the promotion of wound healing.

name: Inula japonica

old.description: East Asian Inula used in TCM for phlegm, nausea, and respiratory conditions.

description: Inula japonica was traditionally recorded for a broad set of medicinal applications, particularly those involving the chest and respiratory system. The plant belongs to the Asteraceae family, and its use was recorded in China. It was traditionally recorded for bronchitis, cough, shortwindedness, and chest congestion, as well as for fever, chill, and pain. Other recorded applications include antiseptic use and conditions such as ascites, pleurisy, splenitis, and stomach complaints.

name: Ipomoea purga

old.description: Mexican tuberous vine; resin used as powerful cathartic in traditional and colonial medicine.

description: Ipomoea purga, a member of the Convolvulaceae family, is traditionally recorded for its strong laxative effects. In Mexico and Turkey, its use has been documented mainly as a purgative and cathartic, with related applications as a hydragogue and diuretic. These terms describe actions that promote bowel movements and fluid elimination. The plant has also been recorded for use on sores.

description: Ipomoea purpurea, a plant in the Convolvulaceae family, was traditionally recorded for hallucinogenic, laxative, and purgative purposes in the United States and Africa. Its use as a hallucinogen and its role as a laxative and purgative were documented in both regions. The plant was also traditionally recorded in connection with syphilis.

name: Ipomoea Batatas Leaf

description: Sweet potato leaf is traditionally recorded for ciguatera, a fish poisoning, in Haiti and the Dominican Republic. The leaf also appears in the ethnobotanical records of China, Turkey, the United Kingdom, and Hawaii. Its main applications group around digestive support, such as stomach complaints, diarrhea, and use as a tonic during convalescence, alongside respiratory uses including asthma and catarrh. External applications include poultices for burns and insect bites, while other recorded uses include astringent, demulcent, and alterative actions, as well as aphrodisiac, kidney, spleen, and evil eye purposes.

name: Ipomoea turpethum

old.description: Ayurvedic purgative herb; resinoid turpeth used for constipation and digestive cleansing (virechana).

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Ipomoea turpethum, a member of the Convolvulaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Fiji, India, and Java. Its main applications group into two areas: a purgative action and a tonic effect, alongside uses related to parturition and as a bactericide. These applications reflect the plant's place in local practices, where it was valued for its strong laxative properties and for supporting general vitality.

name: Iris Pallida

old.description: Native to the Dalmatian coast, Iris pallida rhizomes are the primary source of orris root in perfumery and herbal medicine.

description: Iris pallida was traditionally recorded for a range of digestive and respiratory purposes, and its use was documented in Turkey, Iraq, and India. This member of the Iridaceae family has been noted as a stomachic and laxative, and as a cholagogue that supports bile flow. It also appears as a diuretic and expectorant, while other applications include balsamic, dentifrice, and teething uses.

name: Ixora coccinea

old.description: South Asian ornamental Rubiaceae; leaves and flowers used in folk medicine for skin, wound healing, and fever.

description: Ixora coccinea belongs to the family Rubiaceae, and its use was recorded in Bombay. The plant is traditionally recorded for a broad range of applications, including digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, and stomachic support, as well as respiratory conditions like bronchitis and catarrh. It is also noted for fever, headache, and gynecological concerns including dysmenorrhea and leucorrhea, alongside uses as an anodyne, antiseptic, astringent, and sedative. Other recorded applications include eye and sore-related uses, as well as hiccup, hemoptysis, and gonorrhea.

name: Jamu Herbs Mix

description: Jamu Herbs Mix belongs to the Zingiberaceae family and is traditionally recorded for use in Malaya and Java. Its applications include respiratory complaints such as asthma and cough, as well as skin conditions grouped under dermatosis, scabies, and scurf. The mix is also traditionally recorded for parturition, as a purgative, and in relation to insanity.

Other traditional uses address the mouth and teeth, including toothache and caries, while astringent and demulcent properties are also recorded. Additional applications include laxative use, support of the stomach, and uses relating to puerperium and sterility.

description: Jasminum grandiflorum, a member of the Oleaceae family, was traditionally recorded for uses including astringent, deobstruent, diuretic, and vermifuge applications in India and Sanscrit regions. The plant was used for its astringent properties, which are typically associated with toning or tightening tissues, and as a deobstruent, a term describing agents thought to clear obstructions in the body. Its diuretic use relates to promoting urine flow, while its vermifuge application refers to expelling parasitic worms. These applications reflect the plant's place in traditional practice in the recorded regions.

description: Jasminum officinale, a member of the Oleaceae family, has recorded traditional use in Turkey, China, Iraq, Europe, and Spain. It was traditionally recorded for a wide range of applications, including as a sedative and central nervous system depressant, for headache and as an anodyne, and for digestive complaints such as dysentery and cirrhosis. Other recorded uses include astringent, tonic, and vermifuge actions, as well as external applications for skin, sores, corns, ringworm, whitlow, and eye and mouth conditions. It was also traditionally recorded for hepatitis, septicemia, otorrhea, and use during the puerperium, and as a lactogogue, pectoral, and vulnerary (wound healing) remedy.

name: Jasminum sambac

description: Jasminum sambac, a member of the Oleaceae family, is traditionally recorded for use as an anesthetic and anodyne, and its record includes applications for the eyes and for the skin. Use was recorded in China, Malaya, Iraq, Malaysia, Samoa and the East Indies. Related applications include a collyrium and use for conjunctivitis, alongside skin applications for dermatosis and sores. Other recorded uses cover fever, dysentery, congestion, headache, insomnia and fracture, as well as a lactifuge purpose.

name: Jatamansi Root

old.description: Himalayan aromatic root used in Ayurveda for nervous conditions; same species as biblical spikenard; calming and anti-epileptic.

description: Jatamansi root, of the family Valerianaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in India, Turkey, China, Nepal, and Europe. Its applications center on the nervous system, with records for convulsion, epilepsy, hysteria, and fainting, alongside sedative and nervine roles. The root is also noted for heart related concerns such as palpitation, arrhythmia, and tachycardia, and for respiratory complaints including cough and bronchitis. Additional traditional uses include digestive issues like dysentery and cholera, and hair care purposes.

name: Jati Belanda

old.description: A Jamu slimming herb used across Indonesia for weight management and cholesterol reduction.

description: Jati Belanda, of the family Sterculiaceae, has been traditionally recorded for obesity, a use that stands out among its many applications. Its use was documented in Haiti, Mexico, Venezuela, the Dominican Republic, Mauritius, and the West Indies. Other recorded applications include respiratory complaints such as asthma, bronchitis, and lung and chest conditions; digestive issues like diarrhea, dysentery, and stomach problems; and skin concerns including leprosy, elephantiasis, scurf, and general skin care. It was also used for fever and malaria, as a depurative and diaphoretic, and for liver and kidney conditions, among other purposes.

description: Jatropha gossypiifolia, a member of the Euphorbiaceae family, was traditionally recorded for snake bite and for a range of digestive and other internal uses. In Mexico and Guatemala, it was also used as a depurative, a purgative, and an emetic, and for stomach ache. The same records note its use for venereal complaints.

name: Jatropha curcas

old.description: Tropical biofuel crop with significant folk medicinal uses for skin, wounds, and dental conditions across Africa and Asia.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Jatropha curcas, a member of the Euphorbiaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal and practical applications across Trinidad, India, Africa, Mexico, Venezuela, and Guatemala. Its uses include skin and hair conditions such as alopecia, eczema, dermatitis, burns, and carbuncles, as well as internal complaints like diarrhea, dysentery, dyspepsia, fever, and dropsy. The plant was also recorded for dental purposes including dentition and as a dentifrice, and for serious conditions such as convulsion, collapse, and hernia. Other recorded applications include anodyne, antiseptic, and emetic uses, along with treatment of guineaworms and gonorrhea.

name: Jatropha gossypiifolia

old.description: Caribbean and South American shrub used in folk medicine for hypertension, diabetes, and wound healing.

description: Jatropha gossypiifolia, a member of the Euphorbiaceae family, is traditionally recorded for snake bite in Mexico and Guatemala. Its other documented applications include use as a depurative, a substance taken to purify the blood, and as an emetic and purgative to induce vomiting and evacuation. The plant is also traditionally recorded for venereal complaints and stomach ache.

description: Jatropha multifida belongs to the family Euphorbiaceae, and its use has been recorded in Mexico, Brazil, Indochina, Venezuela, and the Caribbean islands of St Vincent and Wi. Traditionally, it has been recorded for a range of applications, including digestive complaints such as colic, dyspepsia, and as a cathartic, emetic, purgative, and tonic. It also has recorded uses for fever, leprosy, scabies, sores, wounds, and venereal conditions, as well as bactericidal applications.
traditional_uses: Digestive complaints including colic and dyspepsia

name: Jeffersonia diphylla

old.description: Eastern North American woodland herb related to Berberis; used by Native Americans for rheumatism and syphilis.

description: Jeffersonia diphylla, the only name recorded for this plant in the family Berberidaceae, has a traditional use record from the United States. Its most distinctive recorded application is as a gargle, alongside uses for sore throat. The plant was also traditionally recorded as an aromatic, stimulant, and tonic, and for rheumatism and spasm. Other applications include use as an emetic and expectorant, grouped among its general medicine uses.

description: Ji Xue Teng belongs to the Fabaceae family and is traditionally used in China. Its recorded applications include menstrual amenorrhea and discomfort in the abdomen, as well as concerns related to the waist and knees. It is also traditionally recorded for leukopenia, a condition characterized by a low white blood cell count.

name: Jojoba

old.description: Desert shrub producing liquid wax ester similar to human sebum.

description: Jojoba was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications, including hair and scalp care, eye and head concerns, and the relief of colds and sore throats. It belongs to the family Simmondsiaceae, and its use was recorded in Mexico, Russia, and the United States. Other traditional applications include the management of dysuria, wounds, and sores, as well as use during parturition and as an emetic. It was also recorded in connection with obesity and as a coffee-related application.

name: Job's Tears Seed

description: Job's Tears Seed, a member of the grass family Poaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in China, Japan, India, Panama, Haiti, and Egypt. Among its most distinctive applications is the treatment of abscesses, but the record also includes many other uses. It was traditionally recorded for inflammatory and infectious conditions such as arthritis, bronchitis, catarrh, diarrhea, dysentery, fever, pleurisy, pneumonia, rheumatism, and smallpox. Other applications include diuretic and demulcent purposes, as well as support for bladder complaints, edema, diabetes, and recovery after childbirth.

name: Jin Qian Cao

description: Jin Qian Cao, in the Primulaceae family, was traditionally recorded for uses in China. It was applied to abscesses, wounds, burns, and bites from bugs and snakes, and was also taken for urogenital and bladder complaints, including stones in the bladder and gall. Other recorded uses include as a diuretic, a refrigerant, an alexiteric, and a detoxicant, as well as for infections and inflammation.

description: Jujube Date, of the Rhamnaceae family, has a traditional record that includes its use for insomnia and anxiety, a distinctive application among its many uses. The plant's use was recorded in China, India, Turkey, Iraq, Java, and Europe. It was traditionally recorded for digestive complaints such as dyspepsia, diarrhea, and dysentery, and for respiratory conditions including cough, bronchitis, and throat issues. Other applications include fever, debility, and pregnancy-related uses, as well as wound and sore care.

description: Juncus effusus, in the family Juncaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in China and Turkey. Its applications center on the urinary system, where it was recorded for dysuria, strangury, stone, and as a litholytic and lithontriptic, terms describing agents that break down or expel stones. Other recorded uses include sedative, nervine, and treatments for insomnia and fear, as well as antiphlogistic, depurative, and pectoral applications. Additional traditional labels include discutient, lenitive, and uses for fistula, jaundice, convulsion, and sore.

It was also recorded as a stimulant and sudorific, and for bronchitis, convalescence, and debility. Additionally, it was noted as a taenifuge and in relation to fatality.

It was traditionally recorded as a stomachic and a tonic, uses that sit closely together, and also as a diuretic. Other recorded applications include care of the skin and use as a fumigant, a category that points to burning rather than internal use.

description: Jurubeba is a Solanaceae plant whose use has been recorded in Brazil. It is traditionally recorded for the liver and spleen, and for the bladder and catarrh. These applications group digestive and urinary concerns with a respiratory one. The record does not specify how the plant was used or in what form.

It also appears in records for digestive and systemic issues such as diarrhea, dysentery, constipation, colic, dropsy, and jaundice-related concerns, as well as for asthma, fatigue, and pain. Other traditional uses include fever, bladder complaints, menstrual cramps, and as a soothing or astringent agent.

External applications include astringent and emollient purposes for wounds, sprains, swellings, and skin conditions such as erysipelas, along with hair loss and hoarseness. Other recorded uses cover female and childbirth-related concerns, syphilis, urethritis, leprosy, neuralgia, and headache.

Additionally, it was valued as a balsamic and stomachic, applications that relate to soothing and digestive support.

Digestive issues such as dyspepsia, stomach ache, dysuria, and carminative purposes also feature, alongside external uses for burns and thrush, and a role as an anodyne and intoxicant.

description: Kawakawa, a member of the Piperaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in New Zealand. Among its most distinctive applications is the steam bath, a practice that sets it apart from many other medicinal plants. The plant is also traditionally recorded for a range of skin and tissue complaints, including boils, eczema, wounds, and general skin care. Its internal uses include bladder and kidney support, urogenital and diuretic applications, and a depurative role, while it has also been recorded for aphrodisiac purposes, as a sialogogue, and for stomach ache and toothache.

description: Khat, a plant in the Celastraceae family, is most distinctive for its use as a masticatory, chewed for its stimulating effects. Its use has been recorded in Ethiopia, elsewhere in Africa, Arabia, Yemen, and Kenya. Traditional applications center on central nervous system stimulation, including use as a stimulant and for lethargy, debility, and anorexia. Other recorded uses include aphrodisiac purposes, relief of cough, flu, and chest complaints, and astringent and stomach-related applications, with some records describing a tea and a narcotic use.

Its use has been recorded in Ghana, Upper Volta, and other parts of Africa, where it is traditionally recorded for an unusually wide range of applications, including snake bite and dysentery. Other recorded uses include kidney complaints, stomach problems, and as a laxative or purgative, as well as a taenifuge for tapeworm. The plant is also traditionally recorded for female health, as a lactogogue, and for musculoskeletal and skin issues such as lumbago, rheumatism, piles, sores, and wounds.

description: Korean Red Peony, a member of the family Paeoniaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in China. Among its most distinctive applications is the relief of headache and vertigo, which are grouped with other nervous system related uses such as convulsion. The plant is also traditionally recorded for digestive complaints including diarrhea, and for gynecological concerns such as dysmenorrhea and menoxenia. In addition, it has documented applications as a bactericide and fungicide, and in connection with hepatitis.

Its applications often center on sedation and pain relief, with recorded uses as a narcotic, sedative, and masticatory. Other traditional applications include treating fever, delirium, and an enlarged spleen, as well as use as a vermifuge and for wound care. The plant has also been recorded for fumitory purposes.

description: Korean Mugwort, a member of the Asteraceae family, has traditional applications that center on bleeding control and digestive upset. It was traditionally recorded for hemostatic use and for diarrhea, grouping these as related concerns about the retention and regulation of fluids and blood. The plant also appears as an emetic, a use that stands apart from the others. Additionally, moxa is documented, referring to the burning of prepared mugwort material for warming purposes.

description: Ku Shen was traditionally recorded for a broad range of medicinal applications, especially for digestive and infectious complaints. It belongs to the Fabaceae family, and its use was recorded in China, Japan, and Malaya. The plant was used as an astringent for diarrhea, dysentery, and enteritis, and for bleeding such as enterorrhagia and metrorrhagia. It was also recorded for fever, jaundice, and skin conditions including rash, scabies, and scrofula, as well as for vaginal and parasitic infections.

name: Kutaja Indian

description: Kutaja Indian, a member of the Apocynaceae family, is traditionally recorded in India for an unusually wide range of applications. Among the most distinctive is its use in cases of dog bite and rabies, a striking entry in a record that also covers abscesses, amebiasis, anemia, and a set of astringent and bactericidal purposes. Digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, dyspepsia, cholera, and colic appear frequently, alongside respiratory uses for cough, cold, and bronchitis. The record further notes applications related to blood, hemorrhage, epistaxis, hematochezia, hematuria, and menorrhagia, as well as piles, spleen and splenitis, fever, epilepsy, and labor, parturition, and the puerperium.

name: Lablab purpureus

description: Lablab purpureus, a member of the Fabaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in China, India, the Philippines, and Asia more broadly. The most frequent therapeutic theme is the management of digestive and intestinal complaints, with uses recorded for diarrhea, cholera, and as a carminative. Other traditional applications include fever, epilepsy, and a range of gynecological and systemic concerns such as leucorrhea, menorrhagia, and an enlarged spleen. The plant has also been recorded for localized purposes, including poultices for swelling, remedies for earache and sore throat, and as a tonic.

The plant is also noted as a diuretic, sudorific, and laxative, and has been used as an astringent, depurative, and fever remedy. Additionally, it has been applied as a cataplasm.

Other recorded uses include as an expectorant for coughs, for fever, and as a gargle for sore throat. It was also noted for scurvy.

description: Loquat leaf, of the family Rosaceae, was traditionally recorded for use in China, Indochina, and Japan. Other recorded uses include digestive issues such as diarrhea, nausea, and stomach ache, as well as sedation, depression, and thirst. The leaf was also applied to skin problems like chafe, sores, swelling, and wine-nose, and was listed for epistaxis, hemoptysis, smallpox, and as a refrigerant.

Other recorded uses address the heart and circulation, fever, insomnia, and neurasthenia, along with post-partum and labor-related purposes. The plant has also been noted for its effects on the abdomen, chest, and complexion.

name: Lotus Leaf

Its most distinctive recorded application concerns the blood: it was traditionally noted as a hemostat for hemorrhages ranging from nosebleeds and coughing or vomiting blood to blood in the stool or urine, and for excessive menstrual bleeding. Other recorded uses include digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, dyspepsia, and enteritis, along with fever, cholera, and support during labor and the postpartum period. The leaf was also traditionally recorded for the heart and circulation, for complexion and dark hair, for insomnia and nervous exhaustion, and as a diuretic and soothing agent.
traditional_uses: Hemorrhage and blood in the urine or stool

description: Lotus root, of the family Nelumbonaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in China, India, and Egypt. The plant is also traditionally recorded for digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, and dyspepsia, and for a range of other purposes including fever, insomnia, and post-partum care.

Its use as an anodyne for pain relief and as a hemostat to control bleeding reflects its prominence in folk practice. The plant is also cited as an astringent, a role often linked to toning or drying tissues, and for skin-related purposes. These traditional recordings group into pain relief, bleeding control, and external or tissue-toning applications.

The stamen is also recorded for fever, insomnia, and post-partum care, and has been used as a hemostat, diuretic, and demulcent. Other traditional uses include the treatment of bruises, skin complexion issues, and as a deobstruent, meaning it was thought to clear obstructions.

The plant was also used for skin conditions such as scabies, leprosy, and scrofula, and for inflammatory or spasmodic complaints including adenopathy, piles, and convulsions. Other recorded uses include jaundice, asthma, and syphilis, reflecting a broad range of traditional applications.

Other recorded uses include alterative, depurative, and deobstruent applications, which relate to cleansing or clearing the body, as well as digestive and carminative purposes for the stomach and bowels. It was also recorded as a diuretic, a vermifuge, and a pectoral for the chest, alongside a general tonic role.

Its applications include digestive issues such as diarrhea, colic, gastritis, and stomach ache, as well as pain-related uses for neuralgia, angina, and anal discomfort. The leaf was also recorded for throat conditions like quinsy, for skin eruptions and smallpox, and as a tonic and nutrient in cases of anemia and thirst.

Its applications centered on women's reproductive health, with records for amenorrhea, dysmenorrhea, metrorrhagia, and metroxenia. The plant was also traditionally recorded for circulation and as a decoagulant, as well as for diuretic purposes such as edema, polyuria, and swelling. Other recorded uses include abscess, abdomen, extravasation, and liver.

These include treatment of abscesses, sores, swelling, burns, and scalds, as well as use as an emetic and expectorant. Additional traditional applications cover fever, nausea, dysentery, edema, and nervous conditions, along with an antitussive role.

name: Macleaya cordata

description: Macleaya cordata, a member of the Papaveraceae family, has a traditional record in China and Japan that includes an unusually wide range of applications. Among the most distinctive is its use for dental caries, alongside other oral and skeletal concerns such as osteomyelitis and abscesses. The plant was also traditionally recorded for pain relief, including arthralgia and general soreness, and for skin sores. Other uses include treatment of edema, syphilis, and hookworm infection, as well as a laxative and carminative action and support for circulation.

description: Macropiper excelsum belongs to the Piperaceae family and is traditionally used in New Zealand. It is recorded for a wide range of applications, including skin conditions such as eczema, boils, and wounds, as well as urinary and kidney complaints, bladder issues, and urogenital uses. Other traditional purposes include a steam bath, a sialogogue to promote saliva, a diuretic, a depurative, and an aphrodisiac. The plant is also traditionally recorded for stomach ache and toothache.

name: Madder
