description: Madder, a member of the Rubiaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Europe, Turkey, the USSR, and Spain. Its main medicinal applications include urinary and digestive support, such as for the bladder, kidney, and gall, as well as for arthritis and liver conditions like hepatitis and sclerosis. Other recorded uses are as an astringent, tonic, and diuretic, and for catarrh, bedsores, and menstrual concerns. The plant also appears in homeopathy and has been traditionally recorded for urogenital and splenitis applications.

Other applications include relief for asthma, cough, and hayfever, as well as a mydriatic action to dilate the pupils.

These records group into calming, anticonvulsant, and pain related uses, with the connection to morphinism standing out as the most distinctive entry.

description: Matico Leaf, of the Piperaceae family, has a recorded history of use in Haiti, Mexico, the Dominican Republic, and Latin America. Its applications cluster around the genitourinary and circulatory systems, with traditional use for blennorrhagia, leucorrhea, dropsy, and as a diuretic. The leaf was also recorded as a stimulant, stomachic, and liver remedy, and for rheumatism and ulcer. Skin and sore applications, along with its astringent and hemostatic properties, reflect a further traditional role in wound care.

name: Mauritia flexuosa

old.description: Tall Amazonian palm whose fruit is one of the richest natural sources of beta-carotene and vitamin C.
traditional_uses: Traditional Amazonian indigenous food and medicine plant
Called Tree of Life by Moriche and other Amazonian peoples

image.credit: Dick Culbert from Gibsons, B.C., Canada — CC BY 2.0

description: Mauritia flexuosa, a palm of the family Arecaceae, has a traditional record centred on its intoxicant use, alongside digestive and laxative applications. Use of the plant is recorded in Venezuela, Colombia, Amazonia and South America more broadly. The digestive and laxative applications are closely related, and the plant is traditionally recorded for both digestive complaints and the relief of constipation. The intoxicant application stands apart from these and is the most distinctive element of its ethnobotanical profile.

name: Maytenus ilicifolia

old.description: Thorny shrub of southern Brazil and neighboring countries, traditional Brazilian remedy for gastric ulcers and cancer.
traditional_uses: Traditional Brazilian remedy for gastric ulcers
Used across southern South America for digestive and anti-inflammatory conditions

description: Maytenus ilicifolia, known by its common name and belonging to the family Celastraceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in Brazil and Paraguay. Its most distinctive application is as a contraceptive and antifertility agent, a use that stands out among the plant's other recorded purposes. The plant is also traditionally recorded for soothing the stomach and intestines, for astringent and tonic effects, and for promoting appetite. Additional applications include use as an analgesic, a cicatrizant for wound healing, and as a tea.

name: Mela dubia

old.description: A fast-growing Asian tree used in folk medicine for pain, inflammation, and respiratory conditions.

description: Mela dubia belongs to the Meliaceae family and is traditionally recorded for use in the Philippines, Malaya, and Sumatra. Its main medicinal applications group into two areas: an anodyne use for pain relief and a fever use, alongside internal applications and a vermifuge use for expelling worms. These applications reflect the plant's recorded role in traditional practice across these regions.

name: Melilotus albus

old.description: White sweet clover relative of M. officinalis; similar coumarin content and venous tonic properties.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Melilotus albus, a member of the Fabaceae family, is traditionally recorded for uses that center on the relief of spasms. It has also been noted as an expectorant and for the care of sores. These applications reflect a therapeutic focus on calming internal spasm and supporting respiratory and topical comfort.

name: Melianthus Major

old.description: Striking South African shrub with toxic foliage historically applied externally for rheumatism, wounds, and inflammation despite its dangerous systemic toxicity.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Melianthus major, the only name recorded for this plant in the family Melianthaceae, has a traditional use record limited to South Africa. Its most distinctive application is as a gargle, which is traditionally recorded for sore throat and gingivitis. Other recorded uses include wounds, sores, and necrosis, as well as tinea capitis, a fungal infection of the scalp. The plant is also traditionally recorded in connection with fatality, a label that likely reflects a serious or life-threatening context rather than a specific medicinal use.

name: Mentha longifolia

old.description: Wild mint widespread across Europe, Asia, and Africa; used in traditional medicine across many cultures.

description: Mentha longifolia, a member of the Lamiaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in the United States, Lesotho, Iraq, Turkey, and South Africa. Its applications most often centre on colds and fever, with additional use as a stimulant and for headache. Other recorded uses include anodyne, antiseptic, and carminative purposes, as well as applications for chest complaints, apoplexy, and sclerosis, and it has been taken as a snuff and as a tea.

name: Mesembryanthemum crystallinum

old.description: Succulent annual from South Africa and Mediterranean with glistening water-filled cells; leaves eaten as food medicine.
traditional_uses: Traditional South African use as wound healer
Used as anti-inflammatory and for skin conditions

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Mesembryanthemum crystallinum, a member of the Aizoaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications in Turkey. Its uses included the relief of inflammation and fever, as well as support for lung and pectoral complaints. The plant was also recorded as a demulcent and diuretic, and for urogenital and kidney-related conditions such as ascites and hepatitis. Other traditional applications included dysentery and rhinitis.

name: Mespilus germanica

old.description: Ancient European Rosaceae fruit tree used in folk medicine for digestive conditions and as astringent.
traditional_uses: Digestive conditions in European folk medicine

description: Mespilus germanica, the medlar, is a member of the Rosaceae family whose use has been recorded in Turkey and Europe. Its main traditional applications center on astringent and tonic effects, which are reflected in uses for diarrhea and as a general blood tonic. The plant has also been recorded as a diuretic and for gravel, and as an alterative and for splenomegaly, while its astringent quality appears in several of these labels.

name: Mexican Marigold

old.description: An Aztec sacred herb used as incense, medicine, and as a tarragon substitute, with documented psychoactive properties at high doses.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Mexican Marigold, a member of the Asteraceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Mexico and among the Aztec. Its applications include relief from bug bites and itch, as well as aid for diarrhea and hiccups. It was also recorded as an anesthetic, sedative, and hallucinogen, and for rheumatism and malaria. Other uses include as a fumigant and for hemoptysis.

name: Mikania micrantha

old.description: Invasive tropical Asteraceae used widely in traditional medicine across Asia and Pacific for wound healing and fever.

image.credit: Jeevan Jose, Kerala, India — CC BY-SA 4.0

description: Mikania micrantha, a member of the Asteraceae family, is traditionally recorded for skin injuries and wounds across Fiji, Trinidad, Samoa, Haiti, and Mexico. The most frequent applications relate to stopping bleeding and closing wounds, including use as a hemostat, styptic, tourniquet, and for sores and burns. It is also traditionally recorded for athlete's foot, cough, and fever, as well as for bug bites, snake bites, and scorpion stings.

name: Millettia pinnata

description: Millettia pinnata, a member of the Fabaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Java, India, the Philippines, the Moluccas, Malaya, and Australia. Its applications are broad, including remedies for skin conditions such as scabies, itch, and leprosy, as well as for joint and muscle complaints like arthritis and rheumatism. It is also recorded for digestive issues such as diarrhea, dyspepsia, and piles, and for respiratory complaints including cough and bronchitis. Other traditional uses include fever, diabetes, and a range of internal and external purposes.
traditional_uses: Skin conditions such as scabies and itch

description: Mo Han Lian, a member of the Asteraceae family, is traditionally recorded for use in China and India. Its applications include support for the urinary system, such as cystitis and dysuria, and for digestive complaints like jaundice, hepatitis, and gastritis. The plant is also traditionally recorded for fevers, tuberculosis, and various bleeding episodes, including epistaxis and hemoptysis. Other recorded uses cover skin conditions, snake bite, trauma, and hair oil.

name: Momordica balsamina

description: Balsam apple (Momordica balsamina), a member of the Cucurbitaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for burn care in the Dominican Republic, Turkey, Syria, Ghana, and the United States. Its applications include digestive and liver related uses such as stomachic, laxative, purgative, and liver support, as well as skin and wound care for sores, chafe, and dermatosis. The plant is also traditionally recorded for fever and malaria, rheumatism and gout, and as a tonic, stimulant, and vermicide.

These include impotency, ejaculation, enuresis, polyuria, and hernia. The plant is also traditionally recorded for debility, lumbago, and notalgia, as well as for cholecystitis.

description: Mountain Sagebrush, a member of the Asteraceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in the United States. Its applications include the relief of colds, coughs, and fever, often grouped with its sudorific property, which refers to promoting sweating. The plant has also been documented as a diuretic and for heartburn.

description: Mountain mint, a member of the Lamiaceae family, was traditionally recorded for use in the United States. Its most distinctive recorded application is for sclerosis of the belly, a traditional label for a hardening or induration of the abdomen. Other traditional applications include use as a diaphoretic, to promote sweating, and for spasm. These records describe what was traditionally recorded for the plant, not claims of efficacy.

name: Mucuna Sloanei

description: Mucuna sloanei is a member of the Fabaceae family, and its use has been recorded in Mexico. Traditionally recorded applications include a diuretic action and a purgative effect, which relate to the movement of fluids and the bowels. The plant is also traditionally recorded for evil eye, a cultural concept rather than a medical condition.

Its main applications center on promoting circulation and fluid balance, with recorded uses as a diuretic for edema and dysuria. It was also traditionally recorded for amenorrhea and as a lactogogue, and was used as a nervine. These applications reflect a therapeutic theme of regulating movement and flow within the body.

description: Munyeroo, in the family Portulacaceae, has been traditionally recorded for use in China, India, Haiti, Turkey, Trinidad and Sudan. Its applications center on digestive and urinary complaints, with records for dysentery, dyspepsia, colic, enteritis, bladder and kidney gravel, dysuria and hematuria. The plant is also noted for skin conditions such as eczema, dermatitis, boils, burns and erysipelas, and for fevers, colds and hemorrhage. Other traditional uses include snake and bug bites, gonorrhea and other genital complaints, and general debility.

name: Murraya Paniculata

description: Murraya paniculata, in the family Rutaceae, is traditionally recorded for uses in Malaya, the Philippines, Panama, Java and China. Its most distinctive recorded application is as a dentifrice, and it also appears in records for cough, diarrhea and dysentery, stomach ache, and rheumatism. Other traditional uses include wound care, eye complaints, gynecology, herpes, hysteria, stomatosis, and tapeworm, along with astringent, bactericidal and stimulant purposes.

description: Musta Root, a member of the Cyperaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications across China, Turkey, Egypt, Java, India, and Sudan. Its uses include digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dyspepsia, and gastralgia, as well as menstrual and reproductive concerns like amenorrhea, dysmenorrhea, and leucorrhea. The plant was also recorded for fever, inflammation, and pain, and for urinary and circulatory issues including edema, gravel, and hypertension.

description: Myrica esculenta, in the family Myricaceae, is traditionally recorded for use in Nepal and India, with a strong emphasis on the respiratory system. The plant has been used for asthma, bronchitis, and as a pectoral and lung remedy, while also serving as an astringent for diarrhea and dysentery. Other recorded applications include fever, headache, and toothache, along with use as an antiseptic for sores, a carminative and stomachic for digestive complaints, a diuretic, and a sedative.

description: Nagarjuna was traditionally recorded for a broad range of medicinal applications, from wound care and skin complaints to cough and stomach problems. It belongs to the Clusiaceae family, and its use was recorded in India, Nepal, and Malaya. Related applications include astringent and bactericidal actions, use against Candida and fungi, and relief for piles and rheumatism. It was also recorded in connection with parturition and as a sudorific, stomachic, and general medicine.

name: Myrtus communis

old.description: A Mediterranean aromatic shrub used since antiquity for respiratory, skin, and urinary conditions.

description: Myrtus communis, a member of the Myrtaceae family, has a traditional record that includes use as a mouthwash and for wound care. Its use was recorded in Iraq, Turkey, Europe, Spain, Kurdistan, and Greece. The applications group around digestive complaints such as dyspepsia and stomach upset, urinary and genital conditions including cystitis and leucorrhea, and respiratory issues like bronchitis. Other recorded uses include rheumatism, epilepsy, and hemorrhage, with labels such as astringent, tonic, and sedative reflecting its broader traditional role.

name: Nance

description: Nance, a member of the Malpighiaceae family, has recorded uses in Mexico, Venezuela, Panama, the Dominican Republic, and Guatemala. Traditionally recorded for fevers and colds, it is also used for digestive complaints such as diarrhea, colitis, and gastritis, and for intestinal atony. Other applications include astringent and diuretic purposes, snake bite, skin sores, fungal conditions, and dental issues like pyorrhea and denture-related problems.

name: Nelumbo Nucifera Herb

description: The herb Nelumbo nucifera, in the family Nelumbonaceae, has been traditionally recorded for uses centered on bleeding control and blood-related conditions. In China, India, and Egypt, it was used for hemorrhages such as hemoptysis, hematemesis, hematuria, and metrorrhagia, as well as for bruising and as a hemostat. Other applications include digestive complaints like diarrhea, dysentery, and dyspepsia, along with fever, cholera, and intestinal inflammation. It was also recorded for genitourinary issues, postpartum and labor-related purposes, and for promoting circulation and complexion.

name: Nerium oleander

old.description: Mediterranean ornamental shrub; all parts extremely toxic (oleandrin); historical use in cancer treatment.

description: Nerium oleander, in the family Apocynaceae, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal and other applications across Haiti, Mexico, Turkey, Venezuela, the Dominican Republic, and Europe. Its main medicinal uses included cardiac and cardiotonic purposes, as well as stimulant and tonic applications, while it was also recorded as a diuretic, purgative, and emetic. Skin-related applications included psoriasis, scabies, warts, corns, sores, eruptions, and other skin conditions, and it was further documented as a parasiticide, raticide, and rodenticide. Other recorded uses included treatment of aposteme, atheroma, carcinoma, and epithelioma, alongside sternutatory and cyanogenetic properties and associations with fatality, homicide, and weakness.
traditional_uses: Skin conditions including psoriasis and scabies

description: Newbouldia laevis, a member of the Bignoniaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications across Ghana, Upper Volta, Guinea, Gambia, Senegal, and Africa more broadly. Its uses include remedies for fevers such as malaria, digestive complaints like dysentery and colic, and respiratory issues including coryza and sinusitis. The plant was also recorded for pain relief in headaches, toothaches, and earaches, as well as for gynecological and obstetric purposes such as dysmenorrhea, parturition, and as a lactogogue. Other recorded applications involve convulsions, epilepsy, snake bite, syphilis, and various swellings and sores.

description: Nigella damascena, a member of the Ranunculaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Turkey, Spain, and Europe. Its applications often centre on digestion and the movement of fluids, with carminative, digestive, diuretic, and sudorific uses noted. Other recorded uses include tonic and stimulant actions, as well as applications for the liver and intestines. The plant has also been traditionally recorded as an emollient and for catarrh, alongside uses as a vermifuge and sternutatory.

name: Nigerian Bitter Kola

description: Nigerian bitter kola, a member of the Clusiaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use across Africa, West Africa, Ghana, and Nigeria. Its applications include respiratory complaints such as chest colds, coughs, hoarseness, and throat issues, as well as digestive uses like dysentery and as a purgative. The plant is also documented for sexually transmitted infections, wound care, headache, and parasitic conditions, and it has been used as a chewstick and dentifrice. Other recorded applications include aphrodisiac and malignancy uses.

name: Nopal

old.description: Mexican cactus used as food and medicine by Aztec and indigenous peoples; pads eaten as vegetable; fruits for nutrition; highly studied for diabetes management.

description: Nopal, of the cactus family Cactaceae, is traditionally recorded for skin and wound care across China, Sicily, South Africa, Spain, Mauritius, and Haiti. Applications include burns from radiation, scalds, and sunburn, along with sores, wounds, calluses, and corns, and it is also noted as an emollient. Other recorded uses cover diabetes, diarrhea, and as a diuretic, as well as kidney complaints, piles, internal ulcers, measles, leprosy, and favus. It also appears as a decongestant.

name: Notopterygium incisum

description: Notopterygium incisum, a plant in the Apiaceae family, was traditionally recorded for use in China. Its main applications centered on musculoskeletal and joint complaints, including arthritis, rheumatism, and lumbago. It was also recorded for cold and headache, as well as for sweating.

name: Nigerian Uziza Leaf

old.description: West African pepper plant used in Nigerian folk medicine for digestive, respiratory, and women health conditions.
traditional_uses: treatment of coughs and respiratory infections

description: Uziza Leaf, a member of the Piperaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for a wide range of applications across Zaire, Upper Volta, Java, Ghana, Malaya, and Guatemala. The most frequent therapeutic theme is the relief of fluid accumulation and urinary complaints, with uses documented for anasarca, ascites, and as a diuretic and kidney aid. Other recorded applications include digestive and intestinal issues such as colic, dysentery, and as a laxative or purgative, as well as remedies for cough, rheumatism, and various swellings and wounds. The leaf is also noted for female reproductive purposes, including lactation and placental concerns, and for treating toothache and rib ache.

name: Nymphaea lotus

old.description: An Egyptian water lily with sacred significance used in traditional medicine as a sedative and aphrodisiac.

description: Nymphaea lotus, in the family Nymphaeaceae, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications in India, Sudan, and France. Its uses include respiratory complaints such as asthma, bronchitis, cough, and phthisis, as well as digestive issues like colic, dyspepsia, and dysentery. Other recorded applications cover urinary problems such as dysuria and gravel, skin conditions including leprosy, and piles and menorrhagia.

name: Nutmeg

description: Nutmeg, of the family Myristicaceae, was traditionally recorded for use in Trinidad, Malaya, China, Turkey, Java, and the Moluccas. Its applications include digestive complaints such as dyspepsia, dysentery, and intestinal flux, and it was also recorded as a carminative and astringent. Other uses include fever, flu, and malaria, as well as pain relief for rheumatism, sciatica, and cramps. The plant was also traditionally recorded for aphrodisiac and narcotic purposes, and for conditions of the bladder and spleen.

Other traditional applications include use as an antiseptic, bactericide, carminative, diaphoretic, diuretic, refrigerant, stimulant, tonic, and parasiticide, as well as for toothache and tuberculosis. The plant has also been recorded as an inhalant.

The plant has also been recorded as a tonic, depurative, and diuretic, as well as for wound care and hair care. These varied uses suggest a broad role in traditional practice, though no specific preparation or efficacy is implied.

Other recorded uses are as an apertif and for cyanogenetic applications.

name: Ribes uva-crispa

description: Ribes uva-crispa, a member of the Grossulariaceae family, is traditionally recorded for use in Turkey. Its applications include digestive support, with records for both antacid and laxative purposes, alongside a diuretic use. It is also traditionally recorded for fever and scurvy.

name: Roman Nettle

old.description: Annual nettle of Mediterranean regions; more pungent sting than U. dioica; used in folk medicine similarly to common nettle but also as flagellation treatment for arthritis.

description: Roman Nettle, a plant in the Urticaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for bleeding from several sites, including epistaxis (nosebleeds), hematemesis (vomiting blood), hemoptysis (coughing blood), and metrorrhagia (irregular uterine bleeding). Its use was documented in Iraq and Europe. It was also traditionally recorded for paralysis. These applications reflect a historical focus on hemorrhagic and neurological conditions.

name: Robinia pseudoacacia

description: Robinia pseudoacacia, a member of the Fabaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a broad range of medicinal applications in Turkey, the United States, and Iraq. Other recorded applications cover astringent, diuretic, emetic, emollient, sedative, and antispasmodic actions, along with protisticide and viricide uses.

External applications include wounds, sores, sprains, swelling, and trauma.

These applications reflect the plant's place in historical practice, where it was valued for both its perceived action on the body and its role in formulation.

Its applications include cardiotonic and heart support, alongside astringent and refrigerant properties. The record also notes uses for sore throat and tonsillitis, as well as stomachic, carminative, and laxative purposes. Tonic, nervine, and aperient applications appear as well, with scurvy listed among the documented uses.

name: Rou Gui

The plant has also been used in connection with colic, complexion concerns, perspiration, and the postpartum period. In addition, it is noted as a sedative. These applications reflect the plant's place in traditional practice, where it was recorded for both internal and external purposes.

name: Ru Xiang Resin

description: Ru Xiang Resin, of the Burseraceae family, is traditionally recorded for use in China, India, Iran, Peru, and Morocco. Its applications include internal and external purposes such as alterative, astringent, carminative, diuretic, expectorant, sedative, stimulant, and tonic actions. The resin has also been traditionally recorded for skin and tissue concerns like carbuncle, sore, leprosy, and sclerosis, as well as for urogenital conditions including gonorrhea and spermatorrhea. Other recorded uses include struma and fumigant practices.

name: Rosy Periwinkle Leaf

old.description: In folk medicine context (distinct from pharmaceutical extraction), the leaves are used in South Asian, Caribbean, and African traditions for diabetes and hypertension at culinary doses.

description: Rosy Periwinkle Leaf, of the family Apocynaceae, is traditionally recorded for medicinal use in Trinidad, the Bahamas, the Dominican Republic, Madagascar, Honduras, and Haiti. Its applications include asthma, catarrh, chest colds, sore throat, and laryngitis, as well as diabetes, glycosuria, hyperglycemia, and hypertension. Other traditional uses are as a sedative, tranquilizer, emetic, purgative, hemostat for menorrhagia, and vermifuge. The leaf is also recorded for leukemia, Hodgkin's disease, and as an oncolytic, and for eye conditions such as ceguera and ophthalmia.

name: Rudbeckia laciniata

old.description: Woodland coneflower used by Cherokee for indigestion and fever; roots as food by some tribes.

description: Rudbeckia laciniata belongs to the Asteraceae family and its use was recorded in the United States. Traditionally recorded for Bright's Disease and kidney complaints, it was also used as a diuretic and for gonorrhea. These applications group around urinary and kidney-related purposes.

name: Rubus Fruticosus Herb

description: Blackberry has been traditionally recorded for astringent and tonic purposes, and for complaints of the digestive tract including diarrhea and dysentery. Its use was documented across Europe, Turkey, Spain, India, Italy and Sicily, and the plant belongs to the Rosaceae family. Records also note applications for cough and fever, for diuretic and depurative ends, and for wounds, along with use as an intoxicant and in liqueur. A tea has been recorded as well, and a resolvent role was noted, meaning a use for dispersing swelling or congestion.

It was also recorded for sores and swelling, and a tea was noted among its uses. These applications reflect how the plant was regarded in the recorded tradition rather than any established medical effect.

It is also noted as an antiseptic, a use that aligns with applications for itch and gonorrhea. These applications reflect a pattern of addressing both surface irritations and internal infections. The plant's traditional role thus spans several distinct but related purposes.

It was also traditionally recorded for dropsy, a condition involving fluid retention, and as a vermifuge for expelling intestinal worms. Other recorded uses include applications for excrescences, which are abnormal outgrowths.

It is traditionally recorded for digestive complaints such as dyspepsia, gastritis, and biliousness, and for respiratory conditions including asthma, cough, and catarrh. Other applications include fever, rheumatism, piles, scurvy, and skin problems, along with uses as a dentifrice and for gonorrhea. The plant is also recorded for its effects on the nerves, as a tonic and stimulant, and for properties described as astringent, diuretic, laxative, and purgative.
traditional_uses: Digestive complaints including dyspepsia and gastritis

The leaf also appears in records for inflammatory and infectious skin conditions, as well as for sedative and tonic purposes.

Additional traditional uses include astringent, tonic, stomachic, and cordial actions, as well as treatments for diarrhea, dysentery, fever, inflammation, piles, sores, burns, and furunculosis. Other recorded applications are anodyne, apertif, diuretic, sudorific, parturition, uterus, and vulnerary, the last referring to wound healing.

It was also documented as a stomachic and pectoral remedy, and for leucorrhea and menorrhagia. Other recorded uses include alterative, depurative, and resolvent applications, as well as a vulnerary for wound healing.

The plant is also traditionally recorded for fever and malaria, and for anodyne and toothache purposes. Other recorded uses include debility, female complaints, gonorrhea, leprosy, measles, orchitis, piles, and as an emetic and chewstick.

Other recorded uses include alterative, diuretic, and laxative applications, as well as a preventive purpose. These labels reflect how the plant has been described in ethnobotanical use rather than confirmed medical effects.

Other recorded uses include astringent, sedative, and stimulant actions, as well as applications for colic, diarrhea, and otitis.

name: Sassafras

description: Sassafras was used in the United States and Turkey for a wide range of purposes that were traditionally recorded for the plant. It belongs to the Lauraceae family. External uses include a mouthwash and dentifrice for oral care, a wash for the eyes and skin, and a massage preparation for soreness and swelling. Other recorded uses are as a stimulant, tonic, astringent, and diaphoretic, and as a fungicide, viricide, and pediculicide.

It was also traditionally recorded for nosebleeds, hemorrhage, tonsillitis, and boils.

The plant was also recorded for respiratory conditions including cough, bronchitis, and as an expectorant, and for inflammatory and skin problems such as eczema, mange, and bruise. Other traditional applications include fever, diabetes and hyperglycemia, menstrual disorders, and as an astringent, diuretic, purgative, and emetic.

Its main medicinal applications group around digestive and urinary support, with aperient and diuretic uses, alongside depurative and antiseptic roles. It was also traditionally recorded for scurvy and as a stimulant, and for discutient purposes, meaning it was applied to help disperse swellings or collections.

name: Scutellaria Barbata

old.description: TCM herb used to clear heat and fire toxin, resolve damp, and activate blood circulation. Widely studied for anticancer properties. One of the most researched Chinese cancer herbs.

description: Scutellaria barbata is a plant in the Lamiaceae family, and its use was recorded in China. It was traditionally recorded for fever and as an alexiteric, a term for agents used against poisons or venom, including snake bite. Other applications include anodyne use for pain, diuretic use, and relief of sore throat. It was also recorded for boils, lymphadenitis, and enlarged liver or spleen, as well as for schistosomiasis and neophasia.
traditional_uses: Lymphadenitis and enlarged liver or spleen

name: Seagrape Leaf

old.description: A Caribbean and Pacific coastal plant used medicinally for diarrhea, rheumatism, and edema.

image.file: Sea Grape Coccoloba Uvifera Leaf The Lucayan National Park of the Bahamas in Grand Bahama.jpg

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Seagrape Leaf belongs to the Polygonaceae family and is traditionally recorded in Mexico, the United States, Trinidad, Haiti, and the Dominican Republic. Its main medicinal applications group around digestive and systemic uses. The leaf is traditionally recorded for diarrhea and dysentery, often in the context of its astringent properties. It is also traditionally recorded for fever and as a tonic, and for venereal applications.

name: Sea Lavender

old.description: European coastal salt marsh plant used in traditional folk medicine for diarrhea, bleeding, and as an astringent tonic. The roots are highly tannin-rich.

provenance.notes: Automatically matched to: Commission E, NCCIH. No PubMed citations yet.

description: Sea lavender, a member of the Plumbaginaceae family, was traditionally recorded for astringent and anti-diarrheal purposes. Its use has been documented in Turkey, Spain, and the United States. The plant was employed to address diarrhea and dysentery, and it was also valued as a hemostat to help control bleeding. These applications reflect its historical role in folk medicine, though no claims of efficacy are made here.

name: Selaginella lepidophylla

old.description: Desert spikemoss with remarkable desiccation tolerance; used in Mexican folk medicine for childbirth and fertility.

description: Selaginella lepidophylla, in the family Selaginellaceae, is traditionally recorded for use in Mexico. Its main applications group around the liver and biliary system, with recorded uses for bilious conditions, dyspepsia, and liver complaints. It is also traditionally recorded for the urinary system, including calculus, cystitis, and kidney conditions, and as a diuretic.

name: Sedum Acre Herb

old.description: Low-growing European stonecrop with peppery leaves used historically for hypertension and wound healing; toxic at high doses.
traditional_uses: treatment of hypertension in European folk medicine

provenance.notes: 1 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Biting stonecrop, Sedum acre, is a member of the Crassulaceae family whose use has been recorded in Turkey, Spain, France, Caledonia, Belgium and Finland. The most distinctive application in its record is the treatment of warts and corns, a use that aligns with its traditional role as a rubefacient, meaning a substance applied to redden the skin. Other recorded applications include promoting urine flow and bowel movements, inducing vomiting, and addressing fever, hypertension, scurvy, scrofula and cancre. These uses reflect a broad historical practice of applying the herb both internally and externally for a range of conditions.

name: Securidaca Longipedunculata

old.description: Southern and West African tree used across multiple cultures for respiratory conditions, pain, sexually transmitted infections, and as a powerful purgative.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Securidaca longipedunculata, known as the ordeal tree, is a member of the Polygalaceae family. Its use has been recorded across Africa, including Ghana, Guinea, Botswana, Ethiopia, and Nigeria, where it is traditionally recorded for a wide range of applications. These include fevers such as malaria, venereal conditions such as syphilis and gonorrhea, and skin complaints such as psoriasis and herpes zoster. Other recorded uses are snake bite, convulsions, rheumatism, and as a purgative or vermifuge.

name: Selaginella tamariscina

old.description: Selaginella tamariscina is a botanical used in Traditional Chinese Medicine. description: Selaginella tamariscina, of the family Selaginellaceae, is traditionally recorded for bleeding control, with uses spanning China and India. The plant appears most often in connection with hemostatic and astringent purposes, including metrorrhagia, hematuria, hemoptysis, and piles. Other recorded applications include cough, diuretic use for gravel, and prolapse of the rectum. It is also traditionally recorded for amenorrhea, leucorrhea, puerperium, internal ulcers, and longevity.

name: Selenicereus grandiflorus

description: Selenicereus grandiflorus, a cactus in the family Cactaceae, is traditionally recorded for use in Mexico. Its most distinctive recorded application is for dropsy, a term for fluid retention or swelling. The plant is also traditionally recorded for rheumatism and for fungoid conditions, a label that likely refers to fungal growths or similar complaints. These applications reflect the plant's place in local medicinal practice.

Other uses relate to urinary health, including cystitis, oliguria, and as a diuretic, along with alexiteric and venereal applications. The plant has also been recorded in relation to hepatoma, leukemia, and lymphoma.

name: Senburi

description: Senburi, a member of the Gentianaceae family, is traditionally recorded in Japan for diarrhea and dysentery, with a particular focus on the intestines. It also has a documented use as a stomachic, indicating a role in supporting stomach function. The plant's applications center on the digestive system, addressing both acute and general stomach complaints.

name: Senecio scandens

Its applications include use against flu, malaria, and jaundice, as well as for inflammation and various skin and eye complaints. The plant has also been recorded for dysentery and tenesmus, for soothing soreness, and for bites from dogs and snakes. Additional traditional labels include alexiteric, emetic, and refrigerant uses.

description: Sesame Herb, of the family Pedaliaceae, has been traditionally recorded for hair loss (alopecia) and hair care, including hair oil, hair tonic, and hair blackening. Its use is documented across China, Haiti, Turkey, Malaya, Venezuela, and Mexico. The plant has also been recorded for digestive complaints such as constipation, diarrhea, dysentery, and colic, and for respiratory conditions including cough, cold, and catarrh. Other traditional applications include labor and lactation support, as well as use for debility, liver and kidney complaints, and skin eruptions and burns.

name: Sesbania grandiflora

description: Sesbania grandiflora, commonly known as the vegetable hummingbird, is a member of the Fabaceae family. Its use has been recorded in Java, Malaya, Mexico, Johore, and Hawaii, where it is traditionally recorded for a wide range of applications. These include digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, sprue, and gastrosis, as well as eye and mouth conditions like ophthalmia, stomatitis, and thrush. The plant is also noted for treating fevers, skin issues such as scabies and smallpox, and throat problems including sore throat and tonsillitis.

name: Seseli libanotis

It belongs to the Campanulaceae family, and its use was recorded in China. The plant also appears as an expectorant and was used for nausea. These applications reflect a focus on respiratory and bleeding-related conditions.

name: Setaria Italica

description: Setaria italica, a member of the grass family (Poaceae), has been traditionally recorded for use in China. Its applications are broad and include digestive complaints such as diarrhea and cholera, as well as fever and rheumatism. The plant is also noted for effects on the reproductive system, including uses related to pregnancy, parturition, and the uterus, along with applications for vaginitis and as an antilactogogue. Other traditional uses include abscess, dog bite, pellagra, and as an aphrodisiac for virility, alongside astringent, diuretic, emollient, laxative, refrigerant, sedative, and intoxicant properties.

name: Shankhpushpi Morning Glory

The respiratory applications include asthma and bronchitis, while other recorded uses are alopecia, fumitory, and gonorrhea.

description: Shalaparni, a plant in the Fabaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications across India, Malaya, Upper Volta, and Java. Its uses include remedies for fever and catarrh, as well as digestive complaints such as diarrhea and dysentery. It was also recorded as a diuretic and for urogenital issues including gravel and stone, and as a vermifuge. Other traditional applications include a tonic, alterative, expectorant, sedative, and steam bath, with specific use for headache and toothache.

name: She Gan Rhizome

It also appears in records for fever and malaria, as well as for digestive and eliminative purposes including constipation, dyspepsia, and as a diuretic and expectorant. Other traditional applications include abscesses, inflammation, liver and chest conditions, and support during parturition.

name: Shi Wei

Other traditional applications include fever, hematuria, hemoptysis, and general urogenital complaints.

In addition, Shirish is traditionally recorded for rejuvenation and as a tonic, reflecting a broader role in supporting overall vitality.

It was also recorded for respiratory complaints such as cough and phlegm, and for its cathartic, purgative, and emetic effects. Additionally, the plant was used as a sponge.

name: Sida

Other applications include use as a poultice for sores and swelling, a gargle for mouth and throat issues, and a remedy for snake bite. The plant is also documented for urogenital and gynecological concerns, among many other traditional purposes.

The plant has been used as a demulcent, emollient, diuretic, and sedative, and for genitourinary concerns including bladder issues, leucorrhea, dysmenorrhea, and as an aphrodisiac. Records come from Malaya, Samoa, Java, Nicaragua, Guatemala, and Borneo.

Other recorded applications include depurative, emollient, laxative, stomachic, and tonic uses, reflecting a broad range of traditional therapeutic themes.

The plant was also recorded as a diaphoretic and sudorific, both referring to the promotion of sweating, and was used in connection with fever. description: Bog bilberry (Vaccinium uliginosum), of the heather family Ericaceae, has a traditional record spanning Europe, Turkey and Spain. Its most distinctive recorded use is as a narcotic, a label that sets it apart from the other applications in its record. The remaining uses are grouped around the digestive tract: it was traditionally recorded for stomachic purposes and for gastritis, enteritis and intestinal complaints, with cystitis also noted. Catarrh appears in the record, and the plant was also used in liqueur making.

name: Uvaria chamae

old.description: A West African shrub used in traditional medicine for malaria, pain, and infection.

description: Uvaria chamae, a member of the Annonaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use across parts of West Africa, including Ghana, Nigeria, Togo, and Sierra Leone. Among its most distinctive applications is the treatment of fontanelles, the soft spots on an infant's skull, which stands out in an otherwise broad medicinal profile. The plant is also traditionally recorded for fevers, including yellow fever, and for a range of bleeding-related concerns such as hematemesis, hematoptysis, and hematuria, as well as for dysentery and jaundice. Other recorded uses include inflammation, swellings, sores, wounds, piles, and eye complaints such as ophthalmia, alongside applications related to childbirth and as a purgative or astringent.
traditional_uses: Bleeding from stomach, lungs, or urine

name: Vanilla

old.description: The world's second most expensive spice (after saffron), used by Aztecs as medicine and flavoring with real health benefits.

image.credit: Franz Eugen Köhler, Köhler's Medizinal-Pflanzen — Public domain

description: Vanilla, a member of the Orchidaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal and other uses in Egypt, Mexico, and Haiti. Its applications include aphrodisiac and stimulant purposes, as well as soothing digestive complaints such as carminative and tonic effects. It was also recorded for menstrual irregularities (menoxenia) and to support parturition, and for spasms, snake bites, syphilis, and wound healing (vulnerary). Additionally, it was used as a liqueur.

name: Vana Tulsi

old.description: Shrubby basil of Africa and Asia; one of three Tulsi varieties used in Ayurveda; also widely used across Africa for infections and malaria.
traditional_uses: Adaptogenic tonic in Ayurveda (Vana Tulsi variety)

description: Vana Tulsi, a member of the Lamiaceae family, is traditionally recorded for snake bite, one of its most distinctive applications. Use of the plant has been documented in Haiti, Trinidad, Ghana, India, Upper Volta and elsewhere in Africa. Its recorded applications are broad, covering fevers and flu, colds, cough, bronchitis, catarrh and pneumonia, alongside digestive complaints such as colic, dysentery, nausea and piles. Other traditional uses include arthritis, back and lumbar pain, neuralgia, inflammation, conjunctivitis and other eye complaints, gonorrhea and blennorrhagia, and it was also recorded as an anesthetic, anodyne, antiseptic and bactericide.

name: Varuna Bark

old.description: An important Ayurvedic herb for urinary health; the bark is highly effective for treating urinary calculi, BPH, and urinary tract infections.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Varuna bark, of the Capparaceae family, was traditionally recorded for use in Malaya, Baroendoj, and Sempol wada. Its applications center on the digestive system, where it was used as an aperitif, astringent, cholagogue, demulcent, laxative, and tonic. It was also recorded for fever and malaria, for urogenital complaints, and for cramps, along with external uses as a rubefacient and vesicant. Other documented applications include calculus.

name: Vasaka

old.description: Important Ayurvedic respiratory herb whose name means "give voice to." Contains vasicine, which inspired the drug bromhexine.

taxonomy.note: GBIF and NCBI name different taxa/ranks for this herb; no automatic change made
taxonomy.decision: NCBI Taxonomy + ITIS both give this name

description: Vasaka was traditionally recorded for a range of respiratory and systemic complaints, including asthma, bronchitis, cough, and tuberculosis. It belongs to the Acanthaceae family, and its use was recorded in India and Turkey. The plant was also traditionally recorded as an expectorant and for fever, spasm, and as an alterative, a term used for substances thought to restore health gradually. These applications reflect its historical role in herbal practice.

old.description: High Alpine valerian exported from Austria since medieval times used as an aromatic perfume and nerve sedative.

provenance.notes: Automatically matched to: WHO Vol.1 (1999), Commission E, EMA, NCCIH. No PubMed citations yet.

name: Veratrum californicum

old.description: Western North American plant; causes severe birth defects (cyclopia) in livestock; source of cyclopamine.
traditional_uses: historical Native American use for fertility control

description: Veratrum californicum was traditionally recorded for contraceptive and sterilizing purposes, as well as for use as a pediculicide. It belongs to the family Liliaceae, and its use was recorded in the United States. The plant was traditionally recorded for applications related to fertility control and hygiene, including contraception and sterilization, and for the treatment of lice infestations.

name: Velvet Tamarind

old.description: West African tree with edible sour-sweet fruit pods used medicinally throughout the region.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Velvet tamarind, a member of the Fabaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of applications across Africa, including Ghana, Nigeria, Upper Volta, Ivory Coast, and West Africa more broadly. Its uses include astringent and antiseptic-type applications for the mouth and eyes, such as a mouthwash, dentifrice, collyrium for ophthalmia, and remedies for stomatitis and toothache. The plant was also recorded for internal and systemic complaints, including diarrhea, dysmenorrhea, edema, fever, palpitation, and shortness of breath, as well as for abdominal issues, chest complaints, spasms, thirst, and throat problems. In addition, it was traditionally recorded in contexts of female health and labor.
traditional_uses: Mouthwash and dentifrice for oral hygiene

name: Veronica virginica

old.description: Veronica virginica appears in 3 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

provenance.limitations: LNHPD publishes no per-product indication, so uses are empty rather than invented.

description: Veronica virginica, the only name recorded for this plant in the family Scrophulariaceae, was used in the United States. Its most distinctive traditional application was as an emetic, and it was also recorded as a cathartic and a purgative. These related uses all concern the evacuation of the bowels or stomach, and they are grouped here because they describe similar effects rather than separate purposes.

name: Vervain

old.description: One of the most sacred herbs of the ancient Druids and Romans, used as a nervine, digestive, and fever remedy.

provenance.notes: Automatically matched to: Commission E. No PubMed citations yet.

description: Vervain, a member of the Verbenaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal applications across China, Turkey, Eurasia, Sudan, Mexico, and Europe. Its uses include fevers and malaria, liver and gallbladder complaints such as hepatitis and cirrhosis, and women's health concerns like amenorrhea, dysmenorrhea, and as a lactogogue. The plant was also recorded for skin conditions including eczema and scrofula, for respiratory issues such as bronchitis and pertussis, and for rheumatism and arthritis. Other traditional applications include snake bite, dropsy and edema, and use as a diuretic, diaphoretic, and nervine.

name: Vidarikand

old.description: Climbing Ayurvedic plant with large tuberous roots used as a rejuvenating tonic for male and female reproductive health and energy.

image.credit: Dinesh Valke from Thane, India — CC BY-SA 2.0

provenance.notes: Automatically matched to: WHO Vol.4 (2009). No PubMed citations yet.

description: Vidarikand belongs to the Fabaceae family and is traditionally recorded for use in India and Nc. Its applications include arthritis and swelling, which are related to joint and inflammatory conditions. Other traditional uses cover fever, gravel, and syphilis, as well as menorrhagia and use as a lactogogue. These applications reflect a range of recorded purposes, from urinary and reproductive concerns to systemic and inflammatory complaints.

name: Vigna angularis

old.description: Vigna angularis is a botanical used in Traditional Chinese Medicine. Health Canada has licensed 1 natural health product containing it, and 1 of their labels were read for this entry. The regulator records no specific indication beyond the traditional-medicine basis, so this entry claims none.

provenance.limitations: LNHPD publishes no per-product indication for TCM licences and no TCM energetics (nature, flavour, meridians). Those fields are deliberately empty rather than filled from an unlicensed source.

description: Adzuki bean (Vigna angularis) is a member of the Fabaceae family, and its use has been recorded in Elswhere. The most distinctive application in its record is for labor, with other uses traditionally recorded for miscarriage and as a lactogogue. It is also traditionally recorded for fever, constipation, and kidney complaints, as well as for skin conditions such as abscess and boil.

name: Vigna mungo

old.description: South Asian legume with warming properties in Ayurveda; used for nerve strength and musculoskeletal conditions.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Vigna mungo, a member of the Fabaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in India, China, Lesotho, Sudan, Indochina, and Venezuela. Among its most distinctive applications is the treatment of smallpox, a use that stands out in its ethnobotanical record. Other recorded uses include poultices for abscesses, boils, and fistulas, as well as internal applications for fever, dysentery, and cholera. The plant has also been traditionally recorded for rheumatism, scabies, and a range of urinary and digestive complaints.

name: Vigna radiata

old.description: East Asian legume with cooling properties in TCM; sprouts high in enzymes; used for heat conditions and detox.

description: Mung bean, Vigna radiata, is the only name recorded for this Fabaceae plant, and its use has been documented in China, the Philippines, Malaysia, and Africa. Among its most distinctive applications is a poultice, traditionally recorded for abscesses, boils, and swelling. The plant is also traditionally recorded for fevers, cholera, dysentery, and smallpox, as well as for urinary and bladder complaints and as a diuretic. Other uses include support during labor and the puerperium, a lactogogue for breastfeeding, and applications for beri-beri, polyneuritis, and carcinoma.

name: Vigna unguiculata

old.description: African-origin legume used as nutritive food and in folk medicine for digestive complaints.

image.credit: HeraldDesa at English Wikipedia — CC BY-SA 3.0

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata), a member of the Fabaceae family, has traditional use recorded in India, China, Cambodia, and Haiti. Its applications include digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, and stomach issues, as well as urinary and kidney related uses like dysuria and polyuria. The plant is also traditionally recorded for infectious diseases including leprosy, measles, smallpox, and pneumonia, and for skin problems such as burns and sores. Other uses include jaundice and liver complaints, thirst, and as a tonic and astringent.

old.description: Ancient cultivated legume whose seeds, pods, and flowers have medicinal use for Parkinson's and as L-DOPA source.

description: Vincetoxicum atratum, a member of the Asclepiadaceae family, is traditionally recorded for use in China. Its applications include fever and malaria, as well as urogenital concerns such as incontinence. The plant is also noted as a diuretic and has been traditionally recorded for delirium.

name: Viper's Bugloss

old.description: Biennial of disturbed European ground; flowers and leaves used in folk medicine for fever and respiratory conditions though contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids.
traditional_uses: Fever and headaches in European folk medicine
Used for snakebite in historical medicine (Doctrine of Signatures)

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Viper's Bugloss, a member of the Boraginaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Turkey and Spain. Its applications include soothing irritated tissues as a demulcent, promoting urine flow as a diuretic, and aiding in the expulsion of phlegm as an expectorant. The plant has also been recorded for fever, nervous conditions, and pain, as well as for promoting sweating and acting as a tonic. In addition, it has been traditionally recorded for snake bite.

name: Viola Odorata Herb

old.description: Fragrant violet used in European and Unani medicine for respiratory conditions, headache, and skin inflammation.
traditional_uses: respiratory mucus remedy in European folk medicine

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Sweet violet, a member of the Violaceae family, has a traditional record that includes its use as an emetic, a distinctive application among its many entries. Its use was recorded across Turkey, Mexico, Eurasia, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, and Pakistan. The plant was traditionally recorded for respiratory complaints such as cough, catarrh, and lung support, and for digestive purposes including laxative, purgative, and aperient actions. It also appears in records for skin conditions like eczema, for fever, and for sedative and nervine uses.

name: Vitex doniana

old.description: West African Vitex tree whose leaves, bark, and fruit are used in traditional medicine for malaria, fever, and anemia.
traditional_uses: Malaria treatment in West African medicine

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Vitex doniana is traditionally recorded for a range of medicinal applications. It belongs to the Lamiaceae family, and its use has been documented in several African regions, including Nigeria, Ivory Coast, Guinea, and Ghana. The plant was used for gastrointestinal complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, and stomach ailments, and as a laxative. It was also recorded for fever and cold, for gargle, and for conditions including leprosy, rickets, and sterility.

name: Vitex Negundo

old.description: A widely used medicinal shrub in Asia used for respiratory conditions, joint inflammation, and as a female hormonal regulator; extensively used in Filipino traditional medicine as Lagundi.

description: Vitex negundo, a member of the Lamiaceae family, has recorded traditional use in India, China, Fiji, Sanskrit-speaking regions, Samoa, and Iran. Its applications are broad and include fever and malaria, digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, dyspepsia, gastritis, and enteritis, and inflammatory conditions including arthritis, swelling, and sprains. It is also traditionally recorded for respiratory complaints like cold and cough, for skin issues such as boils and abrasions, and for a range of other purposes from madness and angina to piles and splenomegaly.

name: Vitex Trifolia

old.description: Coastal herb used across Pacific Islands and Asia for headache, fever, and respiratory conditions.

description: Vitex trifolia was traditionally recorded for a broad range of medicinal applications, from fevers and inflammation to digestive and respiratory complaints. It belongs to the Lamiaceae family, and its use was documented in Samoa, China, Hawaii, Malaya, India, and Sanscrit. The plant was also recorded for amenorrhea, puerperium, and as a tonic, alongside uses for rheumatism, sprains, backache, and headache. Other applications include cough, catarrh, breathlessness, and tuberculosis, as well as eye and hair care.

name: Vitis labrusca

old.description: Vitis labrusca appears in 26 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 6 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

provenance.limitations: LNHPD publishes no per-product indication, so uses are empty rather than invented.

description: Vitis labrusca belongs to the grape family, Vitaceae, and its use has been recorded in the United States and China. Traditionally recorded applications center on external injuries, including bruises and sprains, as well as eye complaints. These records group together concerns about physical trauma to the body and care for the eyes.

name: Wasabia japonica

old.description: Wasabia japonica appears in 10 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

provenance.limitations: LNHPD publishes no per-product indication, so uses are empty rather than invented.

description: Wasabia japonica, a member of the Brassicaceae family, has been traditionally recorded in Japan for applications centered on pain relief and prevention. The most frequent theme in the documented uses is an anodyne or pain-relieving purpose. It was also recorded for preventive use and for addressing ptomaine, an archaic term for food poisoning. These traditional applications reflect the plant's historical role in Japanese practice, though no claims of efficacy are made here.

name: Waltheria Indica

old.description: Pantropical shrub used in traditional medicine across Hawaii, Africa, and the Caribbean for respiratory conditions, wound healing, and pain.

description: Waltheria indica, a member of the Sterculiaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Ghana, South Africa, Togo, Haiti, Nigeria, and Venezuela. Its applications center on skin and wound care, including sores, eruptions, and emollient use, alongside eye preparations such as collyrium. Fever and related symptoms like giddiness and vertigo are also noted, as are respiratory complaints such as cough and blood in sputum. Other recorded uses include diarrhea, syphilis, and a preventive purpose for fever.

name: Water Avens

old.description: Woodland and wetland perennial; roots used in European folk medicine for digestive and fever conditions; pleasant chocolate flavor.
traditional_uses: Digestive conditions in European folk medicine

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Water Avens belongs to the Rosaceae family and has been recorded in traditional use across the United States, Turkey, and Europe. Its applications center on the digestive system, where it was traditionally recorded for dyspepsia, dysentery, and as a stomachic and digestive aid. It also appears in records for fever and ague, as well as for debility and as a tonic. Other traditional uses include astringent and antiseptic purposes, hemorrhage, dysmenorrhea, and as a vermifuge.

name: Welsh Onion

old.description: Asian origin hollow-stemmed onion used in TCM for cold-expelling and Yang-warming conditions.

provenance.notes: Automatically matched to: WHO Vol.3 (2007), Commission E. No PubMed citations yet.

description: Welsh onion was traditionally recorded for uses related to sweating and fever, including headache. It belongs to the Liliaceae family, and its use was recorded in China. The applications grouped together suggest a role in promoting perspiration and addressing feverish conditions, with headache also noted.

name: Watermint

old.description: Aquatic European mint and parent of peppermint, used in traditional medicine for digestive and respiratory.

image.credit: Burschik at English Wikipedia — CC BY-SA 3.0

description: Watermint was traditionally recorded for digestive complaints and colds, among other uses. It belongs to the Lamiaceae family, and its use was recorded in Turkey, the United Kingdom, Lesotho, and Europe. The main applications group around the stomach and digestion, including carminative, stomachic, and digestive uses, while other recorded uses include astringent, stimulant, emetic, and for gall. Cold was also among the documented applications.

name: Wei Mao

old.description: TCM herb for blood stasis, joint pain, and irregular menstruation.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Wei Mao has been traditionally recorded for pain relief and cough suppression, as well as for digestive and women's health complaints. It belongs to the Celastraceae family, and its use was recorded in China and Japan. Related applications include diarrhea and constipation, with a purgative action noted alongside an antidiarrheal one. It was also traditionally recorded for gynecopathy, for lice, and as a vermifuge.

name: White Clover Leaf

old.description: Ubiquitous lawn plant with gentle medicinal properties; less potent than red clover but nutritive and digestive.

provenance.notes: Automatically matched to: WHO Vol.4 (2009). No PubMed citations yet.

description: White Clover Leaf, of the Fabaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in Turkey, Eurasia, the United States, the USSR, and Iraq. Its applications often center on the relief of swelling and related conditions, with recorded uses for adenopathy, scrofula, sore, swelling, and whitlow. Other traditional applications include rheumatism, gout, and use as a tonic, astringent, and expectorant. The leaf has also been recorded as a depurative, for spasm, and as a preventive for mumps and parotitis, with additional notes on its cyanogenetic and estrogenic properties.

name: White Peony

old.description: A fundamental TCM herb for nourishing liver blood, relieving spasms, and regulating menstruation; one of the most widely used herbs in gynecological formulas.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: White Peony belongs to the family Paeoniaceae and its use has been recorded in China. Traditionally recorded applications include menstrual disorders such as dysmenorrhea and menoxenia, along with digestive complaints like diarrhea. It has also been noted for convulsions, headache, and vertigo, and for hepatitis. In addition, it has been recorded for bactericidal and fungicidal purposes.

name: White Poplar

old.description: European and Central Asian poplar with salicin bark used in traditional medicine for rheumatism.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: White poplar, a member of the Salicaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use across China, Turkey, Eurasia, Iraq, and Italy. Its applications include fever and malaria, as well as rheumatism and a range of skin conditions such as herpes and complexion concerns. The plant is also noted for its astringent and antiseptic properties, and it has been used for digestive complaints like colic and flux, along with hemorrhage and hematochezia. Other recorded uses include diuretic and tonic purposes, and applications related to bones, caries, and goiter.

old.description: Young grass of the common wheat plant, popularized as a nutritional supplement. Rich in chlorophyll, vitamins, minerals, and enzymes.

name: Wild Bergamot Monarda

old.description: Purple-flowered bee balm species used widely by Native American tribes for respiratory, antiseptic, and digestive conditions.
traditional_uses: treatment of colds and respiratory infections in Native American medicine

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Wild Bergamot, a member of the Lamiaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in the United States. Its applications include support for the respiratory system, such as for colds, coughs, bronchitis, and catarrh, as well as for sore throat. It was also recorded for skin concerns like acne, eruptions, and pustules, and for digestive purposes as a carminative and stomachic. Other traditional uses include addressing fever, acting as a diaphoretic and tonic, and relieving headache and toothache.

name: Wild Chrysanthemum

old.description: TCM herb stronger than Ju Hua for clearing heat and toxins; used for carbuncles, sore throat, and hypertension.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Wild Chrysanthemum belongs to the Asteraceae family and its use has been recorded in China, Japan, Indochina, and India. It is traditionally recorded for inflammatory and infectious skin conditions such as abscesses, boils, swellings, and wounds, as well as for fever and infections. Other applications include headache and migraine, digestive complaints, hypertension, and as a sedative, tonic, and vermifuge. The plant has also been noted as an alexiteric, antiphlogistic, aperient, bactericide, collyrium, depurative, stomachic, and for encephalomyelitis and mumps.

name: Wild Indigo Root

old.description: North American herb used by Cherokee and Iroquois as an immune stimulant, lymphatic herb, and antiseptic. Used by Eclectic physicians for typhoid and septicemia.

description: Wild Indigo Root, a member of the Fabaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for use in the United States. Its applications include poultices for wounds, bruises, and sores, as well as internal uses as a laxative, cathartic, and emetic. It was also recorded as an antiseptic, astringent, and tonic, and for fever, typhus, and sore throat.

name: Withania coagulans

old.description: Relative of ashwagandha used in Ayurveda and Unani medicine for diabetes, and as vegetarian milk coagulant for cheese.

description: Withania coagulans, a member of the Solanaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of medicinal uses in India and Pakistan. Its applications include digestive complaints such as dyspepsia, colic, and bilious conditions, as well as fever and hepatitis. The plant was also recorded as a diuretic and for strangury, and as a sedative and alterative. Other traditional uses include asthma, toothache, and a dentifrice, along with an emetic and a rennet-like purpose.

name: Wood Avens

old.description: Common perennial weed of hedgerows and woodland edges; roots smell of cloves due to eugenol; used in European folk medicine as digestive bitter and tonic.
traditional_uses: Digestive conditions in European folk medicine
Used since medieval times as food flavoring and tonic

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Wood Avens, a member of the Rosaceae family, was traditionally recorded for a wide range of applications across France, Germany, Turkey, Europe, India, and Iraq. Its uses included addressing fevers and chills, such as ague and malaria, as well as digestive complaints like diarrhea, dysentery, and constipation. The plant was also documented for throat and mouth issues, including sore throat and halitosis, and for its astringent, antiseptic, and tonic properties.

name: Woodfordia fruticosa

old.description: Woodfordia fruticosa appears in 3 licensed natural-health products in Canada, and 3 product labels were read for this entry. Health Canada records no specific indication beyond the product's own claim, so this entry states none.

Its applications include treatment of dysentery, cholera, and cough, as well as fever and hemorrhage. The plant was also recorded for skin and wound care, such as sores, carbuncles, and fractures, and for women's health concerns including pregnancy, parturition, and infertility.

It also appears as a hypnotic, suggesting a role in promoting sleep, and as a tea. These uses reflect the plant's place in regional practices, where it was valued for its stimulating and sedative properties.

name: Wrightia Tinctoria

description: Wrightia tinctoria belongs to the family Apocynaceae and its use has been recorded in India. Traditionally recorded for a range of digestive complaints, it is noted as a carminative, stomachic and vermifuge, and also for biliousness. Other recorded applications include dropsy and hypertension, as well as use as an aphrodisiac and for toothache. The plant has also been listed as a source of rennet.

old.description: Eastern North American shrub with intensely yellow roots used by Cherokee and other tribes for bitter digestive and antimicrobial purposes.

provenance.notes: 2 PubMed citation(s) found. No authoritative monograph match.

description: Yellowroot is traditionally recorded for jaundice, a use that stands out among its applications. This herb belongs to the buttercup family, and its use was recorded in the United States. It was also traditionally recorded for digestive complaints such as dyspepsia and stomach ache, for colds and throat conditions including stomatitis, and as a tonic. In addition, it was recorded in connection with parturition.

name: Xanthorhiza simplicissima

old.description: Small native American shrub with intensely yellow roots rich in berberine; folk remedy for mouth sores and ulcers.

description: Xanthorhiza simplicissima, a member of the Ranunculaceae, is traditionally recorded in the United States for a range of applications. Its most distinctive use is in parturition, or childbirth. Other recorded uses include digestive complaints such as dyspepsia and stomach ache, as well as jaundice, colds, and conditions of the throat and mouth like stomatitis. The plant also appears as a tonic and as a general medicine.

name: Ximenia Americana

old.description: Small thorny tree found in tropical Africa, Asia, and the Americas used in traditional medicine across multiple regions for wound healing, pain, and infections.

description: Ximenia americana, of the family Olacaceae, has recorded uses in Mexico, Argentina, Sudan, Java, Uganda, and South Africa. It is traditionally recorded for digestive complaints such as diarrhea, dysentery, colic, gastritis, nausea, and jaundice, and for respiratory conditions including colds and coughs. Other applications include fever, rheumatism, headache, toothache, and skin and hair concerns, with uses as an astringent, bactericide, cathartic, laxative, purgative, and vermifuge also noted.

description: Ye Jiao Teng, a member of the Polygonaceae family, is traditionally recorded for use in China and Malaya. Its applications cover a wide range of conditions, including nervous system complaints such as insomnia, neurasthenia, and vertigo, as well as joint and bone issues like arthritis, knee problems, and rickets. The plant is also traditionally recorded for blood-related and liver concerns, including anemia, hepatitis, and splenitis, and for skin conditions such as scabies, itch, and scrofula. Other documented uses include fever, constipation, diarrhea, and recovery during the puerperium.

description: Xylopia aethiopica, a member of the Annonaceae family, is traditionally recorded for a range of applications across Ghana, Liberia, Nigeria, and other parts of Africa. Its use is most often associated with respiratory complaints such as cough and bronchitis, and with digestive purposes including dysentery, biliousness, and as a carminative, purgative, and emetic. The plant is also recorded for musculoskeletal and neuralgic conditions like rheumatism, lumbago, and neuralgia, as well as for boils, sores, eruptions, and headache. Additional traditional uses include female fertility, fumitory practice, and as a stimulant and vermifuge.

description: Ye Jiao Teng Vine, in the family Polygonaceae, has a traditional use record from China and Malaya. Its most distinctive recorded application is for insomnia, and it is also traditionally recorded as a sedative and nervine for neurasthenia and vertigo. Other applications include support for the liver and kidney, use in arthritis and trauma, and a range of digestive, circulatory, and skin complaints. The record further notes uses related to childbirth and the postpartum period, as well as for fever and scurvy.

It belongs to the family Ranunculaceae, and its use was recorded in Turkey, the USSR, and Spain. The main medicinal applications group into pain relief and calming effects, alongside uses for fever, fluid balance, and sweating. These applications include analgesic, anodyne, narcotic, and sedative properties, as well as diuretic, sudorific, and fever-related uses.

description: Yerba de Tago, a member of the Asteraceae family, has recorded uses in China, Trinidad, Malaya, Java, India, and the Philippines. It is traditionally recorded for skin and hair complaints such as alopecia, baldness, ringworm, sores, and wounds, as well as for bleeding issues including hemorrhage and enterorrhagia, where it is noted as a hemostat. Other applications include digestive and liver concerns like jaundice, hepatitis, indigestion, and copremia, along with respiratory conditions such as cough, catarrh, and pertussis. It is also recorded for vertigo, giddiness, lumbago, toothache, and as a tonic, purgative, and emetic.

description: Yin Chen Hao, a member of the Asteraceae family, is traditionally recorded for jaundice and related bilious complaints, a use that stands out among its many applications. Its use has been documented in China and Japan, where it was also recorded for fevers including malaria and ague, as well as for catarrh and headache. Other traditional applications include diuretic and urinary uses such as dysuria and oliguria, along with constipation, rheumatism, dysmenorrhea, and pruritis. The plant was further noted as an anodyne, antiphlogistic, bactericide, and fungicide, and was applied as a cataplasm.

Additional recorded uses include support as a tonic and nutrient, as well as applications for freckles and rabies.

It belongs to the family Rutaceae, and its use was recorded in the United States, Haiti, and Mexico. The plant was also recorded as a stimulant, tonic, and alterative, and as a diaphoretic and sudorific to promote sweating. Other traditional uses include poultices for sores and inflammation, as well as remedies for itch, gonorrhea, and throat complaints.

The plant was also recorded for respiratory conditions including asthma and pectoral uses, and for skin applications such as ecchymosis and skin complaints. Other traditional uses included malaria, parasitic conditions, and as a stimulant and preventative.

The plant also appears in records for congestion and as an expectorant, and it has been noted as an emetic. Other traditional applications include epilepsy, lockjaw, numbness, and stroke.

Its other documented uses include anodyne (pain relief), diaphoretic (promoting sweating), diuretic (increasing urine flow), stimulant, and stomachic (supporting stomach function) purposes. These applications group into those affecting the body's eliminative and circulatory processes and those addressing pain and digestive comfort.

description: Ze Lan was traditionally recorded for a range of conditions linked to the abdomen and circulation, including amenorrhea, dysmenorrhea, and swelling. It belongs to the Lamiaceae family, and its use was recorded in China. Other documented applications include fluid balance issues such as edema and polyuria, as well as abscesses and abnormal bleeding like metrorrhagia. The plant was also noted for its effects on the liver and as a decoagulant.

It was also recorded for enlargement of the liver and spleen and for lymphadenitis.

description: Zhi Gan Cao Processed has been traditionally recorded for a wide range of applications, including cough and related respiratory complaints, digestive weakness, and inflammatory or ulcerative conditions. It belongs to the Fabaceae family, and its use was recorded in China and Japan. The main medicinal applications group into respiratory support such as cough, pharyngitis, and laryngitis; digestive and constitutional support such as anorexia, debility, and duodenal or internal ulcers; and other recorded uses including abscesses, sores, piles, hemorrhage, palpitation, vertigo, and tuberculosis. Additional labels such as demulcent, emollient, expectorant, antispasmodic, antitussive, and laxative describe purposes rather than specific diseases.

Its applications often center on respiratory and digestive complaints, with uses documented for cough, chest conditions, flu, and as an expectorant, alongside diarrhea and dysentery. Other recorded uses include a range of genitourinary and inflammatory concerns, such as gonorrhea, blennorrhagia, rheumatism, and wound care, as well as a sedative or soporific role and a tonic purpose. Additional traditional labels include anodyne, diaphoretic, refrigerant, and sweetener, reflecting a broad ethnobotanical profile.
