Its applications center most often on calming and sleep, with sedative and anodyne uses noted alongside records for anxiety, insomnia, and vertigo. Digestive and respiratory purposes also appear, including stomachic and astringent uses, dyspepsia, colic, diarrhea, dysentery, cough, bronchitis, and throat complaints. Further traditional records mention fever, debility, wound and sore care, skin conditions such as scabies, and uses connected with pregnancy and livestock rinderpest.

The plant has also been recorded as a laxative, a febrifuge for fever, and a nervine for spasm, while other applications include pectoral and urogenital uses. Additional traditional labels include depurative, emollient, and cyanogenetic, the last of which is noted here only as a documented application.

Other applications include use as a tonic, sedative, and aphrodisiac, and for female fertility, puerperium, and hemorrhage. Additional traditional uses cover fever, thirst, inflammation, eye concerns, heart and pectoral applications, and as a vermifuge and vulnerary.

Other recorded uses include parturition, nasal polyps, and wound healing, the last reflecting the older label vulnerary.

Much of the record concerns the digestive and respiratory systems, with applications traditionally recorded for indigestion, diarrhea, stomach complaints, cough, bronchitis, catarrh and fever, alongside its use as a soothing demulcent and emollient. External uses include poultices and preparations for burns, chilblains, sores and inflammation, and it also appears in connection with bladder and urogenital complaints, debility and the puerperium.

Other recorded applications include skin conditions like eruptions, itch, and prurigo senilis, and oral concerns such as gingivitis and stomatitis. The plant has also been noted for its astringent, demulcent, and emollient properties, and for uses related to the lungs and as a tonic.

Other recorded uses include laxative and emollient purposes, a nervine application for spasm, and pectoral and urogenital indications. A depurative use and a corn application also appear in the list.

Its applications often center on promoting sweat and urine, with diaphoretic, sudorific, and diuretic labels, alongside uses for menstrual pain and hysteria. Other traditional labels include astringent, narcotic, and resolvent, the last meaning a substance that disperses swelling or induration. The plant has also been noted for cyanogenetic potential and for serious outcomes such as fatality and somnolency.

Its other recorded uses are chiefly laxative and purgative, with a cathartic application also noted, and these are grouped with a cholagogue use. A vulnerary use, meaning a preparation for wound care, and a use for fever are also documented.

It has also been noted for menstrual and women's health concerns including amenorrhea, dysmenorrhea, and menorrhagia, and for inflammatory and rheumatic conditions such as gout and rheumatism. Other recorded uses include astringent, antiseptic, and cardiac applications, along with diabetes, hypertension, and flu.

Related applications include prostatitis and metritis, along with menstrual complaints such as amenorrhea, dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia. Other recorded uses range from rheumatism, gout and inflammation to flu, pneumonia, hepatitis, hypertension and diabetes, and it also appears as a demulcent, astringent, antiseptic, diuretic, stimulant and tonic-type alterative.

description: Wood Sorrel belongs to the family Oxalidaceae, and its use has been recorded in Turkey, the United Kingdom, the United States, France, and Spain. Traditionally, it has been recorded for astringent and refrigerant purposes, as well as for catarrh, fever, and scurvy. It has also been noted for dyspepsia, liver complaints, and urogenital applications including gonorrhea, alongside uses for hemorrhage, quinsy, and lip care. In homeopathy, it has been documented as a remedy.

description: Yellow Dock Root has been traditionally recorded for constipation and other digestive complaints, as well as for skin conditions and general debility. It belongs to the Polygonaceae family, and its use has been documented in the United States, Haiti, Turkey, China, Europe, and Chile. Records describe it as a laxative, purgative, and cathartic for constipation and dysentery, and as an astringent, antiseptic, and emollient for skin problems such as boils, itch, ringworm, and tinea. It also appears as a tonic, alterative, and depurative, with applications for fever, scurvy, and nerves.

description: Xing Ren, in the Rosaceae family, has been traditionally recorded for uses across China, Turkey, Japan, the United States, Iraq, and Spain. Among its most distinctive applications is the pursuit of immortality, a goal that stands apart from the more practical uses in its record. The plant has been traditionally recorded for respiratory complaints such as cough, cold, asthma, bronchitis, and catarrh, and for digestive issues including constipation and as an aperient. Other traditional applications include fever, inflammation, hemorrhage, anemia, and female fertility, along with tonic, sedative, and aphrodisiac purposes.
